meta.name: Blog
meta.about: Guides to common conditions, medicines and tests, and plain-English summaries of the latest announcements from official health bodies such as the NHS, NICE, UKHSA and the World Health Organization. Every article cites its sources and links to the full pages on this site.

ace-inhibitors-arbs-and-amlodipine-compa.name: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and amlodipine compared
ace-inhibitors-arbs-and-amlodipine-compa.headline: ACE inhibitors, ARBs and calcium-channel blockers: how do they differ?
ace-inhibitors-arbs-and-amlodipine-compa.summary: ARBs work much like ACE inhibitors but do not typically cause a dry cough; amlodipine relaxes artery walls and can cause ankle swelling.
keyPoints: The NHS says a doctor may recommend one or more blood pressure medicines, and the choice depends on blood pressure level, age and ethnicity.
A dry cough is a common side effect of ACE inhibitors such as ramipril and lisinopril, and ARBs such as losartan are a common alternative.
Ankle swelling is a common side effect of the calcium-channel blocker amlodipine.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs need regular blood tests to check the kidneys, and the NHS advises against losartan in pregnancy.
The NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction with a swollen throat or tongue, and NHS 111 for some other serious side effects.

body.heading: What do these medicines do?
body.body: The NHS describes ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) and calcium-channel blockers as medicines used to treat high blood pressure. Its examples of ACE inhibitors include enalapril, lisinopril, perindopril and ramipril. Examples of ARBs include candesartan, losartan and valsartan, and examples of calcium-channel blockers include amlodipine, felodipine and nifedipine. ACE inhibitors lower blood pressure by reducing a hormone called angiotensin-2, which narrows blood vessels. ARBs work in a similar way by blocking angiotensin-2. Calcium-channel blockers relax the muscle in the artery walls, which widens the vessels and lowers blood pressure. The NHS also describes amlodipine as a medicine to treat high blood pressure and angina, a type of chest pain.

body.heading: Which type is usually tried first?
body.body: NICE guideline NG136 covers the diagnosis and management of high blood pressure in adults. The NHS says the choice of medicine depends on blood pressure level, age and ethnicity. In its first-step advice, NICE includes offering an ACE inhibitor or an ARB. If an ACE inhibitor is not tolerated, for example because of cough, NICE advises offering an ARB. NICE advises against combining an ACE inhibitor with an ARB to treat high blood pressure. If blood pressure stays uncontrolled, the next step is a combination of an ACE inhibitor or ARB with a calcium-channel blocker or a thiazide-like diuretic, depending on the person's circumstances. The NHS says ARBs are often offered instead of ACE inhibitors because they do not typically cause a dry cough.

body.heading: What side effects are typical of each?
body.body: For ramipril, the NHS lists a dry cough as a common side effect, along with dizziness on standing, headache, diarrhoea, vomiting and mild rash. It says dizziness is more likely when starting the medicine or moving to a higher dose. If a dry cough does not go away, doctors may suggest an ARB such as candesartan, irbesartan, losartan or valsartan. The British Heart Foundation (BHF) lists a dry cough, dizziness, headache and tiredness among the most commonly reported ACE inhibitor effects. For losartan, the NHS lists dizziness, tiredness, headache, tummy pain, feeling or being sick, and swelling in the legs, ankles or feet. The BHF lists dizziness, headache and feeling weak or tired as ARB side effects. For amlodipine, the NHS lists ankle swelling, headaches, dizziness and tiredness among the common effects, and says they are usually mild and last a short time. The NHS says to avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with amlodipine because they can make side effects worse.

body.heading: What about the kidneys and potassium?
body.body: The NHS says blood tests are done before ramipril is started and when the dose changes, to check the kidneys and potassium. It also says regular blood tests are needed with ACE inhibitors to check that the kidneys are working properly. For losartan, the NHS says long-term use can sometimes stop the kidneys working as well as they should, so a doctor checks kidney function with regular blood tests. The BHF also says regular blood tests check kidney function after starting an ARB. The NHS ramipril page says salt substitutes such as Lo-Salt are high in potassium, which can make blood potassium too high with ramipril. It says possible signs of kidney, liver, blood or pancreas problems with ramipril call for a doctor or NHS 111.

body.heading: What do they mean for pregnancy?
body.body: The NHS advises against losartan in pregnancy. It says losartan can reduce the level of fluid around the baby, particularly in the second and third trimesters. The NHS says a doctor can usually switch to another option if pregnancy happens, and that any pregnancy should be planned carefully with a doctor or specialist. The NHS losartan pages differ on breastfeeding: one says it is not usually used, while another says it might be possible after talking to a doctor or pharmacist. For amlodipine, the NHS says it is not usually recommended in pregnancy because similar medicines are safer. It may still be used when other options fail and it is important that the condition is treated during pregnancy. The NHS advises telling the doctor about a pregnancy or a possible pregnancy.

body.heading: Who can advise about side effects or a missed dose?
body.body: For a missed dose of amlodipine, the NHS advice is to leave it out and take the next dose as usual, without taking two doses to make up for it. It also says not to stop amlodipine unless a doctor says so. The NHS says to call 999 for a serious allergic reaction, with signs such as a swollen throat, lips or tongue and difficulty breathing. It lists angioedema, which is swelling of the lips, tongue and face, among the rare serious side effects of lisinopril. For lisinopril, the NHS says NHS 111 is the route for signs such as yellowing skin or eyes, unexplained bleeding or bruising, or severe stomach pain. This guide describes what the sources say and does not replace advice from the person who prescribes the medicine.

alcohol-and-antibiotics.name: Alcohol and antibiotics: what the NHS says
alcohol-and-antibiotics.headline: Can you drink alcohol with antibiotics? What the NHS says, and which ones differ
alcohol-and-antibiotics.summary: It depends on the antibiotic: the NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with common ones, but firm warnings exist for a few.
keyPoints: The NHS says moderate drinking is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics, though alcohol may worsen side effects such as nausea or dizziness.
The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and tinidazole, and NHS 111 Wales names linezolid and doxycycline as antibiotics that alcohol can affect too.
The NHS says amoxicillin can be taken with alcohol, and that azithromycin can too unless it causes dizziness, although the About azithromycin page is more cautious.
UK sources word the advice differently, so the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP for a specific antibiotic.
For a serious allergic reaction to an antibiotic, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about drinking alcohol with antibiotics?
body.body:
The NHS says that drinking alcohol in moderation is unlikely to cause problems with the most common antibiotics. It adds that some antibiotics can cause side effects such as feeling sick or dizzy, and alcohol may make these worse. So the answer depends on which antibiotic has been prescribed.

Antibiotics are medicines that treat infections caused by bacteria. The NHS interactions page says a GP or pharmacist can confirm whether a particular antibiotic is suitable to take with alcohol.

body.heading: Which antibiotics have a specific alcohol warning?
body.body:
A small number of antibiotics carry a firmer warning about alcohol. The NHS says to avoid alcohol completely with metronidazole and with tinidazole. NHS 111 Wales says it may be best to avoid alcohol with linezolid, and says alcohol can affect how doxycycline works.

For linezolid, NHS 111 Wales names undistilled fermented drinks such as wine, beer, sherry and lager. For doxycycline, the NHS common questions page says it is best not to drink alcohol, because alcohol can stop the medicine working properly.

body.heading: What can happen if alcohol is mixed with metronidazole?
body.body:
The NHS says that mixing alcohol with metronidazole can cause nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, hot flushes, a racing heartbeat and headache. Its common questions page says not to drink alcohol while using metronidazole tablets, liquid or suppositories.

The NHS says the advice to avoid alcohol carries on for a period after treatment finishes. NHS 111 Wales gives a longer period for tinidazole than for metronidazole. Apart from alcohol, the NHS says metronidazole users can eat and drink normally.

body.heading: Can alcohol make antibiotic side effects worse?
body.body:
Some antibiotics cause nausea or dizziness, and the NHS says alcohol may make these effects worse. The NHS lists dizziness as a common side effect of azithromycin.

For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says that if the medicine makes a person dizzy, alcohol will make them feel worse. The NHS clarithromycin page gives the same caution about dizziness.

body.heading: What do the NHS pages say about amoxicillin and azithromycin?
body.body:
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin family of antibiotics, and azithromycin to the macrolide family. The NHS common questions page for amoxicillin says alcohol can be drunk while taking it, and that no food or drink needs to be avoided.

For azithromycin, the NHS common questions page says alcohol can be drunk, but not if the medicine causes dizziness. The About azithromycin page is stricter and says not to drink alcohol because it will make a person feel worse. The NHS common questions pages for flucloxacillin and ciprofloxacin also say alcohol can be drunk. The wording differs between pages for the same medicine, so a pharmacist can say how it applies to a particular prescription.

body.heading: Do all UK health sources give the same advice?
body.body:
They do not always match. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS information service, says alcohol should not be drunk while taking antibiotics, or for a period after finishing them. The NHS interactions page is more relaxed about moderate drinking with common antibiotics, then names metronidazole and tinidazole as exceptions.

NHS 111 Wales lists the antibiotics with firmer warnings and says it is a good idea to ask a GP or pharmacist if unsure.

body.heading: Who can give advice, and when is it urgent?
body.body:
For a question about one antibiotic and alcohol, the NHS points to a pharmacist or GP. The NHS says that in very rare cases an allergic reaction to an antibiotic can lead to anaphylaxis, which is a medical emergency.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a skin rash, wheezing, tightness in the chest or throat, trouble breathing or talking, or swelling of the mouth, face, lips, tongue or throat. For less severe reactions, an Oxford University Hospitals leaflet points to a GP or NHS 111.

alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.name: Alcohol units: the UK low-risk drinking advice
alcohol-units-and-low-risk-drinking.summary: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise adults not to regularly drink more than 14 units a week, spread over three days or more.
keyPoints: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units of alcohol a week.
The guidance says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking; 14 units a week is described as a low-risk level, not a safe one.
One unit is 10 millilitres, or 8 grams, of pure alcohol, and the strength printed on a label as ABV can be used to work out units.
For anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: What is the UK low-risk drinking advice?
body.body: The UK Chief Medical Officers advise that, to keep the risk of harm from alcohol low, adults should not regularly drink more than 14 units a week. For someone who drinks as much as 14 units, the advice is to spread it evenly over three days or more. The guidance also says there is no completely safe level of regular drinking, so 14 units is a way to keep risk low rather than a safe amount. Some older leaflets still quote daily limits, but the weekly figure is the one in the current guidance.

body.heading: What is an alcohol unit?
body.body: One unit is 10 millilitres of pure alcohol, which is 8 grams. The strength of a drink is shown on the label as alcohol by volume, or ABV. Units can be worked out by multiplying the volume in millilitres by the ABV percentage and dividing by 1,000. Using that method, a pint of strong lager at 5.2% ABV comes to about three units. As a guide, 14 units is about six pints of average-strength beer or six medium glasses of average-strength wine.

body.heading: What does drinking above the guidance do to health?
body.body: The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says regular drinking above the low-risk level raises the risk of dying from long-term illnesses and from accidents and injuries, and alcohol is a risk factor for seven types of cancer. The guidance also names accidents and injuries among the short-term risks of heavy drinking. Drinking a large amount in a short time carries a particular risk of alcohol poisoning. Mouth cancers are more common among people who drink, and the risk is higher still when drinking is combined with smoking or any form of tobacco.

body.heading: Does keeping to 14 units remove the risk?
body.body: The 2016 review behind the guidance estimated that the lifetime risk of dying from an alcohol-related condition is around 1 per cent, or a little under, for people drinking at the low-risk level. Heavier drinking raises the risk further. The guidance is therefore described as a way to keep risk low, not to remove it.

body.heading: Who is advised not to drink at all?
body.body: For anyone who is pregnant or thinks they could become pregnant, the Chief Medical Officers advise that the safest approach is not to drink alcohol at all.

body.heading: When might someone need support with drinking?
body.body: Signs listed as a reason to seek support include drinking more over time, struggling to cut down, poor sleep, thinking ahead to the next drink, risky behaviour and concern from other people.

body.heading: How does the NHS suggest cutting down?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site points people to their local alcohol support service, or to Drinkline on 0300 123 1110, which it describes as free, confidential help for anyone concerned about their own or someone else's drinking. It also offers the NHS Drink Free Days app for setting a weekly unit target. NHS pages describe a drinks diary as a way to see how much is being drunk, in which situations, and how cutting down could start. Having several alcohol-free days each week is another suggestion, as are choosing lower-strength drinks and alternating alcoholic drinks with soft drinks.

body.heading: What treatment exists for alcohol dependence?
body.body: The NHS says treatment for alcohol use disorder is available from a GP or a specialist alcohol service. Options it lists include counselling, self-help groups, talking therapies such as CBT, and medicines. Alcoholics Anonymous and SMART Recovery are named as self-help groups, and Al-Anon Family Groups as support for families and friends of people who drink. The NHS says a person who is not ready to stop, or who only wants to cut down, will be supported to reduce drinking to a safer level. The NHS says it can be very dangerous to stop drinking suddenly for someone who is dependent on alcohol, and that anyone who gets withdrawal symptoms should get medical help before trying to stop; for severe symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations or a seizure it advises calling 999 or going to A&E.

antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.name: NHS antenatal care: appointments and scans
antenatal-care-on-the-nhs.summary: The NHS offers antenatal appointments with a midwife, two ultrasound scans and optional screening tests. First pregnancies get at least 10 appointments, later ones around 7.
keyPoints: People having their first baby are offered at least 10 antenatal appointments and 2 ultrasound scans, and those who have had a baby before typically have around 7 appointments.
The booking appointment with a midwife is usually the first, and NICE recommends offering it by about 10 weeks of pregnancy.
Screening tests are optional, and NICE says a woman can accept or decline any part of any screening programme.
Exact schedules vary between local maternity services.

body.heading: What antenatal care does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says first-time mothers are offered at least 10 appointments and 2 ultrasound scans. People who have had a baby before typically have around 7 appointments. The exact schedule varies between local maternity services.

body.heading: What happens at the booking appointment?
body.body: The booking appointment is usually the first appointment with a midwife and can take around an hour. The NHS says the booking appointment should ideally happen before about 10 weeks of pregnancy, and NICE recommends offering it by 10 weeks. At this appointment, NICE recommends that staff discuss and offer screening for infectious diseases (HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B), sickle cell disease and thalassaemia, and fetal anomalies.

body.heading: What checks happen at later appointments?
body.body: Later appointments happen at intervals through pregnancy, and the midwife checks blood pressure, urine, bump size and the baby's movements.

body.heading: What scans are offered?
body.body: The scan offered at around 11 to 14 weeks, sometimes called the dating scan, shows how far along the pregnancy is and checks the baby's development. The 18 to 21 week scan, often called the anomaly or 20-week scan, looks at the baby's development and screens for 11 physical conditions.

body.heading: Are screening tests compulsory?
body.body: Screening for Down's, Edwards' and Patau's syndromes is offered in early pregnancy, and it is the woman's choice whether to have it. NICE says the woman can accept or decline any part of any of the screening programmes offered.

body.heading: What else does antenatal care cover?
body.body: The free flu vaccine is offered in every pregnancy, as is the whooping cough vaccine. Maternity services also give advice on supplements such as folic acid and vitamin D, and the NHS page sets out the amounts. Local maternity services vary in the exact schedule and in what they include, so the local service's own plan is the reference.

references.title: NHS: Your antenatal care and appointments

anxiety-signs-and-treatment.name: Anxiety: signs, treatment and getting help
anxiety-signs-and-treatment.summary: Anxiety becomes a health problem when worry is hard to control and affects daily life. Talking therapy comes first, medicine is next, and help is available without a GP referral.
keyPoints: Some anxiety is a normal part of life; it becomes a concern when worry is hard to control and gets in the way of daily life.
Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment, such as cognitive behavioural therapy, before medicine.
People in England can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is anxiety, and when does it become a problem?
body.body: Feeling anxious now and then is a normal part of life. Generalised anxiety disorder, or GAD, is a long-term condition in which a person feels anxious most days, about a wide range of situations rather than one event. That worry gets in the way of daily life.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Alongside worry, symptoms can include feeling restless, trouble concentrating or sleeping, tiredness, irritability, muscle tension, dizziness and heart palpitations (a pounding or fluttering heartbeat). Because many of these also occur in other conditions, a GP can help work out what is going on.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: The exact cause of GAD is not fully understood, and several factors probably combine. Factors named in the sources include inherited genes, past stressful or traumatic experiences, a long-term painful health condition, and past drug or alcohol misuse.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: NICE advises a comprehensive assessment that looks at the number, severity and duration of symptoms, and also at the degree of distress and the effect on daily functioning. Where another condition such as depression is also present, NICE says the more severe disorder is generally treated first. A short two-question screen about feelings of anxiety and the ability to control worry may be used.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body: Adults are usually advised to try psychological treatment before medication. Cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, is a talking therapy that looks at how thoughts, feelings and actions affect one another. CBT and applied relaxation are both talking therapies available on the NHS for GAD. NICE describes CBT-based self-help as a low-intensity step, with written or electronic materials worked through systematically over several weeks. If talking therapy is not enough, medicine is the next option, and the usual first choice is an SSRI, a type of antidepressant. NICE sets out treatment in steps, offering the least intrusive, most effective option first. Step 4 is for complex, treatment-resistant anxiety with marked impairment or a high risk of self-harm, and involves specialist care.

body.heading: What can people do themselves?
body.body: NHS self-help ideas include regular exercise, cutting back on caffeine, which may help reduce anxiety, and eating a healthy diet. The NHS suggests drinking alcohol in moderation and stopping smoking as part of looking after physical health. Many books and courses can teach ways of coping with anxiety.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says to speak to a GP if anxiety is hard to cope with and self-help is not enough. A GP can talk through treatment and refer on, and people can also refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. Charities such as Mind, Rethink Mental Illness and Anxiety UK also offer support.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Anxiety is common and treatable, and there are several routes to help. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which local NHS trusts describe as free and available at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.name: Asthma and COPD: how they differ
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.headline: Asthma and COPD: how they differ in cause, symptoms and treatment
asthma-and-copd-how-they-differ.summary: Asthma is a long-term airway condition whose symptoms come and go; COPD is mostly smoking-related and tends to get worse over time.
keyPoints: Asthma symptoms can come and go, while COPD symptoms usually get progressively worse without treatment.
The main cause of COPD is smoking, though it can affect people who have never smoked.
Clinicians use a person's history, an examination and breathing tests such as spirometry to tell the two apart.
Asthma is mainly treated with inhalers; COPD has no cure, but treatment and stopping smoking can help slow it.
In an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if a person does not feel better after using the reliever inhaler as directed, or feels worse at any time.

body.heading: What is asthma?
body.body:
Asthma is a long-term condition that affects the airways. The NHS says the main symptoms are wheezing, coughing, shortness of breath and a tight chest, and that they often come and go.

Common triggers include exercise, cold air, air pollution and allergens such as pollen or dust. The NHS says the exact cause of asthma is not fully understood, but allergies, a family history of asthma or allergies, and early-life exposure to air pollution or cigarette smoke are among the factors linked with it.

During an asthma attack, sitting up and staying calm is part of the usual NHS advice while using the reliever inhaler as directed, and 999 should be called if there is no improvement.

body.heading: What is COPD?
body.body:
COPD, short for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, is the name for a group of lung conditions that cause breathing difficulties. It includes emphysema and chronic bronchitis.

The NHS says the main cause is smoking, although it can sometimes affect people who have never smoked. Typical symptoms are breathlessness on exertion, a persistent chesty cough with phlegm, frequent chest infections and wheeze. They tend to get worse over time.

With COPD there can also be periods when symptoms suddenly get worse, known as a flare-up.

body.heading: How do doctors tell them apart?
body.body:
NICE says that when someone first presents with symptoms, untreated COPD and asthma can frequently be told apart from the person's history and an examination. NICE advises using features from the person's history and examination to help tell the two conditions apart.

Breathing tests help. Spirometry is a breathing test that supports a diagnosis of COPD, and lung function tests also form part of diagnosing asthma, although a normal result does not always rule asthma out. The site's spirometry page explains the test.

Because symptoms vary and breathing problems have more than one cause, the NHS notes that diagnosing asthma can take time.

body.heading: How are the two treated?
body.body:
The NHS says inhalers are the main treatment for asthma. Reliever inhalers ease symptoms when they occur, and preventer inhalers are used regularly to reduce them. An asthma action plan is usually agreed with a doctor or asthma nurse.

There is currently no cure for COPD, but treatment can help slow its progression and control symptoms, and for people who smoke, stopping smoking is the most important step. Treatment mainly relieves symptoms, with inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help people become more active.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body:
Asthma attacks can be life-threatening. During an asthma attack, the NHS says to call 999 if the person does not feel better after using their reliever inhaler as directed, if they feel worse at any time, or if they do not have an inhaler.

COPD symptoms can suddenly get worse in what is called a flare-up. A person unsure what to do can contact their GP or NHS 111 for advice, and 999 is for emergencies. NHS 111 can advise when it is unclear how serious a flare-up is.

A GP can look into new or ongoing breathing problems, because both conditions are diagnosed using symptoms, an examination and lung function tests.

body.heading: What helps people living with either condition?
body.body:
People with asthma are offered regular asthma reviews, where things such as flu vaccination can be discussed. For people with COPD who smoke, the NHS says stopping smoking is the most important step.

The NHS encourages people with COPD to have the yearly flu jab and a one-off pneumococcal vaccination, and for asthma it advises vaccinations such as the flu vaccine because viruses such as flu can make asthma symptoms worse. Flu jabs can be discussed at an asthma review.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Pulmonary rehabilitation is a programme of exercise and education that can improve how far someone can exercise before becoming breathless. COPD can also come from long-term exposure to harmful fumes or dust, and rarely from a genetic problem that makes the lungs more vulnerable. Having eczema or hay fever, being born prematurely, or growing up around air pollution or cigarette smoke are linked with asthma. Asthma can have normal breathing test results at the time of the test, so one normal result does not always rule it out. NICE says COPD is suspected from symptoms and signs and supported by spirometry, which is also used again if the diagnosis is reconsidered. Flu jabs are given at a GP surgery or a taking-part pharmacy.

back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.name: Back pain: what helps and when to get help
back-pain-what-helps-and-when-to-get-hel.summary: Most back pain settles with time and staying active helps, but new numbness around the genitals or changes in bladder or bowel control need urgent help, and NHS leaflets point to A&E or NHS 111.
keyPoints: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time.
NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends considering a group exercise programme for a specific episode or flare-up.
NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks.
Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment.

body.heading: What causes back pain?
body.body: An NHS back pain page says a strain is a common cause and that serious causes such as a fracture, cancer or infection are very rare. The NHS says a slipped disc is the most common cause of sciatica, and the likelihood rises with age. Other causes of sciatica include spinal stenosis, spondylolisthesis and a back injury. Sciatica is pain that spreads from the lower back down the leg because the sciatic nerve is irritated.

body.heading: What helps back pain?
body.body: NHS sources say that staying active is part of treatment and that most back pain settles with time. NHS inform describes keeping active as an essential part of treatment and recovery. In most cases, back pain gets better after a few weeks. NHS inform says resting in bed does not help back pain and often makes it harder to get going again. The NHS sciatica page suggests asking a pharmacist about painkillers and says paracetamol is unlikely to help sciatica. The NHS back pain page says paracetamol on its own is not recommended for back pain.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend for low back pain?
body.body: NICE guideline NG59 on low back pain and sciatica in people over 16 recommends considering a group exercise programme for a specific episode or flare-up. NICE guideline NG59 says not to offer belts or corsets, foot supports, traction or TENS for low back pain.

body.heading: When should back pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: NHS sources suggest asking a GP or an NHS physiotherapist for advice if back symptoms are still getting in the way of normal activities after about 6 weeks. NHS 111 Wales says physiotherapy is free on the NHS and that, depending on where a person lives, they may be able to refer themselves or may need to see a GP first. Sciatica often improves within weeks, though it can last longer.

body.heading: What are the emergency signs?
body.body: Cauda equina syndrome is a rare but serious condition that needs emergency treatment. NHS sources list its warning signs as changes in bladder or bowel control, numbness or pins and needles around the genitals or back passage, and pain or weakness in both legs. One NHS trust leaflet says to attend the Emergency Department immediately if two or more of these symptoms appear suddenly, and another says to attend A&E or call NHS 111.

bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.name: Bleeding after menopause or between periods
bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.headline: Vaginal bleeding after the menopause or between periods: causes and next steps
bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.summary: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause should be checked by a GP. It is often caused by something other than cancer, but womb cancer is one possible cause.
keyPoints: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP for any bleeding after the menopause, even a small amount of blood, spotting or pink or brown discharge.
The NHS lists bleeding or spotting after the menopause as a main symptom of womb cancer, but it has other, more common causes.
NHS inform says anyone with vaginal bleeding after the menopause is referred urgently, within two weeks.
A scan of the womb lining is often the first test, and a small sample of the lining may follow.

body.heading: What counts as bleeding after the menopause?
body.body: Bleeding after the menopause means vaginal bleeding once periods have stopped, and the NHS lists it among the main symptoms of womb cancer. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP even if the amount is small, or if it is spotting or pink or brown discharge.

body.heading: Does it mean cancer?
body.body: Bleeding has many possible causes, and cancer is a less common one. The causes NHS 111 Wales lists include thinning of the vaginal or womb lining from lower oestrogen, benign polyps and a thickened womb lining. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) can also be linked with bleeding. NHS inform advises always seeing a GP about any unusual vaginal bleeding.

body.heading: What about bleeding between periods?
body.body: The NHS lists bleeding between periods, unusually heavy periods and a change in vaginal discharge as other possible signs of womb cancer. NHS 111 Wales advice on heavy periods lists bleeding between periods or after sex as a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: How quickly will someone be seen?
body.body: NHS inform says that a person with vaginal bleeding after the menopause is referred urgently, to be seen within two weeks. The NHS inform pathway describes Scotland, and referral rules can differ between UK nations.

body.heading: What tests might be offered?
body.body: The first test is usually a transvaginal ultrasound scan, which measures the thickness of the womb lining. A small sample of the womb lining (biopsy) may follow, and some clinics use hysteroscopy, a look inside the womb with a thin camera. Treatment depends on the cause; for thinning of the vaginal lining it can include local oestrogen cream.

bleeding-after-menopause-and-between-per.metaDescription: Any vaginal bleeding after the menopause should be checked by a GP. It is often caused by something other than cancer, but womb cancer is one possible cause.

blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.name: Blood in urine: causes and what happens next
blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.headline: Blood in your urine: common causes and why the NHS wants it checked
blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.summary: Blood in the urine is not usually serious, but the NHS advises seeing a GP every time, even if the amount is small, because cancer is one possible cause.
keyPoints: The NHS says blood in the urine is not usually serious, but it is important to get medical help.
Urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate are the usual causes the NHS lists.
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for blood in the pee, even if there is only a little or it is the first time.
Beetroot, some medicines, bleeding from the back passage or a period can make urine look pink or red.

body.heading: What does blood in urine look like?
body.body: Blood in the urine may look bright pink, red or dark brown. Beetroot, some medicines, bleeding from the back passage or a period can make urine look pink or red, so these do not always mean blood in the urine. The NHS says to get checked even if you are unsure whether it is blood.

body.heading: What are the common causes?
body.body: The NHS lists urinary tract infections, kidney stones and an enlarged prostate as the usual causes. The other symptoms that come with each of these can give a clue to the cause. Kidney inflammation and blood-thinning medicines are also named as possible causes.

body.heading: Could it be cancer?
body.body: Cancers of the bladder, kidney or prostate are on the NHS list of possible causes, which is why the NHS stresses that blood in the urine must be checked. Blood in the urine is the most common symptom of bladder cancer. The NHS notes that blood in the urine is not usually a sign of anything serious.

body.heading: When should you get help?
body.body: The NHS says to see a GP about blood in the urine even if the amount is small. The NHS bladder cancer page says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for blood in the pee, even with no other symptoms, if it is the first time, if there is only a little, or if you are not sure it is blood.

body.heading: What will a GP do?
body.body: A GP will ask about symptoms and may examine the person. A urine sample or blood test may be requested, antibiotics may be prescribed for a suspected infection, or a referral to a specialist may be made. At a specialist clinic, the checks can include an ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder and a look inside the bladder with a thin flexible camera.

blood-in-urine-causes-and-what-happens-n.metaDescription: Blood in the urine is not usually serious, but the NHS advises seeing a GP every time, even if the amount is small, because cancer is one possible cause.

blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.name: Home blood pressure checks: how they work
blood-pressure-at-home-how-it-works.summary: The NHS says blood pressure can be checked at home with a monitor, with the cuff on the upper arm and the person sitting with their back supported; local NHS leaflets also advise avoiding caffeine and smoking beforehand.
keyPoints: High blood pressure does not usually cause symptoms, so measuring it is the way to find out.
Blood pressure is written as two numbers, the first higher than the second.
NHS-linked guidance recommends an upper arm monitor rather than a wrist or finger device.
A GP or nurse advises how often to check blood pressure at home.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure check show?
body.body: The NHS says a blood pressure test can check whether blood pressure is too high or too low. High blood pressure does not usually have any symptoms. Readings are given as two numbers, for example 140/90, measured in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).

body.heading: Can people check at home?
body.body: The NHS says blood pressure can also be checked at home with a monitor. NHS England has a programme of home blood pressure monitoring through GP practices. The NHS says blood pressure is usually considered high at a lower figure when checked at home than when checked by a healthcare professional.

body.heading: How is a home reading usually taken?
body.body: Local NHS guides recommend an upper arm monitor with a cuff that fits snugly, and say that wrist devices are not recommended. Guides describe sitting quietly for about five minutes with feet flat and the back supported, and avoiding caffeine, smoking and exercise for about 30 minutes beforehand. Guides often suggest taking readings twice in the morning and twice in the evening for about a week, with the average worked out afterwards, although the number of readings differs between guides. Guides advise leaving about a minute between two readings, and the GP or nurse advises on timing around medicines because guides differ. One guide recommends choosing a monitor validated by the British and Irish Hypertension Society.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: One NHS integrated care board page says the GP or nurse advises how often to check. Blood Pressure UK advises re-checking after resting for five minutes if a reading is still high. The NHS advises calling 999 for possible heart attack symptoms such as chest pain with sweating or breathlessness, and contacting NHS 111 about frequent headaches, blurred vision or chest pain that comes and goes; the British Heart Foundation advises contacting a GP about symptoms that could be caused by high blood pressure.

bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.name: Bone health: what helps keep bones strong
bone-health-keeping-bones-strong.summary: NHS pages link bone health to weight-bearing exercise, calcium, vitamin D, not smoking and keeping alcohol low.
keyPoints: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for bone strength.
Calcium is important for bone health, and vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium.
Being inactive, having a low body weight, smoking and heavy drinking are listed as risk factors for weaker bones.
The NHS advises adults aged 65 and over to include strength and balance activities on at least two days a week.

body.heading: What helps keep bones strong?
body.body: NHS guidance describes weight-bearing and resistance exercise as particularly important for improving bone density. Running, skipping, dancing, aerobics and jumping are named as higher-impact examples that strengthen muscles, ligaments and joints. Swimming and cycling support general fitness but are not weight-bearing, so they do less for the bones. Lack of physical activity is listed as a risk factor for osteoporosis.

body.heading: What do calcium and vitamin D do?
body.body: The NHS says most adults should be able to get the calcium they need from their daily diet. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, and the NHS says it can be difficult to get enough vitamin D from food alone, so a daily supplement may be considered. Sunlight from about late March or early April to the end of September helps the body make vitamin D, and the NHS suggests considering a daily vitamin D supplement.

body.heading: What raises the risk of weaker bones?
body.body: Osteopenia is the stage of bone loss before osteoporosis, and being underweight is listed among the risk factors for bone loss. Smoking and heavy drinking are also listed, and one source gives the low-risk alcohol guidance of less than 14 units a week. The Royal Osteoporosis Society says too much salt may increase the amount of calcium lost in urine.

body.heading: What changes after 65?
body.body: NHS guidance for people aged 65 and over advises activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week. It also advises 150 minutes (2 and a half hours) of moderate-intensity activity a week, ideally spread across the days. NHS 111 Wales suggests that people diagnosed with osteoporosis talk to a GP or health specialist before starting a new exercise programme. A DEXA bone density scan is often used to help diagnose osteoporosis or to assess the risk of it.

references.title: NHS: Keep your bones strong over 65
NHS inform: Bone health and falls

breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.name: Found a breast lump: what happens next
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.headline: Found a breast lump? Causes, the GP appointment and what the breast clinic does
breast-lump-what-happens-after-you-find-.summary: Most breast lumps are harmless, but the NHS advises seeing a GP about any new lump so it can be checked. A GP examines the breast and refers to a breast clinic if the cause is unclear.
keyPoints: The NHS says most breast lumps are harmless, with fibroadenomas and cysts among the common causes.
NHS 111 Wales advises getting any new breast lump checked by a GP.
If the GP is unsure of the cause, they refer to a hospital breast clinic.
At a breast clinic you may have an examination, a scan and sometimes a biopsy.

body.heading: Are most breast lumps harmless?
body.body: The NHS says most breast lumps are not cancer. Common causes include fibroadenomas, which are solid benign lumps, and cysts, which are fluid-filled sacs. Sometimes a breast lump can be a sign of something more serious, such as breast cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises contacting a GP about any lump in the breast or armpit. The NHS also advises seeing a GP about other changes to the breast that are unusual for you. A new lump is worth getting checked even if it is painless. NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP rather than trying to work out the cause of a lump yourself. The NHS lists a lump or swelling in the breast, chest or armpit, skin dimpling or redness, and a change in the size or shape of a breast among the symptoms to have checked. Nipple discharge, which may be bloody, and nipple changes such as inversion or a rash are also listed. Having one of these symptoms does not definitely mean breast cancer, but the NHS says it is important to have it checked by a GP.

body.heading: What happens at the GP appointment?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales says the GP may ask about any breast screening you have had and whether anyone in your family has had breast cancer. The GP then examines the breasts. If the GP is not sure what is causing the lump, they refer the person to a breast clinic at a hospital.

body.heading: How is an urgent referral decided?
body.body: In England, NICE guidance on suspected cancer sets out who should be offered an urgent referral to a breast clinic. An urgent referral in England aims for an appointment at the breast clinic within two weeks. Referral guidance can differ between the UK nations.

body.heading: What does the breast clinic do?
body.body: Tests at a breast clinic usually include an examination of the breasts and an imaging scan, usually a mammogram or an ultrasound. Sometimes a biopsy is taken, in which a needle removes a small sample of cells from the lump. Some results may be available on the same day, while others, such as a biopsy, can take one to two weeks.

body.heading: How can breasts be checked at home?
body.body: The NHS has a page on how to check your breasts or chest, so that a person knows how they normally look and feel. Its guidance describes looking in a mirror with the arms at the sides and then raised, and feeling each breast along with the area up to the collarbone and under the armpit. The NHS says to contact a GP about any change, including a new lump.

cardiovascular-service-framework-england.name: Heart disease and stroke framework for England
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.headline: Government and NHS England publish a 10-year framework on heart disease and stroke
cardiovascular-service-framework-england.summary: The government and NHS England have published a cardiovascular disease framework that aims to cut premature deaths from heart disease and stroke by a quarter within a decade.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England published a cardiovascular disease modern service framework on 7 July 2026.
It sets a 10-year aim of cutting premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England by a quarter.
The government describes 12 priorities for the first three years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: The government and NHS England say the framework is a 10-year strategic vision to reduce premature deaths from heart disease and stroke in England. It sets out 12 priorities for the next three years. The government says the priorities include finding people at risk of cardiovascular disease, blood pressure and cholesterol treatment targets, stroke care and rehabilitation. It also includes a partnership with Diabetes UK to raise public awareness of the link between type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The government estimates that successful implementation could prevent between 1,600 and 2,400 premature deaths a year from heart disease and stroke in people under 75 in the first three years. It estimates this would rise to between 3,850 and 4,900 deaths a year after a decade. These are the government's projections, not results already achieved. The government describes the framework as part of a shift from reactive care towards prevention.

cdc-2026-2027-respiratory-season-outlook.name: CDC outlook for the 2026-27 respiratory season
cdc-2026-2027-respiratory-season-outlook.summary: The US CDC's outlook dated 23 September 2026 expects the peak of combined COVID-19, flu and RSV hospital admissions to be similar to last season, with low to moderate confidence.
keyPoints: The CDC published its 2026-2027 Respiratory Disease Season Outlook on 23 September 2026.
It expects the combined peak hospitalisation rate for COVID-19, influenza and RSV to be within 20% of the 2025-2026 peak.
The CDC calls the outlook high-level information, not a forecast, and says it may change.
This outlook describes the US, not the UK.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) published a 2026-2027 Respiratory Disease Season Outlook dated 23 September 2026.

The CDC describes it as high-level information on how the season could unfold, and says it is not a forecast.

It expects the peak combined hospitalisation rate for COVID-19, influenza and RSV to be within 20% of the 2025-2026 peak, with low to moderate confidence.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
For influenza, the CDC says there is no evidence that a high-severity season is more likely this year.

For RSV, it notes that the 2025-2026 peak came later than in earlier seasons and that the cause of the late peak is unclear.

The CDC lists a higher peak as a risk, driven by viruses that evade existing immunity or by lower vaccine uptake or effectiveness.

This outlook describes the US season; UK figures and vaccination advice come from UKHSA and the NHS.

chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.name: Chest pain: causes and when to get help
chest-pain-causes-and-when-to-get-help.summary: Most chest pain does not come from the heart, but sudden pain that does not ease or spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E.

For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.

body.heading: What causes chest pain?
body.body: The NHS says that in most cases chest pain is not caused by a heart problem. Common causes that do not involve the heart include heartburn or indigestion, a strained chest muscle, anxiety or panic, and chest infections such as pneumonia or pleurisy. Shingles can also cause chest pain, often with a skin rash. Angina, heart attack and pericarditis are heart conditions that can cause chest pain. Pericarditis is inflammation of the lining around the heart, and the NHS says it often follows a viral infection such as a cold or flu.

body.heading: How do angina and a heart attack differ?
body.body: Angina is chest pain that is a sign of a heart problem, and GTN can be used to ease an attack or before a known trigger such as exercise. Angina attacks usually last less than 10 minutes. The NHS says chest pain is the most common symptom of a heart attack, but symptoms vary from person to person. Other signs include pain spreading to the arms, jaw, neck or back, sweating, breathlessness and feeling or being sick, and some people have these without any chest pain. Unlike the pain of angina, the symptoms of a heart attack are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray. A heart attack can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, or pain that spreads to the arm, jaw, neck or back. Chest pain that comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness is in the same group. The NHS says a person with these symptoms should not drive themselves to A&E. For someone already diagnosed with angina, the NHS treats pain that does not settle after rest or after their usual angina medicine as an emergency that needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When should chest pain be checked the same day?
body.body: For sharp or stabbing chest pain that gets worse with deep breathing, swallowing, coughing or lying down, as can happen with pericarditis, the NHS pericarditis page suggests an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111. Angina that feels worse than before, happens more often, lasts longer or happens at rest is a reason to contact a GP urgently.

body.heading: What happens at the GP or in hospital?
body.body: If a GP thinks someone may have angina, they can be referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist). Tests to find out whether someone is having a heart attack include an electrocardiogram (ECG) and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram. An ECG records the heart's electrical activity. An NHS emergency department leaflet says staff check for serious causes such as a heart attack, a blood clot in the lung and a collapsed lung. The Sussex hospital leaflet says staff may test for troponin, which shows whether the heart is involved, and for D-dimer, which looks for clots in the lungs. The Sussex hospital leaflet says a normal troponin result makes a heart problem less likely, but does not necessarily mean the pain is unrelated to the heart.

body.heading: How are angina and a heart attack treated?
body.body: Tests for a heart attack include an ECG and blood tests, and further tests can include a coronary angiogram, which can show exactly where blood flow to the heart is blocked. A heart attack needs emergency treatment in hospital, and treatment can include medicine, coronary angioplasty (opening blocked arteries with a stent) and coronary artery bypass surgery. NHS treatment for angina aims to help stop attacks and reduce the risk of further problems such as a heart attack. Medicines for angina include GTN, beta blockers, which slow the heart, and calcium channel blockers, which relax the arteries, and surgery may be recommended if medicines are not controlling angina. A GP may ask about lifestyle, such as diet, smoking and drinking, and healthy lifestyle changes alongside treatment can help control angina.

cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.name: High cholesterol: diet, tests and medicines
cholesterol-and-diet-what-the-nhs-says.summary: The NHS says cutting down on saturated fat can help lower cholesterol, and that medicines such as statins are considered when lifestyle changes are not enough.
keyPoints: High cholesterol means too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood, and it usually causes no symptoms.
The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially saturated fat, and swapping to unsaturated fats.
Soluble fibre from foods such as oats, barley, beans and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol.
A blood test measures cholesterol, and an NHS Health Check in England may offer it.

body.heading: What is cholesterol and why does it matter?
body.body: High cholesterol means having too much of a fatty substance called cholesterol in the blood. Too much cholesterol in the blood can build up in the artery walls and make them narrower over time. HDL is often called good cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from the blood, while LDL is often called bad cholesterol because it can build up in artery walls. High cholesterol usually causes no symptoms, which is why a blood test is used to find it.

body.heading: Who is more likely to have it?
body.body: Causes and risk factors listed include eating a lot of food high in saturated fat and a family history of high cholesterol. It can also run in families, and the British Heart Foundation lists ethnicity, being male and having been through the menopause among the factors that raise risk.

body.heading: What does diet change?
body.body: The NHS advises cutting down on fatty food, especially food containing saturated fat. The NHS suggests unsaturated fats instead, such as oily fish, nuts, seeds and olive or rapeseed oil, and lists meat pies, butter, cakes and coconut or palm oil among foods to limit. Soluble fibre from oats, barley, beans, pulses and lentils is described as helping to lower cholesterol. Plant sterols and stanols, added to some foods such as spreads, can also help lower cholesterol. The British Heart Foundation says cholesterol in food has a minimal impact on blood cholesterol levels, and that cutting down on saturated fat matters more.

body.heading: When are medicines considered?
body.body: The NHS says medicine may be needed if cholesterol has not gone down after changes to diet and lifestyle, or if a person is at high risk of a heart attack or stroke. Statins are the most common medicine for high cholesterol, and the NHS says people usually need to take them for life.

body.heading: How is cholesterol tested?
body.body: Testing is a blood test. In England it can be offered as part of an NHS Health Check for people aged 40 to 74 who do not already have cardiovascular disease. A GP may also suggest a test for someone with high blood pressure, diabetes, overweight, smoking or a family history of heart disease. Targets depend on factors such as age and other health conditions, so a clinician advises what applies to each person.

cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.name: Cholesterol test results explained
cholesterol-blood-test-results-explained.summary: A cholesterol test reports total, HDL and non-HDL cholesterol plus triglycerides, and doctors read them with other risk factors.
keyPoints: A standard cholesterol test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured with them.
Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL, and it covers all the harmful types together.
Doctors use cholesterol results with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease.
Where treatment is needed, guidance recommends lifestyle support and often a statin, with the test repeated afterwards.

body.heading: What does a cholesterol blood test measure?
body.body: A lipid profile measures lipids in the blood, such as cholesterol and triglycerides. The sample is taken from a vein in the arm, sometimes after fasting. A standard test reports total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol, and triglycerides are usually measured alongside them. LDL cholesterol is tested less routinely, and doctors order it when the healthcare team thinks treatment may be needed.

body.heading: What do HDL, non-HDL and triglycerides mean?
body.body: HDL is generally treated as the protective part of the total, and a low HDL counts as a risk marker. Non-HDL cholesterol is total cholesterol minus HDL. It adds up the harmful types of cholesterol, so it can be more informative than LDL alone. Lab Tests Online UK notes that non-HDL does not need a fasting sample, which makes it practical. Triglycerides are a type of fat in the blood. Fasting is needed only for some triglyceride tests, because fasting triglycerides are more accurate and are done if the non-fasting result is high.

body.heading: Which numbers count as healthy?
body.body: The NHS lists target levels for healthy adults and stricter goals after a heart attack or stroke. Sources differ slightly on where they place the line for triglycerides, and laboratories differ in their reference ranges. For that reason the laboratory report shows the range used for each result.

body.heading: How does a doctor use the result?
body.body: Doctors use the cholesterol result with age, blood pressure and health conditions to estimate the risk of cardiovascular disease. The QRISK tool estimates cardiovascular risk and helps decide whether treatment is needed. For people who already have cardiovascular disease, the pathways skip QRISK because their risk is already high. A GP or practice nurse takes the sample, and a finger-prick test may be offered in some pharmacies or at an NHS Health Check in England.

body.heading: What helps lower raised cholesterol?
body.body: NHS pathways encourage a diet rich in fruit, vegetables and wholegrains and low in saturated fat. They also encourage regular moderate aerobic activity. In primary prevention, lifestyle support is given for a few months before the level is reassessed. Where treatment is needed, the pathways favour a high-intensity statin. Ezetimibe is a second-line option if the aim is not reached. Someone who has side effects on a high-intensity statin can be offered a lower dose or another statin. The test is repeated after treatment starts to see whether the level has fallen.

body.heading: Why does raised cholesterol matter?
body.body: The BHF explains that cholesterol builds up in the artery walls as fatty material called atheroma. That gradual build-up raises the risk of heart attack and stroke. Risk rises further in people who also have high blood pressure, diabetes or who smoke. Most people with high cholesterol have no symptoms.

body.heading: What is familial hypercholesterolaemia?
body.body: Familial hypercholesterolaemia is an inherited form of high cholesterol. South West London guidance describes the risk of heart attack or stroke at a younger age as especially high in this condition. The BHF lists a high result on a routine blood test, or a heart attack or stroke at a younger age, as warning signs.

body.heading: What do statins do, and who is offered them?
body.body: NHS guidance says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They are also used in people who already have heart disease and in people with inherited high cholesterol. If statins are unsuitable, other cholesterol-lowering medicines can be offered. The BHF says people usually combine healthy lifestyle choices with medicine to lower cholesterol. Essex integrated care board guidance lists a better diet, regular activity and a healthy weight as the basics.

dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.name: Dementia: early signs and how it is assessed
dementia-early-signs-and-assessment.summary: Early signs of dementia include memory loss, trouble with familiar tasks and confusion about time or place. A GP starts the assessment, and a memory clinic may confirm the diagnosis.
keyPoints: NHS pages list memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, difficulty finding words, confusion about time and place, and mood changes as common early symptoms.
Memory can be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines, so the NHS suggests a GP visit for someone who is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly over 65.
A GP typically asks about symptoms, carries out an examination and arranges blood tests to look for other causes of memory problems.
A person may be referred to a memory clinic once reversible causes have been looked into and dementia is still suspected.

body.heading: What are the early signs?
body.body: Early symptoms are often mild and tend to progress very gradually. Alzheimer's disease is the most common form of dementia, and vascular dementia is usually the second most common.

body.heading: Is forgetfulness always dementia?
body.body: The NHS says it is normal for memory to be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines. It suggests talking to a GP if someone is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly if they are over 65.

body.heading: What happens at the GP?
body.body: NICE says a history from someone who knows the person well can be supplemented with a structured tool such as the IQCODE. The NHS says a GP may arrange blood tests to rule out other causes of memory problems. NICE also recommends cognitive testing with a validated brief tool, and says a normal screening result alone should not rule dementia out. The NHS says there is no single test for dementia, and that diagnosis rests on a combination of assessments and tests. Memory and thinking tests usually start with a GP, and a specialist may later arrange brain scans such as a CT or MRI scan.

body.heading: When is a memory clinic involved?
body.body: NICE says dementia should be suspected after reversible causes such as delirium, depression, sensory impairment or the effects of some medicines have been looked into, and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service applies if it is still suspected. The specialist assessment includes a neurological examination and cognitive testing, and a dementia subtype is diagnosed where possible. The first memory clinic appointment is usually long, and people are asked to bring someone who knows them well.

body.heading: What if it is unclear whether it is delirium or dementia?
body.body: NICE says that when it is unclear whether someone has delirium, dementia or both, the delirium is treated first. Delirium is a sudden state of confusion; NHS pages advise calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden confusion, because some causes can be life threatening and need prompt assessment.

depression-signs-and-getting-help.name: Depression: signs and getting help
depression-signs-and-getting-help.summary: Depression is more than feeling unhappy for a few days. The NHS describes lasting low mood and loss of interest, and treatment can include self-help, talking therapy and medicine.
keyPoints: Depression is more than feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days, and it can come with physical symptoms.
Treatment depends on severity and usually combines self-help, talking therapies and sometimes medicine.
People can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service, or a GP can refer them.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is depression?
body.body: The NHS describes depression as more than simply feeling unhappy or fed up for a few days. It can involve feeling sad for weeks or months, to the point that it interferes with work, social life and family life.

body.heading: What are the signs?
body.body: Some people also notice physical symptoms, such as tiredness, sleeping badly, changes in appetite or unexplained aches. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms of depression last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks. Low mood can improve after a short time, but feelings that last most of the day, every day, for more than two weeks may be a sign of depression. Many people with depression also have symptoms of anxiety. Aches and pains can also be part of the picture. Depression can range from mild to severe.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body: Life-changing events such as bereavement, losing a job or giving birth can bring depression on. People with a family history of depression are more likely to experience it, and depression can also arise for no obvious reason.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: Treatment usually depends on how severe the depression is. It usually involves a combination of self-help, talking therapies and medicine. For mild depression, a GP can refer someone for talking therapies, or the person can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service. For moderate to severe depression, a combination of talking therapy and antidepressants is often recommended. People with severe depression may be referred to a specialist mental health team. For mild depression, a doctor may suggest watchful waiting, which means monitoring progress to see whether it improves, alongside lifestyle measures and guided self-help. The NHS describes exercise as one of the main treatments for mild depression, and guided self-help is usually based on the principles of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT).

body.heading: How do antidepressants fit in?
body.body: Antidepressants are one of the treatment options, and SSRIs are usually the type prescribed first. Antidepressants do not work straight away; the NHS says it usually takes around a week before effects start to be noticed. The NHS advises that antidepressants are reduced gradually when they are stopped, to help avoid withdrawal symptoms, and that this should be done with the GP. The NHS says to contact a GP straight away if feelings of hopelessness or suicidal thoughts start, or get worse, after starting an antidepressant.

body.heading: When should someone get help?
body.body: A GP appointment is the usual first step for someone who thinks they may have depression. NHS talking therapies accept self-referral, so a GP is not the only way in.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life are present, the NHS advises asking for an emergency GP appointment, calling NHS 111, or calling Samaritans on 116 123 at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. In England, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2) for urgent help that is not an emergency, which trusts describe as available 24 hours a day. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.name: Under-18 ban on vapes and nicotine in force
dhsc-under-18-sales-ban-vapes-nicotine-p.summary: New rules took effect on 29 October 2026 making it illegal to sell any vape or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, according to a Department of Health and Social Care explainer.
keyPoints: The Department of Health and Social Care published its explainer on 29 October 2026, the day the rules took effect.
Selling any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to under-18s is illegal, online or in shop.
Adults who buy these products for under-18s now commit an offence.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The Department of Health and Social Care says it is illegal to sell any vaping product or non-medicinal nicotine product to anyone under 18, whether online or in a shop. The ban now covers nicotine-free vapes, which were not covered before, and tobacco-free nicotine pouches.

Buying these products for someone under 18, known as proxy purchasing, is now an offence.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The rules restrict free giveaways and substantial discounts used to promote sales and ban most vending-machine sales. Enforcement authorities in England and Wales can issue £200 fixed penalty notices. Legal vaping products remain available to adults.

Separate tobacco rules are due later: from 1 January 2027 it will be illegal to sell tobacco to anyone born on or after 1 January 2009. See the site's smoking page for health information.

dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.name: Dizziness and vertigo: causes and warning signs
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.headline: Dizziness and vertigo: common causes and the signs that need urgent help
dizziness-and-vertigo-causes-and-warning.summary: Dizziness is common and has many causes, from inner ear problems to low blood pressure. The NHS advises calling 999 when it comes with signs of a stroke.
keyPoints: Vertigo is the feeling that you or the room is spinning, and the NHS says inner ear problems are its most common causes.
The NHS says to call 999 for vertigo with double vision, trouble speaking or weakness or numbness in an arm or leg.
A severe headache or feeling very sick with vertigo calls for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.
Dizziness that keeps coming back, or comes with hearing, eyesight or pulse changes or fainting, is a reason to contact a GP.

body.heading: Is dizziness the same as vertigo?
body.body: Dizziness is a broad word that people use for several sensations, including light-headedness and a feeling of spinning. Vertigo is a particular kind of dizziness in which it feels as if you or the room is spinning, even when nothing is moving. The NHS says inner ear problems, which affect balance, are the most common causes of vertigo.

body.heading: What causes light-headedness?
body.body: NHS inform lists labyrinthitis, migraine, low blood sugar and dehydration among the causes of dizziness. A sudden drop in blood pressure on standing up is another listed cause. Less often, an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation, or carbon monoxide poisoning, is on the list.

body.heading: What helps while dizzy?
body.body: NHS inform says dizziness usually goes away on its own. Its self-care advice describes lying down until the feeling passes and then getting up slowly. NHS inform also says not to do anything that could be dangerous while dizzy, such as driving, climbing a ladder or using heavy machinery. Most vertigo improves without treatment, and when treatment is needed it depends on the cause. BPPV usually goes away on its own after several weeks or months, and repositioning manoeuvres are used to treat it. For light-headedness on standing, a GP can measure blood pressure lying down and standing up and may arrange blood tests to check thyroid and sugar levels.

body.heading: What are the common causes of vertigo?
body.body: The NHS vertigo page lists benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), labyrinthitis, vestibular neuritis, Ménière’s disease and migraine among the causes. In BPPV, certain head movements trigger short spells of spinning. Rolling over in bed or tilting the head back to look up are typical triggers. Labyrinthitis is usually caused by a viral infection such as a cold or flu, so antibiotics will not help, and the vertigo usually lasts a few days. Hearing loss and ringing in the ears (tinnitus) can come with labyrinthitis. Ménière’s disease is a rarer cause, with attacks that can include vertigo, hearing loss and tinnitus.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS inform advises contacting a GP if dizziness will not go away or keeps coming back. Changes in hearing, eyesight or pulse, or fainting, are further reasons to make contact. For vertigo, the NHS suggests seeing a GP if it comes on suddenly, does not go away, keeps returning or affects daily life.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if vertigo comes with a severe headache, being sick or feeling very sick, or a very high temperature. It says to call 999 or go to A&E if vertigo comes with double vision or loss of vision, hearing loss, trouble speaking, or weakness, numbness or tingling in an arm or a leg. The NHS also advises not to drive yourself to A&E. Dizziness is among the symptoms the NHS lists for stroke, and any sign of stroke is treated as an emergency: the NHS FAST test stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999.

eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.name: The Eatwell Guide: a balanced diet explained
eatwell-guide-healthy-eating.summary: The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions of food groups in a balanced UK diet, with fruit, vegetables and starchy foods making up just over a third each.
keyPoints: The NHS Eatwell Guide divides food into groups and shows how much of each makes up a balanced diet.
Fruit and vegetables and starchy foods each make up just over a third of the guide, with higher-fibre starchy choices preferred.
NHS advice is at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day, and at least two portions of fish a week, one of them oily.
Foods high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups and are meant to be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: What is the Eatwell Guide?
body.body: The Eatwell Guide is the UK government's picture of a balanced diet, and the NHS explains it on its Live Well pages. It divides the foods people eat into groups and shows roughly what share of the diet each should make up. Foods and drinks high in fat, salt and sugar sit outside the main groups, and the guide says they should be eaten less often and in small amounts.

body.heading: How much fruit, vegetables and starchy food?
body.body: Fruit and vegetables make up just over a third of the food in the guide. The NHS advises at least five portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables a day. A portion of fresh, canned or frozen fruit or vegetables is 80 grams. Starchy foods also make up just over a third of the guide, and the NHS recommends choosing wholegrain or higher-fibre versions where possible.

body.heading: What about protein, dairy and oils?
body.body: The NHS lists beans, pulses, fish, eggs and meat among good sources of protein. The NHS advises at least two portions of fish a week, including at least one portion of oily fish. For dairy and alternatives the guide points to lower-fat and lower-sugar choices where possible. Unsaturated oils and spreads are the choice for oils, eaten in small amounts.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about fat, sugar and salt?
body.body: NHS healthy eating advice includes cutting down on saturated fat and sugar and eating less salt. Fruit juice and smoothies are limited to a total of 150 millilitres a day, because they are high in sugar. The NHS says sugary drinks can be swapped for diet, sugar-free or no-added-sugar versions.

body.heading: Where do drinks, breakfast and weight fit in?
body.body: The NHS tips say that a healthy, balanced diet can help maintain a healthy weight, and that regular exercise may help reduce the risk of serious health conditions. They describe a breakfast high in fibre and low in fat, sugar and salt as one way to be part of a balanced diet.

body.heading: How do salt and saturated fat fit in?
body.body: The NHS advises adults and children aged 11 and over to have no more than 6 grams of salt a day, and younger children less. The NHS says around three quarters of the salt people eat comes from packaged and everyday foods. Salt is linked to high blood pressure, which can lead to heart disease or stroke. Too much saturated fat can increase cholesterol in the blood and so the risk of heart disease, and the NHS suggests swapping towards unsaturated fats such as vegetable oils, oily fish and avocados.

body.heading: What do food labels show?
body.body: UK nutrition labels show energy, fat, saturates, carbohydrate, sugars, protein and salt. Front-of-pack labels use red, amber and green colours to show whether a food is high, medium or low in fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt. The NHS lists sweets, sugary drinks, cakes, biscuits, pastries and breakfast cereals among common sources of added sugar, and says the label and ingredients list can show how much sugar a food contains.
