egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.name: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
egfr-and-creatinine-kidney-blood-tests.summary: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
keyPoints: Creatinine is a waste product measured in the blood, and eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering worked out from it.
As kidney function worsens, creatinine goes up and eGFR goes down.
One abnormal result is not enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, which is confirmed when eGFR stays low over about three months.
A urine test, the albumin to creatinine ratio, is used alongside eGFR because it can show kidney damage.

body.heading: What are creatinine and eGFR?
body.body: Creatinine is a waste product, and the blood test measures how much of it is in the blood. The eGFR, or estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine result. The calculation also takes account of age and sex. Lab Tests Online UK explains that as kidney function worsens, creatinine goes up and the eGFR goes down. Because eGFR comes from a routine blood test, it lets clinicians spot kidney problems before symptoms appear.

body.heading: What does a low eGFR mean?
body.body: A low eGFR means the kidneys are filtering less well than expected. The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases treats a reduced eGFR as one sign of decreased kidney function. The other key sign is kidney damage, usually shown by albumin, a protein, in the urine. eGFR falls naturally with age, which does not always mean kidney disease. The estimate is unreliable when kidney function is changing quickly, as in acute kidney injury.

body.heading: How is chronic kidney disease confirmed?
body.body: One abnormal result is not enough. A diagnosis is usually confirmed only if repeated eGFR tests are consistently lower than normal over about three months. A primary care study warned that relying on a single test could overestimate how many people have chronic kidney disease. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio, or ACR, compares albumin with creatinine in a urine sample. Alongside the eGFR, urine tests give a more accurate picture of how well the kidneys are working. Results are classed by eGFR category and by ACR category, which together show the stage.

body.heading: Who is tested?
body.body: Testing is recommended for people with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, past acute kidney injury or cardiovascular disease. Early chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms, so it is commonly found through routine blood or urine tests. Later symptoms can include tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, blood in the urine and passing urine more often at night. The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms that persist.

body.heading: What are the limits of the test?
body.body: Creatinine-based eGFR may be less reliable in older adults. In that situation another marker, cystatin C, can help. Creatinine can also be influenced by factors other than the kidneys, so the report shows the reference range used.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Chronic kidney disease is most often caused by damage from other conditions, most commonly diabetes and high blood pressure. There is no cure, but care can slow progression. Kidney function is monitored with regular blood and urine tests. Care centres on blood pressure control, managing diabetes, prescribed medicines, diet advice and not smoking. If chronic kidney disease advances, a referral to a kidney specialist may follow.

body.heading: How often are kidney tests repeated?
body.body: NICE guideline NG203 says the monitoring frequency it recommends is a minimum, and that more frequent monitoring may suit some people. The frequency is agreed between the person and their healthcare professional. It also reflects how quickly the eGFR or ACR is changing and other conditions such as diabetes. NICE says ACR monitoring should be individualised, for example more often when the ACR is higher. NICE lists diabetes among the risk factors for which eGFR and ACR testing is advised.

falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.name: Falls in older people and reducing the risk
falls-in-older-people-reducing-risk.summary: Strength and balance exercises and simple changes at home can lower the risk of falls in older people, according to the NHS. NICE recommends offering falls prevention exercise programmes.
keyPoints: The NHS says the risk of falling can be lowered by exercises for strength and balance and by simple changes at home.
NICE guideline NG249 recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.
Clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping rooms and stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip are among the home-safety suggestions.
Regular sight tests are recommended, and in England the NHS provides free sight tests for people aged 60 or over.

body.heading: Why do falls happen?
body.body: Causes of falls include muscle weakness and balance changes with age, conditions that affect mobility or balance (such as arthritis, stroke or Parkinson's), low blood pressure, problems with eyesight or hearing, and dementia. Anyone can have a fall, but it is more likely in older people or those with mobility problems. Some medicines can affect balance and increase the chance of a fall. The NHS advises speaking to a GP or pharmacist if medicines might be affecting balance. Postural hypotension is a drop in blood pressure on standing up from lying or sitting, which can cause dizziness and may lead to a fall.

body.heading: What exercise helps?
body.body: The NHS says regular exercises for strength and balance can improve strength and balance and reduce the risk of falls. The NHS notes there is evidence that regular tai chi can reduce the risk of falls. Programmes are described as best when tailored to the individual and overseen by a trained professional.

body.heading: What can be changed at home?
body.body: Suggestions include clearing clutter and trailing wires, using non-slip mats, keeping stairs well lit and wearing well-fitting footwear with good grip. Regular sight tests are recommended, and free NHS sight tests are available to people aged 60 or over in England.

body.heading: What does NICE recommend?
body.body: NICE guideline NG249 covers falls assessment and prevention in older people and in people aged 50 and over at higher risk, and recommends offering a falls prevention exercise programme.

body.heading: What can a GP or falls team do?
body.body: A GP can check balance with simple tests, review medicines and refer to local falls services. Some areas have a falls team that offers a full assessment to older people who have fallen or are at high risk, and a GP surgery can say what is available locally.

body.heading: What does the NHS advise after a fall?
body.body: Advice after a fall includes calling for help, using a lifeline alarm if there is one, and keeping warm by covering up with a rug, blanket or towel. Advice for someone who is not hurt includes getting up slowly, and changing position regularly while waiting for help if they cannot get up. The NHS says to call 999 if someone has fallen and may have injured their head, back, neck or hip, cannot get up, is confused, drowsy or vomiting, or has severe bleeding; NHS 111 can help if they may be in pain, injured or unwell, and a GP can be seen after any fall.

fda-atezolizumab-stage-iii-colon-cancer.name: FDA approves atezolizumab for colon cancer
fda-atezolizumab-stage-iii-colon-cancer.summary: The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) with chemotherapy on 8 October 2026 as adjuvant treatment for stage III mismatch repair deficient colon cancer.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq) on 8 October 2026 for stage III dMMR colon cancer.
It is given with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin as adjuvant treatment.
The approval rests on a randomised, open-label trial called ATOMIC.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 8 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved atezolizumab (Tecentriq, Genentech) with a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin for adjuvant treatment of stage III mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) colon cancer.

The approval covers adults and children aged two years and older.

A subcutaneous form, Tecentriq Hybreza, is approved with the same chemotherapy for patients aged 12 years and older who weigh at least 40 kg.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The FDA notes that ATOMIC enrolled 711 adults and one paediatric patient.

Adjuvant treatment is given after surgery to lower the chance of the cancer returning.

The FDA says the approval rests on the ATOMIC trial, a randomised, open-label, active-controlled study in people with stage III dMMR colon cancer after complete removal of the primary tumour.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-camzyos-children-obstructive-hcm.name: FDA approves Camzyos for children
fda-camzyos-children-obstructive-hcm.summary: The US FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, on 30 September 2026.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy on 30 September 2026.
The FDA says it is the first treatment to improve functional capacity and symptoms in children with this condition.
Camzyos carries a boxed warning for the risk of heart failure and is available only through a restricted programme.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 30 September 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Camzyos (mavacamten) for children weighing at least 30 kg with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

The FDA describes this as the first treatment to improve functional capacity and symptoms in children with the condition.

It describes the condition as inherited and causing a thickened heart muscle, with symptoms that can include shortness of breath, fatigue and an abnormal heart rhythm that can be life-threatening.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
In the paediatric study, patients were randomly assigned to Camzyos or placebo, and Camzyos reduced the Valsalva left ventricular outflow tract gradient compared with placebo.

The FDA says adult data showed a similar reduction, and that it expects the drug to help paediatric patients weighing at least 30 kg.

Camzyos carries a boxed warning for the risk of heart failure and is available only through a restricted programme called the Camzyos Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS).

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-casgevy-sickle-cell-children-aged-2-.name: FDA approves gene therapy for young children
fda-casgevy-sickle-cell-children-aged-2-.summary: The US FDA approved Casgevy on 1 July 2026 for children aged 2 and older with sickle cell disease, which it calls the first gene therapy for this age group.
keyPoints: The US FDA approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel) for patients aged 2 years and older on 1 July 2026.
It covers sickle cell disease with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises and transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia.
The FDA first approved Casgevy and Lyfgenia for sickle cell disease in December 2023, for patients aged 12 and older.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 1 July 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel) for patients aged 2 years and older.

The FDA says it is the first gene therapy approved for patients aged 2 years and older with sickle cell disease.

The approval covers sickle cell disease with recurrent vaso-occlusive crises, and transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The FDA first approved Casgevy and Lyfgenia for sickle cell disease in December 2023, for patients aged 12 and older.

The FDA notes that Casgevy is the first FDA-approved therapy that uses CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing.

Before the Casgevy infusion, patients receive a high-intensity preparatory treatment called myeloablative conditioning.

This is a US decision; availability in the UK is decided separately by the MHRA and NICE.

fda-dostarlimab-rectal-cancer.name: FDA approves dostarlimab for rectal cancer
fda-dostarlimab-rectal-cancer.summary: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli) on 19 October 2026 for adults with certain locally advanced rectal cancers.
keyPoints: The US FDA granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli, GSK) on 19 October 2026.
It applies to adults with stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer that is dMMR or MSI-H.
The approval rests on interim results from a single-arm, open-label study called AZUR-1.
This is a US decision; UK availability is decided separately.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 19 October 2026 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted accelerated approval to dostarlimab (Jemperli, GSK).

It is approved for adults with stage II or III locally advanced rectal cancer whose tumours are mismatch repair deficient (dMMR) or microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H).

The FDA says it acted four months ahead of its goal date, and that the drug had earlier received breakthrough therapy designation.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:

The FDA says it approved label revisions that add a boxed warning, its most prominent safety warning.

Ferric carboxymaltose is an iron replacement given by injection into a vein.

feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.name: Feeling sick and vomiting in adults
feeling-sick-and-vomiting-in-adults.summary: NHS inform says vomiting in adults usually lasts only 1 or 2 days, but blood in vomit means calling 999 or going to A&E, and vomiting for more than 2 days is a reason to call NHS 111.
keyPoints: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own.
NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen.

body.heading: What causes nausea and vomiting?
body.body: The NHS says feeling sick is common and usually goes away on its own. Diarrhoea or vomiting can point to norovirus or food poisoning, and a headache with a high temperature can suggest an infection such as flu. Other causes include morning sickness in pregnancy, motion sickness, anxiety, alcohol, medicines and recent surgery. NHS inform calls gastroenteritis one of the most common causes of vomiting in adults, and also lists migraine, labyrinthitis, appendicitis and medicines such as antibiotics and opioid painkillers. NHS inform says norovirus usually clears up by itself within a few days, and that there is no specific treatment, so the illness has to run its course. NHS inform says antibiotics will not help norovirus because it is caused by a virus, and that small sips of water help to prevent dehydration.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS describes getting fresh air, sipping cold drinks, trying ginger or peppermint tea, and eating smaller, more frequent meals. It also lists hot, fried or greasy food, eating too quickly and lying down soon after eating as things to avoid. NHS inform advises resting at home and taking small sips of water or squash often so that dehydration does not develop.

body.heading: What are the signs of dehydration?
body.body: NHS inform lists signs of severe dehydration, including confusion, a rapid heartbeat, sunken eyes and passing little or no urine, among the reasons to call NHS 111. NHS inform advises people with diabetes who have been vomiting a lot to call NHS 111, especially if they take insulin, because vomiting can affect blood sugar levels.

body.heading: Which symptoms need urgent help?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee granules, or for green or yellow-green vomit. NHS inform advises calling NHS 111 for a person who keeps being sick and cannot keep fluids down, has been vomiting for more than 2 days, or has lost a lot of weight since becoming ill; its gastroenteritis page lists fever and bloody diarrhoea as reasons to contact NHS 111 or the GP practice urgently. The NHS says to call 999 if sudden sickness comes with tight or heavy chest pain, pain spreading to the arms, back, neck or jaw, or shortness of breath, because these could be signs of a heart attack.

body.heading: When should a GP be involved?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if the sickness has not improved after a few days or keeps coming back, and calling NHS 111 for advice if a GP cannot be seen. The GP can look for the cause and may prescribe anti-sickness medicine. The NHS says a pregnant person who is being sick often and cannot keep food down should tell their midwife or doctor, or contact the hospital, as soon as possible.

fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.name: Fever in adults: causes and when to get help
fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.headline: High temperature in adults: what usually causes it and when to get help
fever-in-adults-causes-and-when-to-get-h.summary: A high temperature in adults is usually a sign of infection and often settles at home. The NHS advises urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP if it does not improve, and 999 for some warning signs.
keyPoints: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection.
Home care in the NHS advice includes resting, drinking fluids and, if needed, taking paracetamol or ibuprofen.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after home treatment or is getting worse.
The NHS meningitis page says to call 999 or go to A&E for a very painful headache, confusion, a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights, or a rash that does not fade when pressed.

body.heading: What causes a high temperature?
body.body: The NHS says a high temperature is usually a symptom of an infection. Infections such as flu and glandular fever can cause a high temperature.

body.heading: What helps at home?
body.body: NHS advice for a high temperature is to rest and drink plenty of fluids. The NHS also says paracetamol or ibuprofen can be taken to help feel more comfortable, following the instructions on the packet or leaflet. NHS inform also suggests wearing loose, comfortable clothing and avoiding alcohol. Staying away from other people while you have a temperature is also advised, to avoid passing on an infection.

body.heading: When is it worth speaking to a GP or NHS 111?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a high temperature is not improving after treating it at home, or is getting worse. NHS 111 is free and open every day of the year, day and night.

body.heading: Which signs mean 999 or A&E?
body.body: The NHS meningitis page lists a rash that does not fade when pressed, a very painful headache, confusion, and a stiff neck with sensitivity to bright lights among the signs that need immediate action. For a rash, the NHS describes the glass test: pressing a clear glass firmly against the skin to see whether the spots fade. Spots that stay visible through the glass are called a non-blanching rash, and rashes can be harder to see on darker skin, so the palms, soles and tummy are worth checking.

fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.name: Fever and rashes in children: when to get help
fever-in-children-when-to-get-help.summary: Most fevers in children can be looked after at home. The NHS says call 999 for signs such as a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade, and NHS 111 or a GP for a baby under 3 months.
keyPoints: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home, with plenty of fluids and regular checks, including overnight.
Call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade under a glass, blue, grey or pale skin, being hard to wake, or difficulty breathing.
For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP.
A GP or NHS 111 should be contacted if a fever lasts 5 days or more.

body.heading: Can a fever be looked after at home?
body.body: The NHS says a child with a fever can usually be looked after at home. It recommends giving plenty of fluids and checking on the child regularly, including overnight.

body.heading: When does a fever need 999?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 for a stiff neck, a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed on it, or a first seizure caused by fever. The same list includes cold hands and feet, blue, grey or pale skin, lips or tongue, being drowsy and hard to wake, extreme agitation or confusion, and difficulty breathing. A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it is described as non-blanching, and the NHS treats it as an emergency.

body.heading: When should NHS 111 or the GP be contacted?
body.body: For a baby under 3 months with a high temperature, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact a GP. For babies aged 3 to 6 months, the NHS also advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when the temperature is high. For older children, the NHS advises calling NHS 111 or contacting a GP when a fever has lasted 5 days or more. Signs of dehydration, such as fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes and no tears when crying, also call for advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What about rashes in babies?
body.body: Healthier Together pages say that most baby rashes are harmless and go away on their own, and that dry or peeling skin in the first week or two is normal. Tiny white or yellow spots on the nose or face (milia) usually clear within a few weeks without treatment. Healthier Together lists signs that need urgent help from a health professional: a rash that does not fade under the glass test, redness around the belly button, and a baby who is pale, very sleepy or breathing hard.

flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.name: Flu or a cold: how they differ
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.headline: Flu or a cold: how to tell them apart, how long each lasts and when to get help
flu-or-cold-how-they-differ.summary: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
keyPoints: Cold and flu symptoms overlap, but flu tends to be more severe and often comes on within hours.
A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up gradually.
Antibiotics do not work against colds or flu, because both are caused by viruses.
Sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or coughing up blood needs 999 or A&E.
NHS 111 or a GP can advise if symptoms get worse or last longer than expected.

body.heading: How do flu and a cold differ?
body.body:
Colds and flu are both viral infections that affect the nose and throat, and their symptoms overlap. Flu and colds differ in how severe they are and in how quickly they start.

Flu tends to be more severe than a cold. A cold mostly affects the nose and throat, while flu can also bring a fever, aches and exhaustion.

Because the symptoms overlap, it can be hard to tell flu and a cold apart from symptoms alone. With a cold a person usually feels unwell but can manage usual activities, while flu can leave a person exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.

body.heading: How quickly do the symptoms start?
body.body:
Speed of onset is another difference the NHS pages point to. Flu tends to come on suddenly, often within hours.

A cold usually builds more gradually. The main signs of a cold are a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, a hoarse voice, a cough, and feeling tired and unwell.

body.heading: How long do they last?
body.body:
Most people start to feel better from a cold within about one to two weeks. Flu usually improves within about a week.

Tiredness can linger for longer after flu, even when the other symptoms have settled.

body.heading: What treatment is there?
body.body:
A cold is caused by a virus and usually gets better by itself. The NHS says the usual approach is to rest and drink fluids while the body clears the infection.

For a cold, a pharmacist can recommend suitable medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person. Antibiotics do not help, because both illnesses are caused by viruses rather than bacteria.

A flu vaccine protects against flu, but it does not protect against colds.

A pharmacist can recommend suitable cold medicines and check which ones are suitable for the person, and some are not suitable for children, pregnant women or people taking certain other medicines.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS separates emergencies from problems that can wait for a call or an appointment.

Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood is an emergency, and the route is 999 or A&E.

For less urgent worries, NHS 111 or the GP can advise. The NHS says to get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for flu symptoms with feeling very unwell, shortness of breath or no improvement.

The NHS says people aged 65 or over, people who are pregnant, and people with a long-term condition or a weakened immune system should get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if they have flu symptoms.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood, with someone else driving or an ambulance rather than the person driving themselves.

body.heading: Is it flu, a cold or something else?
body.body:
Other infections can look like flu or a cold. The UKHSA publishes a guide to the signs and symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and colds, and the NHS pages for each illness set out what to look for.

Symptoms overlap, so the only way to know for sure whether a person has flu or COVID-19 is a test.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Flu symptoms can include a sudden high temperature, an aching body and feeling exhausted. A cold usually causes a runny or blocked nose, sneezing, watery eyes and a sore throat, and does not usually bring a fever or body aches. The NHS offers the flu vaccine every year, in autumn or winter, to people at higher risk of becoming seriously ill from flu.

references.title: UKHSA: Do I have flu, COVID-19 or a cold? Know the signs and symptoms

grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.name: Grief and bereavement: what to expect
grief-and-bereavement-what-to-expect.summary: Grief is a natural response to loss, and the NHS says feelings usually ease gradually. A GP or bereavement service can help when grief is very strong or does not ease.
keyPoints: Grief is a normal response to loss, and the NHS says feelings of sadness should ease gradually over time.
NHS Inform says there is no time limit on grief.
The NHS says to see a GP if someone is struggling to cope, or their own efforts are not helping.
In an emergency, with immediate danger to life, the NHS says to use 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 are routes to urgent support.

body.heading: What does grief feel like?
body.body: Grief can bring shock, numbness, sadness, exhaustion and anger. NHS inform says there is no deadline on feeling better or recovering after a bereavement. NHS inform describes delayed grief, when grief is not fully felt at the time, and says it is never too late to grieve. The NHS lists shock, sadness, tiredness, anger and guilt among common reactions to loss.

body.heading: What can help?
body.body: The NHS suggests talking to someone trusted, joining peer support, taking regular exercise and eating regular meals. The NHS advises against relying on alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with grief. Bereavement support organisations such as Cruse can help, and talking to others can bring comfort.

body.heading: When is it worth getting help?
body.body: The NHS says sadness should ease gradually with time, but medical help may be needed if someone feels increasingly depressed or anxious. It advises seeing a GP when someone is struggling to cope, has had low mood for more than two weeks, or finds their own efforts are not helping. People in England can refer themselves directly to an NHS talking therapies service without seeing a GP first.

body.heading: Where can bereaved people and children find support?
body.body: The NHS has a page on grief after bereavement or loss and a separate page on children and bereavement. Cruse Bereavement Support offers a helpline and information on dealing with grief, and Child Bereavement UK and Winston's Wish support bereaved children and families.

body.heading: What is prolonged grief?
body.body: For some people, painful feelings do not ease as months go by, and the NHS says this may be prolonged grief disorder, which may need a clinician's assessment. Signs the NHS lists include difficulty accepting the death and suicidal thoughts, and it says to seek help from a GP, or urgent help if there are suicidal thoughts.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If grief brings thoughts of suicide, urgent help is available; NHS inform in Scotland points to NHS 111 for people in distress or despair. In an emergency, when someone is in immediate danger or has been physically harmed, the NHS says to use 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

references.title: NHS: Get help with grief after bereavement or loss
NHS inform: Advice and support on coping with grief

hba1c-test-what-it-shows.name: HbA1c test: what it shows and why it matters
hba1c-test-what-it-shows.summary: The HbA1c test shows average blood glucose over the past two to three months and is used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.
keyPoints: HbA1c reflects the average blood glucose level over roughly the previous two to three months.
The test is used to diagnose diabetes, to check how well diabetes is managed and to follow people with prediabetes.
Targets are personal, and a diabetes team may set a higher one for someone with frequent low blood glucose or an older person.
Conditions that affect red blood cells can make HbA1c unreliable, and another test may suit better.

body.heading: What does an HbA1c test show?
body.body: The HbA1c blood test reflects the average level of glucose in the blood over the past two to three months. That is why it differs from a finger-prick reading, which captures one moment. Glucose attaches to a part of the red blood cell, and the more glucose there is in the blood, the more HbA1c is present. Red blood cells live for about two to three months before new ones replace them, which sets the window the test covers. Occasional very high or very low readings are smoothed into one average.

body.heading: What is the test used for?
body.body: Doctors use it to diagnose diabetes. They also use it to keep an eye on levels in people at risk of developing diabetes, a state called prediabetes. In people who already have diabetes, it shows how well blood sugar has been controlled. MedlinePlus says the test is not used to diagnose type 1 diabetes. Home glucose monitors do not diagnose diabetes, and diagnosis rests on blood tests that a GP arranges.

body.heading: How are the results given and what are the targets?
body.body: UK laboratories give HbA1c in millimoles per mole, while some countries use a percentage. Diabetes UK says targets are individual and each person agrees their own with their diabetes care team. A higher target may suit someone who has had many problems with low blood glucose. As people age, the diabetes team may raise the target, because the risks of tight control can outweigh the benefits.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: Diabetes UK says HbA1c is usually tested every three to six months in people with diabetes. It may be done more often when blood glucose is changing quickly, when planning a pregnancy or after a change of treatment. Some people need the test less often, usually later in pregnancy.

body.heading: What can make the result less reliable?
body.body: Conditions that affect red blood cells can make the result less accurate, such as anaemia or an uncommon form of haemoglobin. Diabetes UK advises talking to the doctor about which other test will be more accurate in that case. Pregnancy or illness during the window can also affect the result. An NHS Scotland resource says the HbA1c may change if diet, physical activity, weight or medication have changed. Laboratories often convert the result to an estimated average glucose, which may differ from readings on a home meter.

body.heading: What happens after a result in the prediabetes range?
body.body: Scottish NHS guidance says the GP should explain the risk factors for type 2 diabetes and what changes can reduce the risk. Diabetes UK says the GP should refer people to a free NHS type 2 diabetes prevention course. A blood test to check average blood sugar should be offered at least once a year. A GP appointment is the route to discuss any result.

body.heading: Why does a prediabetes result matter?
body.body: Prediabetes means blood sugar is higher than normal but not high enough for a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes. It also means a high risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Prediabetes usually causes no symptoms, so it is often found only through a routine blood test or an NHS Health Check. Feeling very thirsty, passing urine more often, feeling more tired than usual and losing weight without trying are symptoms of diabetes itself. Anyone with those symptoms is advised to speak to a GP. The NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme is a free programme for people at risk of type 2 diabetes, with support on eating, weight and activity, and a doctor or nurse makes the referral.

headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.name: Headaches: types, causes and warning signs
headache-types-causes-and-warning-signs.summary: Tension-type headache is the most common type, and a headache that starts suddenly and is very severe needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer.
The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury.
Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain.

body.heading: What are the common types of headache?
body.body:
The NHS says the main symptom of a tension headache is pain on both sides of the head, face or neck, which lasts at least 30 minutes and can last much longer. NHS Cheshire and Merseyside describes tension-type headache as the most common headache, usually mild to moderately severe, with a pressing or tightening feel. The NHS says stress is a common cause of tension headaches.

The NHS describes migraine as a throbbing headache that can be severe, is often on one side of the head and can be worse when moving around. Other migraine symptoms include feeling sick and sensitivity to light and sound.

Some people also get an aura, such as seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights. NHS inform says migraine affects around 1 in 5 women and 1 in 15 men. NHS inform describes cluster headaches as rare, coming in bouts of short daily headaches that last a month or two, with pain usually around the eye.

body.heading: Can painkillers cause headaches?
body.body: Great Ormond Street Hospital describes medication overuse headache as a headache that develops and gets worse with frequent use of medicines taken for pain. Great Ormond Street Hospital says medication overuse headache occurs in people who already have tension-type headache or migraine. A Nottinghamshire NHS pathway says headache from overusing painkillers improves or resolves within 3 months of stopping them.

body.heading: Which headaches need a 999 call?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a headache that comes on suddenly and is extremely painful, or one that follows a serious head injury. NHS inform lists other reasons to call 999 or go to A&E, including signs of stroke such as weakness on one side or slurred speech, signs of meningitis or sepsis, and being drowsy or confused.

body.heading: Which headaches need an urgent GP visit?
body.body: NHS inform lists a headache set off by coughing, sneezing, a change in posture or effort as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. A headache that wakes someone from sleep, or keeps getting worse despite treatment, is listed under contacting the GP practice. NHS inform lists a sore scalp or jaw pain when chewing in someone over 50 as a reason to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. NHS inform lists changes in vision, or a new or worsening headache with dizziness, vomiting or weakness, as reasons to contact the GP practice urgently, or phone NHS 111 if it is closed. An NHS formulary guideline describes giant cell arteritis, also called temporal arteritis, as a medical emergency that needs prompt assessment and immediate steroid treatment to prevent permanent loss of vision.

body.heading: How is migraine treated?
body.body: The NHS describes triptans as a painkiller made specifically for migraine, available as tablets, injections and nasal sprays. NHS inform says a GP may recommend a triptan if over-the-counter medicines are not helping. Anti-sickness medicines can help during a migraine even without nausea, and the NHS says they work better when taken as soon as symptoms begin. The NHS lists stress, tiredness, skipping meals and too much caffeine among common migraine triggers.

body.heading: When is a routine GP visit sensible, and what might the GP do?
body.body: The NHS says tension headaches can be treated with painkillers, but advises seeing a GP for several headaches a week or severe ones. A GP may suggest keeping a migraine diary. There is no specific test for migraine, so the GP looks for a pattern of recurring headaches with the typical symptoms. The NHS says an antidepressant medicine called amitriptyline is sometimes recommended to help prevent tension headaches.

healthy-weight-bmi-explained.name: Healthy weight: what BMI shows and what it misses
healthy-weight-bmi-explained.summary: BMI is an NHS check on whether weight suits height, but it cannot tell muscle from fat, so waist size and a GP discussion add to it.
keyPoints: The NHS BMI calculator checks whether a person is a healthy weight for their height.
BMI cannot tell muscle from fat, so very muscular people may be rated overweight and people who lose muscle with age may still fall in the healthy range.
The NHS says Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups have a higher risk of some long-term conditions at a lower BMI.
NHS treatment for obesity ranges from lifestyle changes and weight management programmes to medicines and surgery.

body.heading: What does BMI measure?
body.body: Body mass index, or BMI, is calculated from height and weight, and the NHS calculator uses it to check whether an adult is a healthy weight for their height. The calculator shows which category a result falls in, and the NHS gives a different healthy range for Black, Asian and some other minority ethnic groups. The reason given is that these groups have a higher risk of developing some long-term conditions, such as type 2 diabetes, at a lower BMI.

body.heading: What are the limits of BMI?
body.body: BMI cannot tell the difference between muscle and fat. Very muscular people and athletes may be rated overweight or obese despite low body fat. Adults who lose muscle as they get older may fall in the healthy weight range even though they may be carrying excess fat.

body.heading: Why does waist size matter?
body.body: The NHS gives a method for measuring the waist: find the bottom of the ribs and the top of the hips, place a tape measure midway between them, and measure after breathing out naturally. The NHS and NICE describe a waist measurement of more than half a person's height as linked with increased health risks. The NHS advises seeing a GP for help with losing weight, or if the waist measurement is more than half of height.

body.heading: What treatment does the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS says a GP can advise on weight loss and on options such as weight management programmes, medicines or surgery. Options include lifestyle changes, weight management programmes, medicines and surgery. Local NHS specialist weight management services, often called tier 3, usually have a team that can include a doctor, dietitians, specialist nurses and psychologists. NHS access to weight-loss injections such as semaglutide and tirzepatide depends on eligibility criteria and varies by area; some are offered through specialist weight management services, and tirzepatide is being introduced through GP practices in phases for people with the highest clinical need.

body.heading: What health risks are linked to excess weight?
body.body: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, high blood pressure, several cancers, osteoarthritis and fatty liver disease among conditions linked to excess weight.

body.heading: Why does weight change?
body.body: The NHS describes overweight and obesity as having more body fat than the body needs. It can happen when a person eats or drinks more than the body needs or does not do enough physical activity. Other factors listed include genes, some medicines, and some health conditions such as an underactive thyroid.

body.heading: What does a GP check, and what support is free?
body.body: The NHS says a GP looks for possible underlying causes of obesity, for example a medicine the person is taking. The NHS offers a free 12-week weight loss plan as an app. The NHS says that for someone living with obesity, losing about 3 per cent of starting body weight can reduce the risk of obesity-related complications.

references.title: NHS: Overweight and obesity in adults
NHS inform: Obesity causes and treatments

hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.name: Hearing loss: causes, tests and what helps
hearing-loss-causes-tests-and-help.summary: Gradual hearing loss is common and a GP can arrange hearing tests. Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111, according to the NHS.
keyPoints: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or long-term exposure to loud noise.
A GP can look in the ears and may refer to an audiologist for a hearing test.
Sudden hearing loss in one or both ears needs an urgent GP appointment or help from NHS 111.
NHS hearing aids are free.

body.heading: What causes hearing loss?
body.body: Gradual hearing loss in both ears is usually linked to ageing or to damage from loud noise over many years. Earwax, ear infections and a perforated eardrum are other common causes. Sensorineural hearing loss involves damage to the inner ear or the nerve pathway to the brain, while conductive loss means sound is blocked in the outer or middle ear, for example by earwax, fluid or infection.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP, and what happens?
body.body: Some pharmacies and opticians also offer a free hearing test. A GP can check for problems such as earwax or infection and may refer to an audiologist for further tests. If the GP finds no obvious cause, they should refer the person to an NHS audiologist for a full hearing assessment. In a common hearing test, the person wears headphones, hears sounds at different levels and presses a button each time they hear one. The test shows which pitches are affected and by how much.

body.heading: What if hearing is lost suddenly?
body.body: The NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111 for sudden hearing loss in one or both ears. If neither is reachable, the nearest accident and emergency department is the route. Sudden hearing loss can be permanent, and treatment given early can reduce that risk. For sudden sensorineural loss the cause is often never found, and the usual treatment is steroids, which are most likely to help when given soon after the loss starts.

body.heading: What helps with permanent hearing loss and tinnitus?
body.body: For tinnitus, the first person to speak to is the GP, who can check the ears for treatable causes and may refer to a specialist. Treatable causes such as earwax or infection can often be dealt with by a GP, while permanent loss is usually managed with hearing aids. Hearing aids do not make hearing perfect, but they make sounds louder and clearer, and NHS hearing aids are free.

heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.name: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.headline: Heart attack, cardiac arrest and angina: the differences and when to call 999
heart-attack-cardiac-arrest-and-angina.summary: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle, cardiac arrest is the heart stopping, and angina is chest pain that eases with rest.
keyPoints: A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked.
In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, the person collapses and is not breathing normally.
Angina is chest pain caused by a temporary reduction in the blood supply to the heart.
Angina symptoms usually ease with rest or a nitrate medicine, whereas heart attack symptoms usually do not.
For a suspected heart attack or cardiac arrest the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

body.heading: What is the difference between a heart attack and cardiac arrest?
body.body:
The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that a heart attack and a cardiac arrest are different, and that both are emergencies.

A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked. The BHF describes a heart attack as a sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle, and the NHS says it can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively. The person collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally. The BHF says a heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest.

If a defibrillator is nearby, the 999 call handler will say where it is and may ask someone to fetch it, and CPR should not be stopped.

A cardiac arrest usually happens suddenly and without warning.

body.heading: What is angina?
body.body:
Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the blood supply to the heart muscle is temporarily reduced. The BHF says the discomfort of angina does not damage the heart muscle in the way a heart attack does.

Angina symptoms usually happen during exercise and pass within a few minutes, and they can be eased by resting or by using a nitrate tablet or spray.

Angina symptoms usually pass in a few minutes, but heart pain that lasts longer may be a heart attack, so call 999.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of a heart attack?
body.body:
The NHS lists chest pain that feels tight or squeezing. The pain can spread to the arms, jaw, neck, back or tummy.

Other signs include feeling sick, sweating, shortness of breath and light-headedness.

A key difference from angina is that heart attack symptoms are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray.

Some people with a heart attack also look pale or grey.

Women are more likely to notice symptoms such as shortness of breath, feeling sick, and back or jaw pain, and symptoms can be milder than people expect.

body.heading: What are the signs of a cardiac arrest?
body.body:
A person in cardiac arrest loses consciousness. They do not respond, and they are not breathing or their breathing does not look normal.

Without treatment a person in cardiac arrest may die within minutes, which is why speed matters.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 straight away if someone may be having a heart attack.

If someone seems to be in cardiac arrest, the NHS advises calling 999 and starting CPR, with the call handler giving instructions.

The NHS says to call 999 for the main warning signs of a heart attack, and to call NHS 111 for less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat. The BHF says heart attack pain is not relieved by rest or a nitrate medicine, and that a heart attack is a 999 emergency.

The NHS advises a person who may be having a heart attack to call 999 rather than drive themselves to A&E.

For less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat, the NHS says to call NHS 111.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed and treated?
body.body:
A heart attack is usually assessed with an ECG, which records the heart's electrical activity, and a blood test for troponin, a protein released when the heart muscle is damaged. The site's pages on these tests give more detail.

Treatment in hospital, with medicine or a procedure, aims to restore the blood supply to the heart.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: An NHS ECG is usually the first test, and it can show whether the heart attack needs urgent treatment to open the blocked artery.

references.title: NHS: Symptoms of a heart attack

heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.name: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.headline: Heartburn, acid reflux and GORD: what they are and when to see a GP
heartburn-acid-reflux-and-gord.summary: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest from acid reflux; when it keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD).
keyPoints: Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat.
When reflux keeps happening it is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.
Lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines are the usual first steps, and a pharmacist can advise on options.
Difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss or frequent vomiting need prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111.
A GP can prescribe acid-reducing medicine and arrange tests if symptoms continue.

body.heading: What is heartburn, and how does it relate to GORD?
body.body:
Heartburn is a burning feeling in the chest. NHS sources describe it as caused by stomach acid travelling up towards the throat, which is known as acid reflux.

If it keeps happening, the condition is called gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or GORD.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The main symptoms of acid reflux are heartburn and an unpleasant sour taste in the mouth caused by stomach acid. Some people also have a hoarse voice, bad breath, bloating or feeling sick.

Symptoms tend to get worse after eating, when lying down or when bending over.

body.heading: What can bring it on?
body.body:
NHS sources list several contributors: certain foods and drinks, being overweight, smoking, stress or anxiety, having a hiatus hernia, and pregnancy.

Some medicines, including anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen, can also play a part.

Heartburn can also come with bad breath.

body.heading: What helps?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes are usually the first step. NHS advice includes eating smaller, more frequent meals, avoiding foods that trigger symptoms, and not eating within a few hours of going to bed. Not smoking is also advised.

Antacids and alginates, which are available from pharmacies, can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options.

Antacids and alginates are not meant to be taken regularly for long periods, so a pharmacist can advise on them.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route if lifestyle changes and pharmacy medicines do not help, or if heartburn happens most days.

Some symptoms need prompt attention, by contacting the GP or NHS 111. NHS sources list difficulty swallowing, unintentional weight loss, food getting stuck in the throat and frequent vomiting as reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111.

Chest pain can also be a sign of a heart problem. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not ease, especially with sweating, feeling sick, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it may be a heart attack.

Food getting stuck in the throat is another reason to see a GP.

Vomiting blood, or vomit that looks like coffee grounds, needs emergency medical care.

Severe chest pain can be mistaken for heart-related pain, so treat sudden severe chest pain as an emergency and call 999.

body.heading: What can a GP offer?
body.body:
A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor, a medicine that reduces the amount of acid the stomach makes. A GP may prescribe a proton pump inhibitor for a short time, and some people need a long-term prescription, and the NHS advises anyone whose symptoms continue or return to go back to the GP.

If symptoms continue despite treatment, a GP may refer someone for a gastroscopy, a test to look at the lining of the food pipe.

Surgery to strengthen the valve at the bottom of the food pipe exists but is not usually needed.

Long-lasting reflux can sometimes inflame or ulcerate the food pipe.

heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.name: Heavy periods: causes, tests and treatment
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.headline: Heavy periods: what can cause them, which checks a GP offers and how they are treated
heavy-periods-causes-tests-and-treatment.summary: Heavy periods are common and often have no clear cause, but fibroids, endometriosis and other conditions can be behind them. The NHS advises a GP visit when they affect daily life.
keyPoints: Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, and the NHS says help is available when they affect daily life.
Often there is no underlying medical reason, though fibroids, endometriosis and some other conditions can cause heavy periods.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect life, have lasted some time, come with severe pain, or if there is bleeding between periods or after sex.
Treatment choices include some contraceptives, medicines to reduce bleeding and surgery, and heavy periods do not always need treatment.

body.heading: What counts as a heavy period?
body.body: The NHS describes heavy periods in practical terms, such as needing to change pads or tampons every one to two hours. Some people naturally have heavier periods than others, but the NHS says that when periods are so heavy that they affect life, help is available. Feeling tired or short of breath, or avoiding daily activities because of periods, are other signs that bleeding may be a problem.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body: Heavy periods often have no underlying cause. Fibroids, which are non-cancerous growths in or around the womb, are one of the identifiable causes. Other conditions that can cause heavy periods include endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovary syndrome and pelvic inflammatory disease. Some medicines, such as anticoagulants and some chemotherapy medicines, can also be responsible. Rarely, heavy periods can be a sign of womb cancer.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP if heavy periods affect your life, have lasted for some time, or come with severe pain. Bleeding between periods or after sex is also a reason to see a GP. For severe period or pelvic pain that is worse than usual and not helped by painkillers, the NHS advises getting urgent advice, from NHS 111 if needed.

body.heading: Which tests might a GP arrange?
body.body: A GP can investigate why bleeding is heavy, which may include a physical examination, blood tests or scans. A blood test to look for iron deficiency anaemia is usually offered to people with heavy periods. A pregnancy test, an ultrasound scan and, less often, a hysteroscopy (a look inside the womb with a small camera) may follow.

body.heading: How are heavy periods treated?
body.body: Heavy periods do not always need to be treated. If they affect daily life, options include a hormone-releasing intrauterine system (IUS) or the combined contraceptive pill. Medicines to reduce the bleeding, such as tranexamic acid, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as mefenamic acid or naproxen are also used. Surgical options also exist for heavy periods.

high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.name: High blood pressure: what happens next
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.headline: High blood pressure: how it is found, what causes it and what treatment involves
high-blood-pressure-what-happens-next.summary: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms and is found by measuring it; treatment starts with lifestyle changes and may include medicine.
keyPoints: High blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, and the only way to know is to have it measured.
In most people no single cause is found; age, family history, ethnicity and lifestyle all play a part.
Readings taken at home or by a 24-hour monitor can be used alongside clinic readings to confirm the diagnosis.
Lifestyle changes are the first step, and a GP may prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high or stays high.
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

body.heading: What does a blood pressure reading mean?
body.body:
Blood pressure is the force of blood against the walls of the arteries. A reading gives two numbers: the pressure when the heart beats and the pressure between beats. The site's page on blood pressure measurement explains how they are taken.

Doctors use different thresholds for readings taken in a clinic and for readings taken at home when deciding whether blood pressure is high.

body.heading: Does high blood pressure cause symptoms?
body.body:
Usually not. The NHS says high blood pressure often has no symptoms, so many people do not know they have it, and the only way to find out is to have it measured. Rarely it can cause headaches, blurred vision or chest pain.

Over time, the NHS says, untreated high blood pressure raises the chance of problems such as stroke and heart disease.

body.heading: What causes it?
body.body:
For most people there is no obvious cause, which is called essential hypertension, and it can run in families. In a small number of people there is an underlying cause, such as a kidney or adrenal gland condition.

The NHS says risk rises with age, with Black African or Black Caribbean ethnicity, and with a family history. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, being overweight and not being active are also linked.

The NHS advises calling NHS 111 for frequent headaches or blurred vision, chest pain that comes and goes, or other symptoms thought to come from high blood pressure.

body.heading: How is the diagnosis confirmed?
body.body:
A single clinic reading is usually followed by other checks. NICE advises confirming raised clinic readings with home monitoring or with a 24-hour ambulatory monitor, which takes readings through the day.

Some people have higher readings in a clinic than at home, sometimes called the white coat effect, which is one reason these extra checks are used. A GP may also arrange blood and urine tests and an ECG, which checks the heart rhythm.

A reading taken in a clinic is less accurate than home or ambulatory readings and is not enough on its own to diagnose high blood pressure.

body.heading: What does treatment involve?
body.body:
Lifestyle changes come first for many people. The NHS lists cutting down on salt and alcohol, being more physically active, losing weight where needed, and stopping smoking.

A GP will usually prescribe medicine if blood pressure is very high, if the person has a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, or if it stays high after lifestyle changes. Several types are used, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, calcium channel blockers and diuretics, and the choice depends on things such as age and ethnicity.

Some people need to take blood pressure medicine long term, though if blood pressure stays under control for several years it may be possible to cut back or stop treatment.

Most blood pressure medicines are taken as tablets.

Making lifestyle changes early on may mean some people can avoid needing medicine.

Water tablets (diuretics) work by increasing the amount of salt the kidneys remove.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 for sudden chest pain that does not go away, or chest pain with sweating, sickness, light-headedness or breathlessness, as it could be a heart attack.

NHS guidance for pharmacy staff says a very high clinic reading together with symptoms such as headache, palpitations, new confusion or chest pain should be referred to A&E, using 999 where necessary.

high-crp-what-it-means.name: High CRP: what it means and what happens next
high-crp-what-it-means.summary: A high CRP means there is inflammation or infection somewhere in the body, but not where or why, so doctors read it with symptoms and other tests.
keyPoints: A high CRP shows that inflammation or infection is likely, but it does not show where it is or what is causing it.
CRP is a protein made by the liver that rises after tissue injury, infection or other inflammation.
Doctors read the result together with symptoms, an examination and other tests, and often repeat it to see which way it is going.
A high CRP can have causes that are not diseases, such as later pregnancy, the contraceptive pill or hormone replacement therapy.
The laboratory report shows the reference range used, and ranges differ between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a CRP test measure?
body.body:
CRP stands for C-reactive protein, a protein that the liver makes. Its level in the blood rises when there is inflammation somewhere in the body. Tissue injury, infection and other kinds of inflammation can all push the level up.

Doctors usually request the test when they suspect an infection or inflammation, for example after surgery. It is also used to help assess long-term inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis and lupus. The sample is taken from a vein, and the sources list no special preparation.

body.heading: What does a high CRP mean?
body.body:
A high or rising CRP suggests that there is an acute infection or inflammation. It does not show where the inflammation is or which condition is causing it. For that reason the test is not diagnostic on its own. Lab Tests Online UK adds that CRP is not specific for bacterial infection and is raised in many other conditions as well.

A small rise is hard to interpret by itself, so doctors consider it alongside the whole clinical picture. In someone who already has a long-term inflammatory condition, a high level can point to a flare-up or to treatment that is not working. The cause of a high CRP cannot always be found.

body.heading: Which conditions can raise CRP?
body.body: MedlinePlus lists cancer, heart attack, infection, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and related diseases, and rheumatic fever among the conditions that can raise CRP. Not every cause is an illness. CRP can be higher in the later stages of pregnancy, in women who use the contraceptive pill and in women who take hormone replacement therapy. Lab Tests Online UK also links obesity with higher levels. StatPearls describes smoking, diabetes and other long-term conditions as associated with low-grade inflammation that can raise CRP.

body.heading: What happens after a high CRP result?
body.body:
The doctor reads the result alongside signs and symptoms, a physical examination and other tests. That can help show whether someone has an acute inflammatory condition or a flare-up of a long-term one. The doctor may then arrange further tests or treatment.

The test is often repeated to follow progress, because CRP falls as inflammation settles. A falling level suggests that the inflammation is easing. Lab Tests Online UK says results from a test requested by a GP take about seven working days on average to come back from the hospital. A CRP result does not say how urgent an illness is, so severe symptoms such as sudden chest pain or collapse need a 999 call, and feeling more and more unwell needs NHS 111 or the GP the same day.

body.heading: Is hs-CRP the same test?
body.body: High-sensitivity CRP, or hs-CRP, is a separate and more sensitive version of the test. It has been used to estimate the risk of heart disease in people who seem healthy. Lab Tests Online UK notes that current UK guidelines on cardiovascular risk assessment do not recommend hs-CRP testing.

body.heading: Can medicines or other factors change the result?
body.body: StatPearls states that some medicines, including non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and statins, can lower CRP. Long-term conditions linked with low-grade inflammation can lift it. Because of these influences, a single value is rarely read on its own.

body.heading: Where else is CRP used?
body.body: Regional NHS guidance on suspected giant cell arteritis, an inflammation of blood vessels, asks for a CRP before steroids are started. NHS 111 Wales says that if both ESR and CRP are normal, it is unlikely that polymyalgia rheumatica will be diagnosed. During follow-up of polymyalgia rheumatica, blood tests can check the level of inflammation in the body. NHS Tayside referral guidance asks for a CRP and an anti-CCP antibody test, with hand and foot X-rays, when rheumatoid arthritis is suspected. It advises referral for persistent symptoms even when CRP is normal and antibodies are negative. Lab Tests Online UK adds that CRP is used to monitor people after surgery or other invasive procedures for signs of infection during recovery.

high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.name: High white blood cell count: what it means
high-white-blood-cell-count-causes.summary: A high white blood cell count is a non-specific sign, most often from infection, and doctors read it with the type of cell raised.
keyPoints: A high white cell count can be caused by infection, inflammation, some medicines, stress or smoking, and less often by a blood disorder.
The differential count shows which type of white cell is raised, which helps narrow down the cause.
A mild, lasting rise is often linked to chronic inflammation, infection or smoking, while an unexplained very high count leads to urgent referral to haematology.
A single high count does not diagnose anything, and doctors may repeat the test.

body.heading: What does the full blood count measure?
body.body: NHS inform says a full blood count checks the types and numbers of cells in the blood, including red cells, white cells and platelets. The test gives a total white cell count and a differential that splits white cells into types. Those types include neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils. Neutrophils are the main defence against bacterial infection.

body.heading: What does a high white cell count mean?
body.body: A raised count is a non-specific signal, which means it does not point to one cause. A high count can indicate infection, inflammation, or leukaemia and other blood disorders. Infection, most often bacterial infection, is the most common cause. Results vary with age and time of day, and older people sometimes do not show a raised count even when they have an infection.

body.heading: What else can raise it?
body.body: Inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis can raise the count, and so can allergies. Some medicines, for example corticosteroids, can raise it. Tissue damage such as burns can raise it. Severe physical or emotional stress, for example from an injury or surgery, can raise it. Smoking and pregnancy can also raise the count.

body.heading: What does the differential add?
body.body: A high neutrophil count usually suggests bacterial infection, inflammation or physical stress on the body. A high lymphocyte count can occur with viral infections or with conditions such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia. Leukaemia and Hodgkin disease can cause persistently high counts, which is why doctors follow up unexplained rises.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A hospital guideline from Hampshire says a mild, lasting rise is likely to come from a chronic inflammatory or infective process, or from smoking. The same guideline says an unexplained, very high count prompts an urgent referral to haematology. Doctors read the count with symptoms, the differential and sometimes a repeat test or a blood film. Reference ranges differ with age, sex and laboratory, so the report shows the range used. Feeling unwell with a fever is a reason to contact NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and severe breathing difficulty or collapse needs a 999 call.

body.heading: When might a blood disorder be considered?
body.body: A GP may order a blood test if leukaemia is suspected, and a very high number of abnormal white cells can point towards it. In that case the person is referred urgently to a specialist in blood conditions, called a haematologist. Symptoms listed by the NHS across leukaemia types include tiredness, bleeding or bruising easily, night sweats, weight loss and frequent infections. The NHS stresses that having these symptoms does not mean someone has leukaemia, and that many are caused by more common conditions. For chronic myeloid leukaemia the NHS advises a non-urgent GP visit if symptoms appear.

how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.name: How long antidepressants take to work
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.headline: How long antidepressants take to work, and what the NHS says about side effects and stopping
how-long-antidepressants-take-to-work.summary: The NHS says antidepressants usually start to help after 1 to 2 weeks and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
keyPoints: The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect and can take up to 8 weeks to work fully.
For sertraline and citalopram the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, with some people feeling better after 1 to 2 weeks.
Early side effects such as feeling sick, headaches and trouble sleeping are common, and the NHS says they usually ease after a couple of weeks.
The NHS and NICE both say that stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so changes to the dose are decided with the prescriber.
If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 (free, any time) are other routes.

body.heading: How long do antidepressants take to work?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants usually take 1 to 2 weeks to start having an effect. They can take up to 8 weeks to work fully. For sertraline, the NHS says it usually takes 4 to 6 weeks to work fully, although some people start to feel better after 1 to 2 weeks. For citalopram, the NHS gives the same pattern, with a usual 4 to 6 weeks before the full benefit and some improvement possible after 1 to 2 weeks.

Both medicines belong to a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs. For citalopram, the NHS advises against stopping after only 1 or 2 weeks just because it seems not to be helping, since the full benefit takes longer to appear.

body.heading: What can happen in the first weeks?
body.body:
The NHS lists nausea, headaches and diarrhoea among the common side effects of sertraline. It also lists dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth and sleep problems. For citalopram, common effects include tiredness, feeling nervous, dry mouth and sweating. The NHS says common side effects like these are usually mild and go away after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine.

The NHS lists sexual problems, such as a lower sex drive, among the common side effects of citalopram. Sertraline can make a person feel more or less hungry than usual, so weight may go down or up at the start, the NHS says. The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol with sertraline because it can stop the medicine working properly. It also says grapefruit juice can increase the amount of sertraline in the body and the risk of side effects.

If side effects last beyond 1 or 2 weeks, the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor about them.

body.heading: What if nothing seems to change?
body.body: The NHS says a GP may recommend trying a different antidepressant if the first one is not helping. People respond differently to different antidepressants, so a change of medicine can sometimes help. Anyone worried about their progress can raise it with a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Why is stopping suddenly a question for the prescriber?
body.body:
The NHS says antidepressants should not be stopped suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms. For citalopram, the NHS says the doctor will usually recommend reducing the dose gradually over several weeks, or longer after a long course. For sertraline, the NHS says stopping is usually done by reducing the dose gradually.

NICE says reducing the dose in stages, known as tapering, helps to lessen withdrawal effects, and that the taper is agreed with the person's healthcare professional. NICE guidance for adults with depression also says people who want to stop should talk to the person who prescribed the medicine. Tapering is typically needed, and most people manage to stop successfully. The NHS adds that stopping too early can make depression come back.

body.heading: How long does treatment usually last?
body.body: The NHS says a course of antidepressants usually lasts for at least 6 months after a person starts to feel better. For citalopram, the NHS says most doctors recommend taking antidepressants for 6 months to a year. For sertraline, the NHS says most doctors recommend treatment for 6 months to a year after a person no longer feels depressed. The decision to stop or continue depends on symptoms and how well the medicine is working, and is made with the prescriber.

body.heading: Where can someone get help in a crisis?
body.body: If a person or someone else is in immediate danger, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option. Samaritans can be called free on 116 123 at any time of the day or night. In England, adults aged 18 or over can refer themselves directly to NHS talking therapies without a GP referral. These services are for anxiety and depression and are not for urgent crisis help.

references.title: NHS: How and when to take sertraline
NHS: Urgent support, Every Mind Matters
