ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.name: Ibuprofen and paracetamol together: NHS view
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.headline: Can you take ibuprofen and paracetamol together? What the NHS says
ibuprofen-and-paracetamol-together.summary: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen together if needed, but children should not be given them at the same time.
keyPoints: The NHS says adults can take paracetamol and ibuprofen at the same time if needed, and NHS inform says the two can be taken together if required.
For children, the NHS says paracetamol and ibuprofen should not be given at the same time but one at a time.
The NHS lists groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check first, including people with repeated stomach ulcers or bleeding, asthma, or severe kidney failure.
Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen, so using several products can make it easy to take more than the recommended amount.
The NHS says to call 999 for signs of a serious allergic reaction, and to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor for other serious effects such as stomach bleeding or kidney problems.

body.heading: What is each medicine used for?
body.body: Ibuprofen belongs to a group of painkillers called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or NSAIDs. The NHS describes ibuprofen as a painkiller that also treats inflammation. It describes paracetamol as a painkiller for pain and high temperature. For a dental abscess, NHS inform says ibuprofen is the preferred painkiller, and paracetamol can be taken instead if ibuprofen cannot be taken for medical reasons. The NHS also says that if you need pain relief while taking warfarin, paracetamol is the one to take instead of ibuprofen.

body.heading: Can adults take both at the same time?
body.body: For adults, the NHS says paracetamol can be taken at the same time as ibuprofen if needed. It also says paracetamol can be taken with other painkillers that do not contain paracetamol, such as ibuprofen, aspirin or codeine. NHS inform, the NHS information service for Scotland, also says the two can be taken together if required. For a dental abscess, it says that if one painkiller does not work, taking both paracetamol and ibuprofen may help. The advice is different for children. For them, the NHS says paracetamol can be given alongside ibuprofen but not at the same time, and the two should be given one at a time.

body.heading: Who is told to check with a pharmacist or doctor first?
body.body: The NHS lists several groups who should avoid ibuprofen or check with a professional before using it. These include people who have had an allergic reaction to aspirin or other NSAIDs, with signs such as wheezing, a runny nose or skin reactions. They also include people who have had a hole in the stomach, bleeding in the stomach or a stomach ulcer more than once, and people with severe heart, kidney or liver failure. Asthma, hay fever and allergies are also on the NHS list. The NHS also says to avoid ibuprofen in pregnancy unless a doctor or pharmacist advises it, and to check with a pharmacist or doctor when breastfeeding. People over 65 are more likely to get stomach ulcers with ibuprofen, according to the NHS. Other medicines can interact with ibuprofen. The NHS interactions page lists warfarin and other anticoagulants, medicines for high blood pressure, steroids such as prednisolone, certain antibiotics and some antidepressants. It advises against taking ginkgo biloba with ibuprofen because it can increase the chance of bleeding. For other herbal products, it says there is not enough information to say whether they can be taken with ibuprofen. NHS inform advises anyone already taking other medication to check with a pharmacist first.

body.heading: Why do other products containing the same ingredients matter?
body.body: Many cold and flu products contain paracetamol or ibuprofen. NHS inform says this makes it easy to take more than the recommended dose. The NHS says to avoid taking other medicines that contain paracetamol at the same time as paracetamol, such as cold and flu remedies, because too much can be dangerous. It adds that taking two different medicines that contain paracetamol carries a risk of overdose, and that too much paracetamol can sometimes damage the liver. For ibuprofen, the NHS says to check the label of cold and cough remedies for aspirin, ibuprofen or other NSAIDs. Taking ibuprofen with other NSAIDs such as aspirin or naproxen is not advised without speaking to a pharmacist or doctor, because side effects such as stomach ache become more likely.

body.heading: What side effects do the NHS pages describe?
body.body: The NHS lists common side effects of ibuprofen as indigestion, stomach aches, feeling sick, being sick and headaches. Serious ones include stomach ulcers or bleeding in the stomach, and allergic reactions. The NHS also lists kidney problems, such as swollen ankles or blood in the urine, as a reason to get urgent advice. For paracetamol, the NHS says there may be no obvious symptoms at first after taking too much, so feeling well does not rule out harm.

body.heading: When should someone get help, and from whom?
body.body: For signs of a serious allergic reaction to ibuprofen, such as swollen lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or difficult breathing or a tight throat, the NHS says to call 999. The NHS also says to call 999 for severe chest or stomach pain, which can signal a hole in the stomach or gut, and for difficulty breathing or worsening asthma symptoms. Vomiting blood or black, tar-like poo can be signs of bleeding in the stomach, and the NHS says to get urgent advice from NHS 111 or a doctor. Swollen ankles or blood in the urine can point to a kidney problem, and the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a doctor. If too much paracetamol has been taken, the NHS says to contact NHS 111 for advice, even when the person feels well. For questions that are not urgent, NHS inform says to speak to a pharmacist if unsure.

inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.name: INR blood test and warfarin explained
inr-blood-test-warfarin-explained.summary: The INR blood test shows how long blood takes to clot, and it is how the effect of warfarin is monitored so the dose can be adjusted.
keyPoints: The INR measures how long the blood takes to clot, and it is the main way warfarin treatment is monitored.
Warfarin has no fixed dose, so the dose is adjusted from INR results by an anticoagulation clinic.
New medicines, alcohol and diet can change the INR.
The main side effect of warfarin is bleeding, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, and 999 for bleeding that will not stop.

body.heading: What does the INR measure?
body.body: INR stands for international normalised ratio. It is a standard blood test that measures how long the blood takes to clot. One NHS trust explains that it compares the clotting time of a person taking warfarin with that of someone who is not.

body.heading: Why is the INR checked on warfarin?
body.body: Warfarin does not have a fixed dose. The dose needed depends on how much the medicine slows the clotting of the blood, and the INR test measures that effect. The main side effect of warfarin is an increased risk of bleeding, and the risk is highest when the INR is too high.

body.heading: How often is it done?
body.body: At the start, testing is frequent. Once the result is stable, the gaps between tests lengthen. Some people need tests more regularly than others. The INR results go to the warfarin clinic, which advises on the ongoing dose and the date of the next test.

body.heading: What can change the INR?
body.body: New medicines can change the effect of warfarin, so one NHS service asks for an INR test soon after any new medicine is started or stopped. Alcohol, diet and other medicines can also move the result. Sources name cranberry and grapefruit juice and binge drinking as able to raise the INR. They also name ibuprofen and similar painkillers as able to increase the risk of bleeding.

body.heading: What should people know about bleeding?
body.body: Signs of bleeding include bleeding gums, blood in vomit, blood in urine or stool, and prolonged bleeding from small cuts. For women, heavier periods can be a sign. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if there are symptoms of bleeding or other serious side effects. The British Heart Foundation says to call NHS 111 or the GP when worried about bleeding, and 999 if bleeding after an injury cannot be stopped. NHS inform says to phone 999 or go to A&E when bleeding cannot be stopped, and it lists coughing or vomiting blood among the signs. A blow to the head counts as an emergency even without visible bleeding.

body.heading: What else do people on warfarin carry or watch?
body.body: People on warfarin are given an anticoagulant alert card to carry. The card lets medical staff identify that someone takes warfarin if there is an accident. Foods high in vitamin K, such as leafy green vegetables, can affect how warfarin works. Dietary advice from an NHS trust stresses eating a steady amount of such foods, because the clinic adjusts the dose to match. The NHS says the food and drink restrictions do not usually apply to the newer anticoagulants such as apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran.

joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.name: Joint pain: causes and when to see a GP
joint-pain-causes-and-when-to-see-a-gp.summary: Joint pain has many causes, including osteoarthritis, injury and gout, and the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for a hot, swollen joint with a fever.
keyPoints: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers.
The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly.

body.heading: What causes joint pain?
body.body: Gout is a form of arthritis in which small crystals form inside and around the joints. Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system targets the joints, with stiffness that is often worse in the morning or after a period of inactivity. The NHS says rheumatoid arthritis is usually first felt in the small joints of the hands and feet. The NHS arthritis overview says gout often affects the big toe joint, which can become painful, swollen and hot. Psoriatic arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness and swelling, and is linked with the skin condition psoriasis, which causes a red, scaly rash.

body.heading: What can ease joint pain at home?
body.body: The NHS says to rest the joint but not stop moving it altogether, and that a pharmacist or GP can advise about painkillers. NHS 111 Wales says being overweight often makes osteoarthritis worse, because it puts extra strain on some joints. NHS 111 Wales describes exercise as one of the most important treatments for osteoarthritis, and says hot or cold packs can relieve symptoms in some people. NHS 111 Wales says osteoarthritis has no cure but does not necessarily get worse over time.

body.heading: When is a GP appointment sensible?
body.body: The NHS suggests a GP appointment if joint pain stops normal activities or affects sleep, keeps getting worse or coming back, or has not improved after 2 weeks of treating it at home. It also lists joints that stay stiff for more than 30 minutes after waking. For gout, the NHS advises seeing a GP for a first episode, or when the usual treatments are not helping.

body.heading: Which joint pain needs urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for severe pain and swelling in one joint that started suddenly. A warm, swollen joint that is hard to move, with a high temperature or feeling hot and shivery, may mean a joint infection called septic arthritis.

body.heading: How is the cause found?
body.body: A GP examines the joints for swelling, checks how easily they move and asks about symptoms. Blood tests such as ESR, CRP and a full blood count may be used, and X-rays or MRI scans may show inflammation and damage. No blood test can definitively prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, although several tests can show signs of it. If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP usually refers the person to a rheumatologist. A rheumatologist is a doctor who specialises in conditions of the joints and immune system.

kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.name: Kidney stones: symptoms and treatment
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.headline: Kidney stones: symptoms, how they are diagnosed and how they are treated
kidney-stones-symptoms-and-treatment.summary: Kidney stones form when chemicals in urine build up; small ones may cause no symptoms, while larger ones can cause severe pain, and some may need a procedure.
keyPoints: Kidney stones form when chemicals from urine build up in the kidneys, and small stones may cause no symptoms.
Larger stones can cause severe pain that comes and goes, sometimes with nausea or blood in the urine.
A GP can often diagnose kidney stones from symptoms and history, with urine and blood tests and sometimes a scan.
Most stones can be treated at home with medicines and plenty of fluids; larger stones may need to be broken up or removed.
Severe pain, a high temperature or feeling hot, cold or shivery needs urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP.

body.heading: What are kidney stones?
body.body:
Kidney stones are hard lumps that form in the kidneys. The NHS says they are caused by chemicals from urine building up in the kidneys.

Small stones often cause no symptoms and may pass unnoticed.

body.heading: What symptoms can they cause?
body.body:
Larger stones can cause severe pain. It can come and go in waves.

Other symptoms can include nausea or vomiting, blood in the urine, sweating, a high temperature and a urine infection.

body.heading: What causes them?
body.body:
The NHS says kidney stones can be caused by dehydration, by some medicines, and by some medical conditions. Not drinking enough water raises the chance of getting one.

Other things that raise the risk include a diet high in protein and low in fibre, being inactive or bed-bound, repeated kidney or urine infections, and a close family member who has had stones.

body.heading: How are kidney stones diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP can usually diagnose kidney stones from the symptoms and medical history. Urine and blood tests may be used.

If the pain is severe, the NHS says the person may be referred to hospital for a scan. If a scan is needed, the NHS says adults have a CT scan, while pregnant women and children under 16 have an ultrasound scan.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
Most kidney stones can be treated at home. The NHS says this usually means painkillers, anti-sickness medicine, medicines that help a stone pass, and drinking plenty of water.

Larger stones may need to be broken up or removed. One option is shockwave lithotripsy, where shock waves are aimed at the stone to break it up. Other procedures use a thin scope to reach the stone.

body.heading: When should someone get urgent help?
body.body:
The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 for anyone with kidney stone symptoms who is in severe pain, or has a high temperature, or feels hot, cold or shivery.

A high temperature can be a sign of infection, so it needs prompt advice from a GP or NHS 111. Hospital leaflets advise A&E for anyone who cannot pass urine, and 999 in an emergency.

Hospital leaflets also advise A&E when pain is not controlled by painkillers.

Signs of infection with a stone can include a high temperature, burning when passing urine, and feeling tired or unwell.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Shockwave lithotripsy can be uncomfortable, so painkillers are usually given first, and more than one session may be needed. In ureteroscopy, a thin telescope is passed through the urethra and bladder into the ureter, and it is done under general anaesthetic.

knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.name: Knee pain: causes and when to get help
knee-pain-causes-self-care-and-when-to-a.summary: Knee pain can often be treated at home, and NHS 111 is the route for a badly swollen knee or a hot, red knee with a high temperature.
keyPoints: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease.
The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks.
The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

body.heading: What causes knee pain?
body.body: The NHS knee pain page lists causes including sprains and strains, tendonitis, torn ligaments, tendons or meniscus, a dislocated kneecap, bursitis, gout and Osgood-Schlatter's disease. The NHS knee pain page links sprains and strains to overstretching, overusing or twisting the knee, often during exercise. An NHS trust leaflet lists pain, stiffness after rest and swelling as symptoms of osteoarthritis. NHS inform says the exact cause of knee osteoarthritis is unclear, and risk factors include ageing, a previous knee injury, being overweight and family history. An NHS trust page says changes seen on an X-ray do not necessarily match how bad the symptoms are. NHS inform says strengthening the muscles around the knee helps manage osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What can ease it at home?
body.body: The NHS says knee pain can often be treated at home by reducing weight on the knee, using an ice pack and taking painkillers such as paracetamol or ibuprofen.

body.heading: When should knee pain be seen by a GP or physiotherapist?
body.body: Hampshire and Isle of Wight NHS guidance suggests seeing a GP if knee pain has not eased within a few weeks. The NHS says people may be able to refer themselves to community musculoskeletal (MSK) physiotherapy services without seeing a GP. An NHS trust leaflet describes physiotherapy as the mainstay of treatment for pain at the front of the knee. An NHS trust leaflet on hip and knee osteoarthritis describes regular exercise, over-the-counter pain relief and losing a small amount of body fat.

body.heading: Which signs need urgent help?
body.body: The NHS advises calling NHS 111 if the knee is badly swollen or has changed shape, or if there is a very high temperature with redness or heat around the knee, which can signal infection.

levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.name: Levothyroxine: timing and other medicines
levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.headline: Levothyroxine: why timing and other medicines matter, as the NHS describes
levothyroxine-timing-and-other-medicines.summary: The NHS says levothyroxine replaces a missing thyroid hormone and is taken at the same time each day on an empty stomach.
keyPoints: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid that replaces a hormone the body is not making enough of.
The NHS says it is taken at the same time each day, on an empty stomach, before the first meal, any caffeinated drink or other medicines.
MedlinePlus, a US source, says calcium, iron, multivitamins and some antacids are best spaced apart from thyroid medicine.
The NHS says regular blood tests continue until the right amount is reached, then usually once a year.
The NHS says treatment is usually lifelong, and both the NHS and MedlinePlus say not to stop without medical advice.

body.heading: What does levothyroxine replace?
body.body: The NHS describes levothyroxine as a medicine for an underactive thyroid, also called hypothyroidism. The NHS says an underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. It explains that the tablets simply replace a hormone that is missing, which is why they do not usually cause side effects. The NHS also says that in the UK, combining levothyroxine with a second thyroid hormone, T3, is not routinely used because there is not enough evidence that it works better than levothyroxine alone.

body.heading: Why does the NHS say to take it at a consistent time?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine is usually taken once a day, at the same time each day. It also says the tablet is taken on an empty stomach, before the first meal of the day, any drink with caffeine such as tea or coffee, or any other medicine, and swallowed with water. NHS inform Scotland says the morning is usually recommended, though some people prefer night. MedlinePlus, a US source, says thyroid medicine works best on an empty stomach and suggests asking a provider whether bedtime suits. A systematic review of studies, published in a journal and held on PubMed Central, reported that morning and bedtime dosing were equally effective. The NHS says that for a forgotten tablet, take it when remembered unless the next one is nearly due, and do not take two together to make up.

body.heading: How can food, coffee and other medicines affect it?
body.body: The NHS says other medicines, supplements and foods can affect how well levothyroxine is absorbed, which is why it is taken before food, caffeinated drinks and other medicines. A systematic review on PubMed Central, Levothyroxine Interactions with Food and Dietary Supplements, found that coffee, soy products, fibre, calcium or iron supplements and enteral nutrition all decreased absorption, although the evidence was limited. It reported that keeping a gap between levothyroxine and these products is one way to avoid the problem. MedlinePlus, a US source, lists fibre supplements, calcium, iron, multivitamins, aluminium hydroxide antacids and bile-acid binding medicines as products to space apart from thyroid hormone. NHS trust leaflets also advise against taking calcium or iron at the same time. Sources differ on the gap needed, so a pharmacist or the prescriber can advise for one person, using the leaflet in the pack.

body.heading: Why are regular blood tests needed?
body.body: The NHS says a person starts on a low amount that is adjusted over time, with regular blood tests until the right amount of levothyroxine has been reached. It says that once the amount is right, a blood test is usually done once a year to monitor hormone levels. MedlinePlus, a US source, also says hormone levels are checked at the start and then at least once a year. The NHS advises telling the GP when pregnant or planning to be, because further tests are needed and the amount of levothyroxine is likely to need changing.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping?
body.body: The NHS says to keep taking the medicine unless advised to stop. It says an underactive thyroid is a lifelong condition, so people usually need levothyroxine for the rest of their lives. MedlinePlus, a US source, says to keep taking it even when feeling well and not to stop without talking to a doctor. A pharmacist or GP is the usual route for questions about changes to treatment.

body.heading: What side effects can happen, and who can advise?
body.body: The NHS says levothyroxine does not usually have side effects, because the tablets replace a missing hormone. It says most side effects happen when the amount is too high, and they often improve once the amount is changed. Effects listed include trouble sleeping, headaches, feeling anxious, sweating and hair loss, and too much can also bring chest pain, diarrhoea and being sick. The NHS says serious side effects are rare and names an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), with a swollen throat or tongue, a raised itchy rash or difficulty breathing, and thyroid crisis, with a high temperature, a fast or irregular heartbeat, dizziness or faintness, or jaundice. The NHS page says to call NHS 111 when someone taking levothyroxine thinks they might be having serious side effects. For other side effects, the NHS says to speak to a doctor or pharmacist. If more than the prescribed amount has been taken, the NHS says to speak to a pharmacist as soon as possible, and to call NHS 111 if one cannot be reached or it was done on purpose.

liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.name: Liver blood tests: what the results mean
liver-function-tests-what-results-mean.summary: Liver blood tests point towards a possible problem but cannot name the cause, and abnormal results are common and often not serious.
keyPoints: Liver blood tests, once called liver function tests, are a group of tests that include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin.
A result outside the reference range does not always mean liver disease, and a normal result does not always rule it out.
The pattern of results helps point towards liver cell injury or a problem with bile flow.
Yellowing of the skin or eyes needs an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111, according to the NHS.

body.heading: What are liver blood tests?
body.body: Liver blood tests are a group of blood tests, once known as liver function tests or LFTs. They usually include ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin. They are often done as routine tests, so abnormal results are sometimes found by chance when blood is taken for another reason.

body.heading: What do ALT and AST show?
body.body: ALT and AST are enzymes that leak into the blood when liver cells are injured. ALT is more specific to the liver, while AST can also be high when muscle is damaged elsewhere in the body. Common causes of this pattern include viral hepatitis, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, alcohol-related liver disease, autoimmune hepatitis and drug-induced liver injury.

body.heading: What do ALP, GGT, bilirubin and albumin show?
body.body: Raised ALP and GGT point towards a problem with the flow of bile. Causes include blocked bile ducts, for example by stones, and some long-term diseases of the bile ducts. ALP also comes from bone, so GGT helps to show whether the liver is the source. Raised bilirubin causes jaundice, a yellowing of the eyes and skin. Bilirubin can also be raised without liver disease, as in Gilbert's syndrome, where the other liver tests are normal. Albumin is affected only when liver disease is at a severe stage, and low albumin also has other causes such as malnutrition, kidney protein loss and inflammation.

body.heading: Does an abnormal result mean liver disease?
body.body: Abnormal results can occur in conditions that do not involve the liver, and normal results can be found in people with serious liver disease. The British Liver Trust says it is quite common to get a result that is not normal, and this does not always mean a liver condition. It adds that the liver can take a lot of damage before it causes problems, so a normal result is a good sign but not a guarantee. Illness, shock, burns, injury, severe exercise, pregnancy and a reaction to medicines can all change one or more of the tests. Sometimes a repeat test is all that is needed.

body.heading: What happens after an abnormal result?
body.body: Laboratories compare each result with their own range, so results are compared only with the range of the laboratory that did the test. If the results suggest a liver problem, a GP may calculate a FIB-4 index, which gives an indication of the amount of scarring in the liver. People at high risk of liver disease, or with symptoms, are referred or have more tests. Further tests can look for the cause, such as viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease or an effect of alcohol or medicines.

body.heading: When is yellowing of the skin urgent?
body.body: The NHS says jaundice can be a sign of something serious such as liver disease. It advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or contacting NHS 111 when the skin or whites of the eyes look yellow. On brown or black skin the yellow colour is easier to see in the whites of the eyes. Itchy skin, darker urine and paler stools can come with it.

body.heading: What are fatty liver and alcohol-related liver disease?
body.body: NHS guidance names non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, in some pathways now called MASLD, as a common cause of abnormal liver tests. NHS inform says the mainstay of care for non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is lifestyle advice to reduce weight and increase physical activity. It adds that there is currently no specific medicine for it. Where alcohol is the cause, one pathway advises cutting out alcohol and repeating the test after a month. Local guidance suggests repeating the tests after reviewing medicines or a recent illness before moving on to scans. If results stay abnormal, guidance supports an ultrasound scan of the liver and bile ducts and blood tests for viral and autoimmune causes. A standard ultrasound does not assess scarring, so another scan may be needed. Jaundice, weight loss, a swollen abdomen, confusion, bleeding or a low albumin warrant urgent referral, according to local NHS guidance.

loneliness-and-health.name: Loneliness and health: effects and what helps
loneliness-and-health.summary: Severe or long-lasting loneliness can affect mental and physical health, according to the NHS. Staying in touch, joining groups and asking a GP about social prescribing can help.
keyPoints: The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia, and of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression.
Regular contact with friends and family, joining a group or club, and volunteering are NHS suggestions for easing loneliness.
A GP can talk about social prescribing, which links people with a link worker for local support.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is loneliness, and is it a health issue?
body.body: Loneliness is the distress of feeling alone or disconnected, and it is not the same as spending time by yourself. The NHS says severe or long-lasting loneliness might increase the risk of some physical conditions, such as dementia. It also says it might increase the risk of mental health conditions such as stress, anxiety, low mood or depression. Common triggers include bereavement, a break-up, moving away, becoming a parent or carer, and long-term illness.

body.heading: What helps with loneliness?
body.body: NHS suggestions include keeping in touch with friends and family. The NHS also suggests joining a group, for example around something you enjoy. Volunteering is another NHS suggestion. The NHS also suggests doing activities you enjoy. The NHS also suggests talking openly about how loneliness feels, and notes that comparing yourself with others, especially on social media, can make you feel lonelier. For older people, the NHS suggests keeping in touch by phone or video chat, and volunteering.

body.heading: What can a GP or the NHS offer?
body.body: The NHS suggests speaking to a GP about social prescribing, which connects people with a link worker who can point to local support. NHS talking therapies can help with common problems such as stress, anxiety and depression. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to cope with loneliness, because they can contribute to poor mental health. The NHS says a GP can help if low mood lasts or if things tried at home are not helping.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If loneliness feels overwhelming, free support lines are open at any time of day or night. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS advice is to call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), open at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

low-ferritin-what-it-means.name: Low ferritin: what it means and what next
low-ferritin-what-it-means.summary: A low ferritin level means the body's iron stores are low, and doctors then look for the cause, which is often blood loss.
keyPoints: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, so a low level means there is not much iron in store.
Ferritin can fall before blood iron levels fall, which makes it the most sensitive early marker of iron deficiency.
Iron deficiency is often caused by blood loss or pregnancy, so doctors look for the source.
Inflammation, infection and liver disease can raise ferritin, so it is often read alongside CRP.
The report shows the reference range used by the laboratory, which differs between laboratories.

body.heading: What does a ferritin test measure?
body.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron in the body. The test estimates how much iron is held in store. Doctors order it when they suspect the body has too little or too much iron, and it is most often requested for suspected low iron. Lab Tests Online UK calls it the most sensitive early marker of iron deficiency.

body.heading: What does a low ferritin level mean?
body.body: A low ferritin points to iron deficiency. The NHS explains that when ferritin is low, there is not much iron stored in the body. Stores can drop well below normal before the iron level in the blood itself falls, so ferritin can show the problem early. Low iron can exist without anaemia, and symptoms such as tiredness can still be present. Ferritin can also fall when protein levels are very low, as in some cases of malnutrition.

body.heading: Why do iron stores run low?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is caused by a lack of iron, often because of blood loss or pregnancy. NHS formulary guidance lists heavy periods, bleeding in the digestive tract, coeliac disease and a poor diet among the causes. It also lists ulcers, medicines such as aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers, and bowel cancer as possible digestive causes, which is why the cause is looked for. Guidance for NHS Scotland says a low ferritin should be investigated for causes such as coeliac disease.

body.heading: What symptoms go with low iron?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness, shortness of breath, noticeable heartbeats and pale skin as common symptoms. Less common symptoms include hair loss, ringing in the ears, itchy skin, a sore tongue and a craving for non-food items. That craving, called pica, can be for items such as ice, paper or clay. The NHS advises seeing a GP when symptoms like these appear, and a GP appointment is the usual route for a ferritin test.

body.heading: Why can a ferritin result be misleading?
body.body: Ferritin is not only a store of iron. Lab Tests Online UK says levels can be high in inflammatory conditions, infection and liver disease. Because inflammation can push ferritin up and hide a shortage of iron, CRP is often checked alongside it. A high ferritin can signal long-term iron overload, especially haemochromatosis, but further investigation is needed before that diagnosis is made.

body.heading: What happens next?
body.body: A GP usually takes a blood test, and ferritin is the key marker of how much iron is stored. If the cause is not clear, the GP may arrange further tests to find the source. Once the cause has been found, such as an ulcer or heavy periods, the GP recommends treatment for it. Iron tablets are the usual first treatment, and the NHS says they are taken for about six months. Side effects of iron tablets, mainly in the digestive system, are common. Iron can also be given by infusion into a vein, which is used less often. Repeat blood tests over the following months check that the iron level is returning to normal.

body.heading: What helps iron stores recover?
body.body: The NHS says iron deficiency anaemia is treated with iron tablets and with iron-rich foods. NHS guidance points to dark green leafy vegetables and dried fruit as food sources. Formulary guidance also lists iron-fortified bread, meat, apricots, prunes and raisins. NHS guidance says drinking orange juice after an iron tablet may help the body absorb the iron. Tea, coffee, milk and dairy foods, and wholegrain cereals can stop the body absorbing iron from other foods and tablets. NHS 111 Wales says iron tablets taken with or soon after food can reduce side effects, and that tablets should be continued even if side effects occur. Somerset formulary guidance adds that treatment continues for some months after the iron level is corrected, so that stores can be replenished. Tablets can cause constipation or diarrhoea, tummy pain, heartburn, nausea and darker stools.

body.heading: What about pregnancy?
body.body: A Scottish maternity guideline states that iron requirements are higher in pregnancy than in women who menstruate. It recommends that women who start oral iron continue it through pregnancy and for some months after the birth.

menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.name: Menopause: symptoms and the help available
menopause-symptoms-and-help-available.summary: HRT is the main medicine for menopause symptoms, and non-hormone options exist. The NHS says a GP can talk through the options, and NICE advises discussing benefits and risks of HRT.
keyPoints: The NHS calls hormone replacement therapy (HRT) the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms.
NICE advises offering HRT for hot flushes and night sweats after discussing the short- and long-term benefits and risks.
Options that do not use hormones include cognitive behavioural therapy and lubricants or moisturisers for vaginal dryness.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of menopause?
body.body: NICE guidance covers hot flushes and night sweats, vaginal and urinary symptoms, and effects on mood. The perimenopause is the time of change before periods stop, and symptoms can begin then. The NHS lists hot flushes, night sweats, low mood or anxiety, mood swings, brain fog, difficulty sleeping and changes to periods. Others include headaches and migraines, joint and muscle pain, weight gain, skin changes and a lower sex drive. The NHS says a person may have a number of symptoms, or none. Menopause is confirmed once a person has had no period for 12 months. The NHS says menopause usually affects people between the ages of 45 and 55, though it can happen earlier.

body.heading: What is HRT?
body.body: The NHS says the main medicine for menopause and perimenopause symptoms is hormone replacement therapy, or HRT. Oestrogen comes as skin patches, a gel or spray, implants or tablets. Anyone who still has a womb also needs a progestogen to protect the womb lining.

body.heading: How soon does treatment work?
body.body: According to the NHS, hot flushes or night sweats often improve within a few weeks. Other symptoms, such as mood changes and vaginal dryness, can take a few months to improve.

body.heading: What are the benefits and risks?
body.body: The NHS says HRT can lower the risk of osteoporosis, the thinning of the bones. Some types of HRT slightly raise the risk of breast cancer, and HRT tablets carry a small increase in the risk of blood clots. Because benefits and risks differ from person to person, the NHS and NICE both describe a discussion with a clinician.

body.heading: What else is available?
body.body: Vaginal oestrogen, as a pessary, cream, gel or ring, can treat vaginal dryness and other genitourinary symptoms of the menopause. For people who cannot or choose not to take HRT, the NHS lists cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), which can help with low mood and anxiety caused by menopause and perimenopause. Vaginal lubricants and moisturisers are also used. The NHS suggests that regular exercise may reduce hot flushes, and that spicy food, caffeine, smoking and alcohol can be triggers.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body: The NHS says people with menopause or perimenopause symptoms can talk to a GP about their options. The NHS advises seeing a GP about any vaginal bleeding after periods have stopped for 12 months or more, even if it has only happened once.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Menopause can affect mood and sleep. If low mood becomes severe or there are thoughts of self-harm, help is available at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

metformin-what-to-expect.name: Metformin: what to expect when starting
metformin-what-to-expect.headline: Metformin: what the NHS says to expect when starting it
metformin-what-to-expect.summary: The NHS describes metformin as usually the first medicine for type 2 diabetes. Side effects are mostly stomach-related and mostly ease.
keyPoints: The NHS says metformin is usually the first medicine prescribed for type 2 diabetes.
Common side effects are stomach-related; the NHS says most ease after a couple of weeks, and taking tablets with a meal or slow-release tablets can help.
The NHS says long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deficiency, so a doctor may check B12 levels.
The NHS says illness with vomiting, diarrhoea or fever risks dehydration, and metformin may need pausing before surgery or scans using dye.
For side effects, a GP or diabetes team can advise; the NHS says call NHS 111 for other serious side effects and 999 for suspected lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis.

body.heading: What is metformin used for?
body.body: The NHS describes metformin as a medicine used to treat type 2 diabetes, and says it is usually the first choice prescribed for it. It can also be prescribed to help improve ovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome, which the NHS pages call PMOS. The NHS says it reduces the amount of sugar the liver releases into the blood and helps the body respond better to insulin. The NHS also says it does not usually cause weight gain.

body.heading: How is metformin taken?
body.body: The NHS says metformin comes as two kinds of tablet: standard tablets and slow-release tablets. Standard tablets act quickly and may be taken several times a day, while slow-release ones work gradually, so they are taken less often. The NHS says the prescriber sets the amount, and that when standard tablets are first started the amount is usually increased slowly, which reduces the chance of side effects. It says it is best to take metformin with, or just after, a meal, and that tablets are swallowed whole with water rather than chewed. For diabetes, the NHS says treatment is usually for life, and that stopping suddenly makes blood sugar levels go up. The prescriber's instructions and the leaflet in the pack remain the guide for any one person.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and do they settle?
body.body: The NHS lists feeling sick, being sick, diarrhoea, tummy pain, loss of appetite and a change in taste among the common side effects. It says most of these should ease after a couple of weeks as the body gets used to the medicine, although some can last longer. The NHS says taking the tablets with a meal and increasing the amount slowly can reduce them. If side effects are too troublesome, it says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets. Diabetes UK also says early stomach-related effects usually settle within a few weeks. For people on standard-release tablets who have these effects, Diabetes UK advises speaking to a GP or diabetes team, who can say whether slow-release tablets might suit them.

body.heading: What about vitamin B12?
body.body: The NHS says that taking metformin for a long time can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, which can leave a person feeling very tired. Diabetes UK likewise says prolonged use, especially at higher doses, can lower vitamin B12 levels, which matter for red blood cells and nerves. The NHS says a doctor can check B12 levels in the blood, and that vitamin B12 supplements help if levels get too low. Diabetes UK says anyone with symptoms of deficiency should ask their diabetes team or GP about a blood test.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about illness, dehydration, alcohol and scans?
body.body: The NHS says that being ill with vomiting, diarrhoea or a high temperature while taking metformin carries a risk of dehydration. On alcohol, the NHS advises limiting how much is drunk while taking metformin, because alcohol can increase the risk of serious side effects, and says drinking more than its suggested limit can raise the risk of low blood sugar. The NHS also says a doctor may tell a person to stop metformin a few days before an operation or medical tests, and that it may need pausing before scans that use iodine-based dye. Anyone unsure what to do when unwell or before a procedure can ask a GP or pharmacist.

body.heading: Who may not be able to take metformin?
body.body: The NHS says most adults and children aged 10 and over can take metformin, but it is not suitable for everyone. Situations to raise with a doctor before starting include a past allergic reaction to metformin or another medicine, uncontrolled diabetes, liver or kidney problems, a severe infection, heart failure treatment or a recent heart attack, and heavy alcohol use. The NHS says metformin can be taken in pregnancy, alone or with insulin, after checking with a doctor, and that it can usually be taken while breastfeeding because only tiny amounts pass into breast milk. It also says there is no evidence that metformin lowers fertility in men or women.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed, or serious symptoms appear?
body.body: The NHS says not to take two doses to make up for a forgotten one. For side effects that are troublesome, the NHS says a doctor may suggest slow-release tablets, and Diabetes UK points people to a GP or diabetes team. The NHS describes serious side effects as uncommon and lists lactic acidosis (too much acid in the blood), anaphylaxis (a severe allergic reaction) and liver inflammation (hepatitis). It says to call 999 if lactic acidosis or anaphylaxis is suspected, and to call NHS 111 for any other serious side effect. NHS 111 is also the NHS route if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.

mhra-approves-lurbinectedin-small-cell-l.name: MHRA approves lurbinectedin for lung cancer
mhra-approves-lurbinectedin-small-cell-l.summary: The MHRA approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) on 23 September 2026 for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, as maintenance treatment with atezolizumab.
keyPoints: The MHRA approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) on 23 September 2026 for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer.
It is approved in combination with atezolizumab as maintenance treatment.
The MHRA says it will keep the safety and effectiveness of lurbinectedin under close review.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA says it has approved lurbinectedin (Zepzelca) for adults with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. It is approved in combination with atezolizumab as maintenance treatment, for adults whose cancer has not progressed after first-line induction treatment with atezolizumab, carboplatin and etoposide.

The MHRA describes a main study of 483 adults with extensive-stage disease.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The MHRA explains that lurbinectedin attaches to DNA inside cancer cells, which damages it and blocks cell growth, leading to cell death. The MHRA says it will keep the safety and effectiveness of the medicine under close review.

Approval by the MHRA is a licensing decision. It is separate from decisions on NHS funding. The site's lung cancer page explains the condition.

mhra-new-safeguards-antidepressant-safet.name: MHRA adds antidepressant safety safeguards
mhra-new-safeguards-antidepressant-safet.summary: On 15 October 2026 the MHRA announced new safeguards for antidepressant safety information after a review of 28 antidepressants, covering suicidal thoughts and behaviours and sexual dysfunction that continues after stopping.
keyPoints: The MHRA announced the measures on 15 October 2026 after a review by an expert working group of the Commission on Human Medicines.
The review looked at how two risks are communicated to patients for 28 antidepressant medicines.
The measures include a boxed warning in patient leaflets, a patient card and a new safety leaflet.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA says an expert working group of the Commission on Human Medicines has finished a detailed review of how the potential risks of 28 antidepressant medicines are communicated to patients. The review began after concerns from patients and families about the information in patient information leaflets.

The two risks are suicidal thoughts and behaviours, and sexual dysfunction that continues after treatment is stopped.

body.heading: What changes
body.body:
The MHRA lists a new boxed warning in the leaflets, to highlight information on suicidal thoughts and behaviours and point to where help can be found. A new patient card, in digital or paper form, reinforces key safety messages. A new safety leaflet is being developed with other health system partners and can be given out by healthcare professionals. The MHRA has also published a public assessment report on the review.

If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999. For urgent mental health help, NHS 111 offers a mental health option, and Samaritans are free to call on 116 123 at any time. The site's SSRI, sertraline and citalopram pages cover this group of medicines.

mhra-recall-xeal-pharma-clopidogrel-oral.name: MHRA recalls Xeal Pharma clopidogrel liquids
mhra-recall-xeal-pharma-clopidogrel-oral.summary: The MHRA issued a Class 2 recall on 26 October 2026 of all strengths of Xeal Pharma's clopidogrel oral liquids, which contain less than the labelled amount of clopidogrel.
keyPoints: The MHRA issued the Class 2 medicines recall (reference EL(26)A/43) on 26 October 2026.
The recall covers all strengths of Xeal Pharma's clopidogrel oral suspension and oral solution, which contain less than the labelled amount.
The notice says no reports of patient harm have been received.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The MHRA notice covers all strengths of Xeal Pharma's Clopidogrel Oral Suspension and Clopidogrel Oral Solution, which contain less than the labelled amount of clopidogrel. The notice attributes this to a formulation error. Affected batches contain 76% of the required amount, and the recall covers all batches produced before the notice.

Pharmacists and wholesalers are told to stop supplying the affected batches and to quarantine remaining stock.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
Based on Xeal Pharma's risk assessment, the notice says patient harm is not anticipated in patients receiving the product for long-term preventative treatment, and that no reports of patient harm have been received. The notice says these are unlicensed products and that no licensed clopidogrel oral suspension or solution is available.

Xeal Pharma has confirmed that future stock will be made with the correct strength. Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet medicine, and the site has a page on it.

migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.name: Migraine and tension headache compared
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.headline: Migraine and tension-type headache compared: features, treatment and warning signs
migraine-and-tension-headache-compared.summary: Tension headache is usually a dull, tight pressure on both sides of the head, while migraine often throbs and brings nausea or sensitivity to light.
keyPoints: Tension-type headache usually causes a pressing or tightening pain on both sides of the head, with mild to moderate severity.
Migraine is often a throbbing pain that can be moderate to severe, with nausea, vomiting and sensitivity to light and sound.
Some people have an aura before a migraine, and attacks last longer than a typical tension headache.
Painkillers help both, but frequent use of painkillers can itself cause headaches.
A sudden, extremely painful headache, or a headache with loss of vision, confusion or drowsiness, or a rash that does not fade under a glass, needs 999 or A&E.

body.heading: What does a tension headache feel like?
body.body:
Tension-type headache typically causes a dull, pressing or tight-band pain felt on both sides of the head. An NHS-linked self-care leaflet describes tension-type headache as mild to moderate and not made worse by ordinary daily activity.

The NHS says tension headaches last at least 30 minutes and can last for several days. MedlinePlus says tension headaches usually do not cause nausea or vomiting.

The NHS says tension headaches can be eased with painkillers and activities that help with relaxing.

body.heading: What does a migraine feel like?
body.body:
An NHS-linked self-care leaflet describes migraine as usually moderate to severe, on one or both sides of the head, and it can be made worse by ordinary daily activity. Nausea, vomiting, and sensitivity to light and sound are common.

Attacks typically last for hours, and some people have an aura, a set of temporary symptoms such as visual disturbance, before the headache starts.

Early warning symptoms, such as feeling very tired, can start hours or even a day or two before the head pain.

Aura can include seeing zigzag lines or flashing lights, numbness, dizziness or difficulty speaking.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For tension-type headache, NICE advises considering aspirin, paracetamol or an NSAID for the acute treatment, and the NHS mentions activities that help with relaxing. NICE says treatment to help prevent the underlying headache may be offered alongside stopping the medicines that are causing medication-overuse headache.

The NHS migraine page advises taking painkillers as soon as the headache starts. For the acute treatment of migraine, NICE advises offering an oral triptan together with an NSAID, or an oral triptan together with paracetamol.

Taking painkillers or triptans too often can cause medication-overuse headache, which NICE says is treated by stopping the medicines, with advice from a healthcare professional.

body.heading: When is a headache an emergency?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for a sudden and extremely painful headache, a headache after a head injury, loss of vision, confusion or drowsiness, a seizure, new numbness or weakness, or a rash that does not fade under a glass.

These signs can mean a serious condition, and getting help promptly matters.

Headaches with vomiting, or vision or eye problems, can need an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111.

Migraine that is new in pregnancy or soon after having a baby is something to speak to a healthcare professional about promptly.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP if headaches happen several times a week or are severe, or if painkillers and relaxing activities do not help.

The site's page on headache sets out causes and warning signs in more detail.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: NHS migraine treatments include painkillers, medicines called triptans, and medicines that help with feeling or being sick. NICE says medication-overuse headache is treated by stopping the painkillers or triptans causing it, with support from a healthcare professional, and headaches may get worse before they improve. A throbbing pain at the front or on one side of the head, or feeling sick or finding light or noise painful, can point to migraine rather than a tension headache.

mirvetuximab-ovarian-cancer-nhs-rollout.summary: NHS England has begun offering mirvetuximab soravtansine to hundreds of women with ovarian cancer that has stopped responding to platinum-based chemotherapy.

It follows a recommendation by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE).
NHS England describes it as the first new addition to NHS treatment for this type of cancer in over 20 years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: NHS England says hundreds of women with hard-to-treat ovarian cancer can have mirvetuximab soravtansine on the NHS from 4 June 2026. Following the NICE recommendation, it is for epithelial ovarian, peritoneal or fallopian tube cancer that has become resistant to platinum-based chemotherapy and whose tumours contain the folate receptor alpha (FR alpha) protein that the drug targets.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The drug combines a homing antibody with a cancer-killing medicine. NHS England says it may have more tolerable side effects than traditional chemotherapy.

nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.name: NHS talking therapies and how to self-refer
nhs-talking-therapies-how-they-work.summary: NHS talking therapies offer CBT and counselling for anxiety and depression. In England you can refer yourself, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
keyPoints: NHS talking therapies are free psychological treatments for anxiety and depression, such as CBT and counselling.
In England people aged 18 or over can usually refer themselves, without a GP referral and without a diagnosis.
In immediate danger, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS 111 has a mental health option for urgent help, and Samaritans (116 123) is free to call.

body.heading: What are NHS talking therapies, and what help do they offer?
body.body: NHS talking therapies services treat common problems such as anxiety and depression with psychological treatments. Treatments include cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and counselling. Formats include a self-help workbook with a therapist's support, an online course, one-to-one sessions in person, by phone or by video, and group sessions. CBT is based on the idea that thoughts, feelings, behaviour and physical sensations are connected, and it helps people notice and challenge unhelpful patterns. It is an active, practical therapy that includes exercises and homework. Talking therapies can also help with mental health problems that come with long-term physical conditions, such as diabetes, heart conditions or long-term pain.

body.heading: Who can refer themselves?
body.body: People can refer themselves directly, without a referral from a GP. Eligibility is mainly about age and location: people aged 18 or over who live in England can self-refer, and some areas also accept 16 and 17 year olds. A diagnosed mental health condition is not needed. Some local services ask people to be registered with a GP in their area, so the local service's own page has the details. This route describes NHS talking therapies in England.

body.heading: What happens after referral?
body.body: Someone from the service usually gets in touch to carry out an assessment. The therapist then recommends a treatment based on the symptoms and how severe they are. Waiting times vary by area, so the local service can say how long the wait is.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Talking therapies are not an emergency service. For urgent help, the routes below are open at any time. If someone is in immediate danger, the NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which NHS trusts describe as available at any time. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

nice-endometriosis-tests-primary-care.headline: NICE draft guidance proposes two non-invasive endometriosis tests for NHS primary care
nice-endometriosis-tests-primary-care.summary: NICE draft guidance proposes that two non-invasive tests for endometriosis could be used in NHS primary care while more evidence is gathered.
keyPoints: NICE draft guidance proposes that two non-invasive diagnostic tests for endometriosis could be used in NHS primary care while more evidence on their accuracy is gathered.
The two tests are Endotest, which analyses a saliva sample, and EndoSure, which measures electrical signals in the gut.
NICE says the average wait for an endometriosis diagnosis is more than nine years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: NICE has published draft guidance proposing that two non-invasive diagnostic tests for endometriosis could be used in the NHS in primary care while more evidence on their accuracy is gathered. Endotest analyses a saliva sample for tiny biological markers called microRNAs. EndoSure detects endometriosis by measuring electrical signals in the gut.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: NICE says the average wait for an endometriosis diagnosis is more than nine years. A third test, DotEndo, which is a blood test, is not among the tests in the draft recommendations. Because this is draft guidance, the recommendations may change after consultation.

nice-finerenone-chronic-heart-failure.name: NICE backs finerenone for heart failure
nice-finerenone-chronic-heart-failure.headline: NICE final draft guidance recommends finerenone for chronic heart failure
nice-finerenone-chronic-heart-failure.summary: NICE final draft guidance recommends finerenone for adults with chronic heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction.
keyPoints: NICE has published final draft guidance that recommends finerenone for adults with chronic heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction.
NICE estimates that up to 280,000 people in England could be eligible for finerenone.
NICE says about half of the estimated 635,000 people in England with heart failure have preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: NICE has published final draft guidance that recommends finerenone for adults with chronic heart failure that has preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. Finerenone belongs to a group of medicines called mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists. NICE estimates that up to 280,000 people could be eligible for it.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: NICE says that of the estimated 635,000 people in England who have heart failure, about half have preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. The announcement also reports around 100,000 hospital admissions for heart failure in England in 2023 to 2024. NICE recommended dapagliflozin in 2023 for the same group of people, and it was the first NICE-recommended treatment for this type of heart failure. nih-extra-year-school-dementia-diagnoses.summary: An NIH-funded study reports that one extra year of secondary school in the UK was linked to fewer dementia diagnoses later in life, with the largest effect in people at higher genetic risk.
keyPoints: An NIH news release dated 23 October 2026 describes an NIH-funded study of schooling and dementia.
The study used a UK reform that raised the minimum school-leaving age by one year.
It reports fewer dementia diagnoses later in life, with the largest effect among people at higher genetic risk.
This is research news from a US agency, not UK guidance.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
A US National Institutes of Health (NIH) news release dated 23 October 2026 describes a study that found an extra year of secondary school was associated with fewer dementia diagnoses later in life.

The NIH funded the study, which was led by researchers at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and the University of Southern California.

The researchers analysed a UK education reform that raised the minimum school-leaving age by one year, treating it as a natural experiment.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
The release says the effect was largest among people at higher genetic risk of dementia.

The researchers estimated a reduction of 0.88 percentage points in Alzheimer's disease and related dementia over 50 years, which the release calls sizeable given how low overall dementia rates were in the study population.

The release notes that as the group ages, the gap between those who stayed in school and those who left may grow or shrink.

This is research news from a US agency; it does not change UK guidance.

numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.name: Numbness and tingling: causes and when to act
numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.headline: Numbness, tingling and pins and needles: common causes and when to get help
numbness-and-tingling-causes-and-when-to.summary: Pins and needles are usually brief and harmless, but numbness or tingling that lasts, keeps returning or comes with weakness needs checking. The NHS says to call 999 for sudden numbness on one side.
keyPoints: The NHS describes pins and needles as a pricking, tingling or numbing feeling, usually in the arms, hands, legs or feet.
Brief episodes often follow sitting or sleeping in one position, while longer-lasting symptoms can have other causes such as nerve damage or some medicines.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if pins and needles keep coming back or last a long time.
Sudden weakness in an arm, a drooping face or slurred speech are signs of stroke, and the NHS says to call 999.

body.heading: What are pins and needles?
body.body: The NHS describes pins and needles as a pricking, burning, tingling or numbing sensation. It usually affects the arms, hands, legs or feet. Brief spells are common after sitting or sleeping on a limb and usually pass.

body.heading: Why does it keep happening?
body.body: The NHS lists possible reasons for longer-lasting pins and needles, including a trapped nerve in the back or neck, nerve damage, poor diet and heavy drinking. Some treatments and substances are also listed, including chemotherapy, some medicines, lead and radiation. Conditions the NHS links to particular patterns include diabetes, Raynaud’s, hyperventilation, sciatica and multiple sclerosis.

body.heading: What is peripheral neuropathy?
body.body: Peripheral neuropathy is damage to the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. Its main symptoms include numbness and tingling in the feet or hands, burning or stabbing pain, loss of balance and muscle weakness in the feet. Causes the NHS lists include diabetes, long-term heavy alcohol use, low vitamin B12 and an underactive thyroid. The NHS advises seeing a GP early if these symptoms appear, and blood tests may be arranged, especially for diabetes and vitamin B12 deficiency.

body.heading: What about the wrist and hand?
body.body: Carpal tunnel syndrome is pressure on a nerve in the wrist that causes tingling, numbness and pain in the hand and fingers. The symptoms are usually worse at night. The NHS says to see a GP if symptoms are getting worse or not going away, or if home treatment is not helping. When the diagnosis is unclear, a nerve conduction test or scans may be used.

body.heading: When is numbness an emergency?
body.body: The NHS lists face drooping, arm weakness and speech problems among the main symptoms of stroke. The NHS stroke test, FAST, stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999. The NHS advises calling 999 straight away, even if the symptoms disappear while waiting for the ambulance, and NHS inform says not to drive if you think you have had a stroke or TIA. A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a short-lived version of stroke symptoms, and the NHS says an assessment in hospital is still needed if the symptoms go away.

opioid-painkillers-explained.name: Opioid painkillers: what to know
opioid-painkillers-explained.headline: Opioid painkillers: how they work and what the NHS says about the risks
opioid-painkillers-explained.summary: Opioids such as morphine are prescription painkillers for severe pain; the NHS lists constipation and sleepiness as common side effects.
keyPoints: The NHS describes morphine as a strong opioid painkiller, available only on prescription and used for severe pain, such as after an operation or serious injury, or from cancer.
Constipation, feeling sick and sleepiness are the most common morphine side effects the NHS lists, and the chance of side effects is higher with a higher dose.
The NHS says the body can become used to tramadol over time, so higher doses may gradually be needed, and that it is possible to become addicted.
The NHS says morphine should not be stopped suddenly because withdrawal symptoms may follow, and that a doctor reduces the dose gradually over time.
The NHS says to call 999 for breathing difficulties or a seizure, NHS 111 can give urgent advice about side effects, and a GP may be a good place to start for help with drug addiction.

body.heading: What are opioid painkillers used for?
body.body: The NHS describes morphine as a strong opioid painkiller that is available only with a prescription. It is used to treat severe pain, such as pain after an operation or a serious injury, or pain from cancer or a heart attack. The NHS also says it is used for longer-lasting pain when weaker painkillers no longer work. Morphine acts in the central nervous system and brain to stop pain signals reaching the rest of the body, and it also eases the anxiety and stress that pain produces. The NHS describes it as a controlled medicine and says that, because addiction is possible, the dose is reviewed so that a person takes only what is needed to control the pain.

body.heading: Does morphine come in different forms?
body.body: According to the NHS, morphine can be given in several ways, including as an injection into a vein, as tablets or liquid, and as slow-release forms. An injection into a vein gives the quickest relief, working almost straight away. Tablets and liquid act more slowly than an injection, and slow-release forms take longer to start working but last longer. The NHS says the amount of pain a person has, rather than the stage of their illness, decides whether morphine is prescribed.

body.heading: What are the common side effects?
body.body: The NHS says the most common side effects of morphine are constipation, feeling sick and sleepiness. Dizziness, confusion, headaches and an itchy skin or rash can also occur. The NHS says the higher the dose of morphine, the more chance of side effects. Morphine slows digestion, which is why it can cause constipation, and the NHS says a laxative is likely to be needed to help prevent or treat it. Feeling sick should normally wear off after a few days, and the NHS says that taking the dose with a meal or snack helps. Drowsiness typically fades as the body adjusts, and the NHS says to speak to a doctor or pharmacist with any concerns.

body.heading: What are tolerance and addiction?
body.body: The NHS tramadol page says the body can become used to the medicine with long-term use, which means higher doses are gradually needed to get the same effect. The NHS says it is possible to become addicted to tramadol, and it lists people with a history of addiction to alcohol, strong painkillers or recreational drugs among those who may not be able to take it. For morphine, the NHS says addiction is possible and that the dose is reviewed. NICE guidance on medicines associated with dependence links long-term treatment and higher doses taken long term with a greater risk of dependence. NICE chronic pain guidance recommends against starting opioids for chronic primary pain.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping morphine?
body.body: The NHS says not to stop taking morphine suddenly, because withdrawal symptoms may follow. It lists agitation, panic attacks, palpitations, sweating and restlessness as examples. The NHS says a doctor will gradually reduce the dose over time. NICE says clinicians should explain the risk of stopping abruptly, and its guidance favours slow dose reduction, noting that the pace of safe withdrawal differs between people. For questions about stopping, the NHS points to the prescriber or a pharmacist.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about alcohol and driving?
body.body: For tramadol, the NHS advises not drinking alcohol, because side effects such as feeling sleepy are more likely. For morphine, the NHS says it may be best not to drink alcohol, because it may make a person feel sleepier or increase the risk of serious side effects. The NHS says not to drive a car, ride a bike or use heavy tools or machinery if tramadol makes a person sleepy or dizzy, and gives similar advice for morphine when drowsy or dizzy. The NHS also says that recreational drugs can raise the risk of serious side effects with tramadol.

body.heading: When is it an emergency, and where can help for addiction be found?
body.body: The NHS says serious side effects of morphine are uncommon, and include an allergic reaction (anaphylaxis), slowed breathing and changes to vision. It says to call 999 for breathing difficulties or a seizure, and also for signs of anaphylaxis such as sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue. For urgent advice about side effects, the NHS points to NHS 111. For help with drug addiction, the NHS says a GP may be a good place to start, as they can discuss the problem and help get a person into treatment. The GP will usually refer to a local drug service, and the NHS adds that many drug treatment services accept self-referrals.

osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.name: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.headline: Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis: how they differ
osteoarthritis-and-rheumatoid-arthritis-.summary: Osteoarthritis makes joints painful and stiff; rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the joint lining.
keyPoints: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK and mostly affects the knees, hips and small joints of the hands.
Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.
Rheumatoid arthritis usually affects joints on both sides of the body and brings long morning stiffness, as well as tiredness.
Osteoarthritis is managed with exercise, weight management and pain relief; rheumatoid arthritis needs medicines that reduce inflammation.
Early assessment matters for rheumatoid arthritis, so a GP appointment is the first step for persistent joint swelling or stiffness.

body.heading: What do the two conditions have in common?
body.body:
Both osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) are types of arthritis, and both cause joint pain and stiffness.

They are not. They have different causes, tend to affect different joints and are treated differently.

body.heading: What is osteoarthritis?
body.body:
Osteoarthritis is a condition that makes joints painful and stiff. The NHS says it is the most common type of arthritis in the UK.

The protective cartilage on the ends of the bones gradually breaks down. The NHS lists several things that raise the risk of osteoarthritis, including age, joint injury, extra weight, being female and family history.

It most often causes problems in the knees, hips and small joints of the hands. The NHS says osteoarthritis does not necessarily get any worse over time.

There is no cure for osteoarthritis, but treatment can help with symptoms.

Hot or cold packs can ease osteoarthritis symptoms.

body.heading: What is rheumatoid arthritis?
body.body:
Rheumatoid arthritis is a long-term condition that causes swollen, stiff and painful joints, most often in the hands and feet. It is an autoimmune disease: the immune system attacks the lining of the joints.

The NHS says it usually affects joints on both sides of the body, and that morning stiffness often lasts longer than it does in osteoarthritis. Some people also have tiredness, a fever or weight loss.

The trigger is not clear, but a higher risk is linked with being female, having a family history of the condition and smoking.

Rheumatoid arthritis can also cause firm lumps called rheumatoid nodules under the skin.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
For osteoarthritis, the NHS recommends regular exercise, keeping to a healthy weight, suitable footwear and aids that reduce strain on the joint. Medicines can be used to relieve the pain of osteoarthritis, and physiotherapists and occupational therapists can provide structured exercise plans and advice on aids.

Surgery, most often a hip or knee replacement, is generally considered when other treatments are not enough.

Rheumatoid arthritis is treated with medicines that slow the disease and reduce inflammation, known as disease-modifying drugs, sometimes alongside biological treatments. Painkillers and steroids can ease symptoms, and physiotherapy and occupational therapy are part of care. There is no cure, but treatment can help to reduce inflammation, relieve pain and prevent or slow joint damage.

body.heading: How are they diagnosed?
body.body:
A GP asks about symptoms and examines the joints. Osteoarthritis can often be diagnosed from the symptoms and an examination.

For suspected rheumatoid arthritis, blood tests that look for inflammation are used, and the site's pages on CRP and ESR explain two of them. Scans such as X-rays may be done to check for joint inflammation and damage.

No single blood test can prove or rule out rheumatoid arthritis, so doctors combine blood tests, scans and an examination.

Osteoarthritis does not usually need X-rays or blood tests, but they may be used to rule out other causes such as rheumatoid arthritis.

If rheumatoid arthritis is suspected, the GP may do blood tests and refer the person to a specialist.

body.heading: When should someone see a GP?
body.body:
A GP appointment is the usual route for joint pain, swelling or stiffness that does not settle. The NHS emphasises that early diagnosis and treatment of rheumatoid arthritis can help to prevent joint damage.

If the skin around a joint is red or hot, or sore joints come with a high or low temperature, the NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111.

For sore joints with a high or low temperature, or red or hot skin around a joint, the NHS says to ask for an urgent GP appointment or get help from NHS 111.
