panic-attacks-what-they-are.name: Panic attacks: what they are and what helps
panic-attacks-what-they-are.summary: A panic attack is a rush of intense fear with physical symptoms such as a racing heartbeat. The NHS describes how attacks pass and how talking therapy and medicine can treat repeated attacks.
keyPoints: A panic attack causes physical symptoms such as a pounding heart, fast breathing and shaking, and many people fear the next attack.
The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes, although some last longer.
Cognitive behavioural therapy is offered for repeated panic attacks, and in England people can refer themselves to an NHS talking therapies service.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: What is a panic attack?
body.body: A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear or anxiety. A single panic attack does not necessarily mean someone has panic disorder, which is when attacks keep coming back.

body.heading: What does it feel like?
body.body: Common physical signs include a pounding heart, fast breathing and shaking. The NHS says a panic attack usually lasts between 5 and 20 minutes. Panic can feel like heart or breathing problems, so the NHS advises speaking to a GP rather than self-diagnosing. The NHS says that although panic attacks are frightening, an attack will not cause physical harm.

body.heading: What can help during an attack?
body.body: The NHS advice is to stay where you are if you can, breathe slowly and deeply, and remind yourself that the attack will pass and is not life threatening. NHS self-help guides describe the feelings as normal bodily reactions that are not harmful, and suggest waiting for them to pass rather than adding frightening thoughts. Grounding techniques, such as focusing on the senses, can also help.

body.heading: How are repeated attacks treated?
body.body: Cognitive behavioural therapy is a recommended psychological treatment, and in England people can refer themselves to a talking therapies service or ask a GP to refer them. Medicines used include SSRI antidepressants, and a tricyclic antidepressant may be used if SSRIs are not suitable. NICE says psychological therapy, medicine and self-help have all been shown to work, and that the benefits of psychological treatment lasted longest.

body.heading: What causes panic disorder, and when should someone see a GP?
body.body: The exact cause of panic disorder is not fully understood, and it is thought to be probably a combination of physical and psychological factors. A GP asks the person to describe their symptoms and may carry out a physical examination to rule out other causes. The NHS says to see a GP if attacks keep happening.

body.heading: What can people do day to day?
body.body: The NHS suggests activities such as yoga and Pilates, breathing exercises for stress, and regular exercise to help ease anxiety. NHS self-help guides note that escaping or avoiding panic can stop an attack in the moment but can also keep the problem going.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: Panic attacks are frightening but pass. If a person feels unable to stay safe, urgent help is open at any time. If you or someone else is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.name: Pelvic pain in women: causes and when to act
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.headline: Pelvic pain in women: common causes, red flags and which NHS route to use
pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.summary: Pelvic pain in women often comes from period pain, ovarian cysts or endometriosis, but a few causes are serious. The NHS says to call 999 for severe or worsening pain.
keyPoints: The NHS lists period pain, ovarian cysts, endometriosis and pregnancy-related pain among the common causes of pelvic pain in women.
Rarer causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease and womb or ovarian cancer.
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E if the pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area.
Pain that comes and goes or does not go away is a reason for a routine GP appointment.

body.heading: What causes pelvic pain?
body.body: The NHS says pelvic pain is more common in women. Common causes include period pain, an ovarian cyst, endometriosis and pain related to pregnancy. Rarer but more serious causes include ectopic pregnancy, pelvic inflammatory disease, womb cancer and ovarian cancer.

body.heading: What is pelvic inflammatory disease?
body.body: Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) is an infection of the female reproductive organs. PID is often caused by a sexually transmitted infection such as chlamydia or gonorrhoea. Bacteria that normally live in the vagina cause some cases.

body.heading: When is a routine GP appointment appropriate?
body.body: The NHS suggests booking a GP appointment if pelvic pain comes and goes or does not go away. Bloating that does not go away, weight loss or changes in bowel habit are further reasons. Pain during sex is also a reason to see a GP.

body.heading: When should you call NHS 111 or an urgent GP?
body.body: The NHS advises asking for an urgent GP appointment or getting help from NHS 111 for pelvic pain with difficulty peeing or pooing, blood in urine or stool, unusual vaginal discharge, or a very high temperature. The same advice applies if the person is or may be pregnant. For an ovarian cyst, sudden severe pelvic pain is a reason for an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

body.heading: When is it an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if pelvic pain is severe, getting worse, or hurts when you move or touch the area. Fainting or feeling dizzy, pain at the tip of the shoulder, difficulty breathing, heavy vaginal bleeding and sudden confusion are also on the 999 list. For PID, the NHS says to call 999 or go straight to A&E for severe pelvic pain or heavy vaginal bleeding, and not to drive yourself.

body.heading: Which tests might follow?
body.body: If PID is suspected, a GP may take a sample of vaginal discharge to test, and an ultrasound scan may be used. Some people with PID have a negative swab result, so a negative swab does not rule it out.

pelvic-pain-in-women-causes-and-when-to-.metaDescription: Pelvic pain in women often comes from period pain, ovarian cysts or endometriosis, but a few causes are serious.

persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.name: A cough that will not go: causes and tests
persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.summary: The NHS advises a GP visit for a cough lasting over 3 weeks, and an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood.
keyPoints: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell.

The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak.
The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines.

body.heading: What causes a cough that lasts?
body.body: The NHS cough page lists smoking, heartburn (acid reflux), allergies and infections such as bronchitis as causes. NHS guidance describes asthma, bronchiectasis, acid reflux and postnasal drip as causes of a long-lasting cough. Some NHS hospital trust leaflets list ACE inhibitors, a type of blood pressure medicine, as a cause of a long-lasting cough. NHS inform says a persistent cough is often of unknown cause. The NHS says bronchitis often gets better without treatment in around 3 weeks. A chest infection usually gets better on its own in about 7 to 10 days, although the cough and mucus can last up to 3 weeks. Antibiotics are generally not used for viral chest infections such as flu or viral bronchitis.

body.heading: What can help at home?
body.body: The NHS says most coughs can be managed at home with rest and fluids, and a pharmacist can advise on cough medicines. A local NHS self-care leaflet says there is little evidence on whether over-the-counter cough medicines relieve symptoms.

body.heading: When should a cough be seen by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if a cough has lasted more than 3 weeks, if weight is being lost for no reason, or if the immune system is weakened. A South East London Cancer Alliance page urges people with a persistent cough to contact their GP. The NHS lung cancer symptoms page lists symptoms including chest or shoulder pain, weight loss without trying, and tiredness.

body.heading: When is a cough urgent?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or a call to NHS 111 for a cough with chest pain or a feeling of being very unwell. The NHS cough page advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood or finding it hard to breathe, and the NHS bronchitis page says to call 999 if someone is struggling to breathe, for example choking or gasping and unable to speak. For people with bronchiectasis, the NHS says to call 999 if more than a few streaks of blood are coughed up.

body.heading: What does the GP do?
body.body: A GP may listen to the chest. NHS inform says a GP may arrange tests such as a chest X-ray, breathing or lung function tests, and a sample of phlegm. NHS pages say antibiotics are not usually prescribed for coughs, and a GP may refer people to a specialist if the cause is unclear.

persistent-cough-causes-tests-and-when-t.metaDescription: The NHS advises a GP visit for a cough lasting over 3 weeks, and an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for coughing up blood.

physical-activity-guidelines-adults.name: How much exercise adults need each week
physical-activity-guidelines-adults.summary: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week, plus strength work.
keyPoints: The NHS lists at least 150 minutes of moderate activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week for adults aged 19 to 64.
Strengthening activities for the major muscle groups on at least two days a week are in addition to the aerobic minutes.
The NHS talk test separates moderate activity, where a person can talk but not sing, from vigorous activity, where only a few words fit between breaths.
The guidance also advises reducing long periods of sitting, and the 2019 update dropped the older rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes.

body.heading: How much activity do adults aged 19 to 64 need?
body.body: The NHS says adults aged 19 to 64 should aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate intensity activity a week, or 75 minutes of vigorous intensity activity a week. It also describes a mix of moderate and vigorous activity as a way of reaching the target. The NHS adds that 75 minutes of vigorous activity a week can give similar health benefits to 150 minutes of moderate activity. The guidance says activity should be spread across the week, and that all adults should aim to be active every day.

body.heading: What counts as moderate or vigorous?
body.body: The NHS uses a talk test: at moderate intensity a person can still talk but not sing. Brisk walking, cycling, dancing, water aerobics and pushing a lawn mower are listed as moderate activities. At vigorous intensity breathing becomes hard and fast, and a person cannot say more than a few words without pausing for breath. Running, swimming, fast or uphill cycling, skipping and team sports are listed as vigorous activities. The UK Chief Medical Officers' guidelines say very vigorous activity, such as sprinting or stair climbing, can count too, in shorter periods or mixed with other intensities.

body.heading: What are strengthening activities?
body.body: The NHS says adults should do strengthening activities on at least two days a week, working all the major muscle groups: legs, hips, back, abdomen, chest, shoulders and arms. Lifting weights, push-ups, sit-ups, heavy gardening such as digging and carrying heavy shopping are given as examples, along with yoga, pilates and tai chi. The NHS says these sessions are needed in addition to the aerobic minutes, because they do not count toward the 150 minutes. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance adds that any strengthening activity is better than none.

body.heading: Does sitting still matter?
body.body: The NHS guidance advises reducing the time spent sitting or lying down, and breaking up long periods of not moving with some activity. The Chief Medical Officers' guidance says adults should aim to minimise time spent sitting and, where possible, break up long inactive periods with at least light activity.

body.heading: What do the guidelines say about benefits and short bouts?
body.body: The NHS says exercising even once or twice a week can reduce the risk of heart disease or stroke. The 2019 revision of the UK guidelines removed the earlier rule that activity must come in bouts of at least ten minutes. The guidance says there is no minimum amount of physical activity needed for some health benefit.

body.heading: What does regular activity do for health?
body.body: The NHS says regular activity lowers the risk of conditions including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression and dementia. It also says activity can improve self-esteem, mood, sleep quality and energy.

body.heading: What changes for adults aged 65 and over?
body.body: NHS guidance for older adults advises being active every day, even lightly. It recommends activities that improve strength, balance and flexibility on at least two days a week, and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week. The NHS advises speaking to a GP first for anyone who has not exercised for some time or who has medical conditions or concerns.

reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.name: Reliever and preventer inhalers explained
reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.headline: Reliever and preventer inhalers: what is the difference?
reliever-and-preventer-inhalers.summary: A reliever inhaler eases symptoms when they happen, while a preventer is taken every day to reduce airway inflammation.
keyPoints: A reliever is used when symptoms appear, and a preventer is taken every day, even when a person feels well, to reduce airway inflammation, according to Asthma + Lung UK.
NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler.
The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a steroid inhaler to help prevent thrush; Asthma + Lung UK says a spacer can also reduce steroid side effects.
The NHS and Asthma + Lung UK both link needing a reliever more often than usual with asthma that is not well controlled; Asthma + Lung UK advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.
Asthma + Lung UK says to call 999 if the reliever is not helping in an asthma attack, and to ask for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment after managing an attack alone.

body.heading: What is the difference between a reliever and a preventer inhaler?
body.body: A reliever inhaler is used when symptoms appear. Blue reliever inhalers contain salbutamol, a short-acting bronchodilator, which is a medicine that quickly opens the airways. A preventer inhaler is taken every day, even when a person feels well, and works over time to reduce airway inflammation. The two do different jobs. NHS Inform says a person with asthma should not be given a blue reliever inhaler to use on its own and should always have a preventer inhaler. Asthma + Lung UK adds that relying only on a reliever makes symptoms and asthma attacks more likely.

body.heading: How are they used, and what else is there?
body.body: Salbutamol is the usual blue reliever. A preventer such as beclometasone is an inhaled steroid. Asthma + Lung UK says a GP or nurse should discuss switching from a blue-only reliever to an anti-inflammatory reliever, known as an AIR inhaler, which combines a reliever with a low-dose steroid. The NHS says steroid inhalers should not be stopped without medical advice. In COPD, the NHS says short-acting bronchodilator inhalers are usually the first treatment. A steroid inhaler may be suggested if breathlessness continues on a long-acting inhaler or flare-ups stay frequent, and it is usually combined with a long-acting medicine in one inhaler.

body.heading: What does a spacer do?
body.body: A spacer is a chamber used with a pressurised metered-dose inhaler, the kind that sprays out a puff of medicine. Asthma + Lung UK says using a spacer can also prevent side effects from steroid medicines in preventer or combination inhalers. It also says a tight seal around the mouthpiece helps make sure the full dose is received, and that a whistling sound from the spacer means the person is breathing in too fast.

body.heading: Should the mouth be rinsed after a steroid inhaler?
body.body: The NHS says to rinse the mouth with water or brush the teeth after each dose of a beclometasone inhaler, to help prevent thrush. Asthma + Lung UK gives similar advice, saying to rinse the mouth with water and spit it out after using an inhaler that contains steroid, to reduce the chance of side effects. The NHS steroid inhaler page also advises using a spacer. The rinsing advice applies to inhalers that contain steroid.

body.heading: What are the side effects?
body.body: The NHS lists shakiness, a faster heartbeat and headaches as the typical side effects of salbutamol. It says serious side effects are rare. Muscle pain or weakness, muscle cramps, or an irregular or more noticeable heartbeat can be a sign of low potassium levels, and the NHS says to call a doctor or NHS 111 straight away if these happen. For beclometasone, the NHS lists oral thrush and a dry or sore throat as common side effects, and its steroid inhaler page also lists a hoarse or croaky voice. If thrush develops, the NHS says a pharmacist can recommend an antifungal mouth gel, and the beclometasone inhaler is kept up while the gel is used. The NHS says to call 999 for swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, fast or struggling breathing, or skin, lips or tongue turning blue, grey or pale, and for chest pain after using more than the recommended dose. If more than the recommended dose has been used and the heartbeat is fast or noticeable, the NHS says to contact NHS 111.

body.heading: What can needing a reliever more often mean?
body.body: The NHS says needing a salbutamol inhaler more often than usual could be a sign that the condition is not well controlled. Asthma + Lung UK says regularly needing a reliever inhaler points to asthma that is not under control, and advises speaking to a GP, asthma nurse or pharmacist.

body.heading: When is it urgent?
body.body: Asthma + Lung UK says an asthma attack is an emergency, and that 999 should be called for an ambulance if the reliever is not helping. It says to call 999 if a person feels worse at any point, and to call 999 straight away if there is no reliever inhaler to hand. It adds that even a person who feels able to get to A&E should call 999 for an ambulance, so they can be treated on the way to hospital, and that the call handler should be told it is an asthma attack. After an attack treated with the reliever alone, Asthma + Lung UK advises asking for an urgent same-day GP or nurse appointment.

sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.name: Sepsis: warning signs and when to act
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.headline: Sepsis: the warning signs in adults and children and when to call 999
sepsis-warning-signs-and-what-to-do.summary: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection; the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if sepsis is suspected.
keyPoints: Sepsis can be life-threatening and needs urgent hospital treatment; it can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis.
Signs in adults include confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing and blue, pale or blotchy skin.
Signs in babies and children include fast or difficult breathing, unusual sleepiness, poor feeding, and a rash that does not fade under a glass.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if someone may have sepsis, and not to drive there.
Treatment is in hospital and usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids into a vein.

body.heading: What is sepsis?
body.body:
Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection. The NHS says it can develop very quickly and needs urgent treatment in hospital.

It can follow an infection such as pneumonia, a urinary tract infection or cellulitis. The exact cause is not always clear.

body.heading: What are the signs in adults?
body.body:
The NHS lists confusion or slurred speech, uncontrollable shivering, muscle pain, difficulty breathing, and blue, pale or blotchy skin. Passing no urine all day, or very little, is another sign.

Not everyone with sepsis has every sign.

A rash that does not fade under a glass is rare in sepsis, but it can be a sign of meningitis, so call 999 or go to A&E.

In adults, a very high or very low temperature can also be a sign.

body.heading: What are the signs in babies and children?
body.body:
For babies and young children, the NHS lists fast or difficult breathing, blue, pale or blotchy skin, being unusually sleepy, and a rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.

In babies and young children, poor feeding can also be a sign.

body.heading: Who is at higher risk?
body.body:
Anyone can get sepsis, but the chance is higher in babies under 12 months and people over 75. It can sometimes occur in people who are otherwise fit and healthy.

People with a weakened immune system, for example from chemotherapy or from taking corticosteroids or other medicines that suppress the immune system, are also at higher risk.

People with diabetes and people who have recently had surgery are also more likely to develop sepsis.

body.heading: When should someone call 999?
body.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if an adult or child shows signs of sepsis, or if there is a worry that it could be sepsis. It advises asking someone to drive, or calling for an ambulance, rather than driving oneself.

For a worry about an infection when sepsis is not suspected, the NHS says to call NHS 111 or contact the GP. When it is unclear whether it could be sepsis, the NHS says it is still better to call 999.

body.heading: How is sepsis treated, and what happens afterwards?
body.body:
Sepsis is treated in hospital. Treatment usually includes antibiotics, oxygen if needed, and fluids given into a vein. Some people need intensive care.

Recovery can take a long time, and some people take months or longer to feel back to normal. Some people have longer-lasting problems after sepsis, such as tiredness and changes in mood, which is sometimes called post-sepsis syndrome.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Sometimes surgery is needed to remove the source of infection. Post-sepsis syndrome can also cause problems with memory or concentration, and support such as physiotherapy or counselling may help.

shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.name: Shortness of breath: causes and next steps
shortness-of-breath-causes-and-next-step.summary: Breathlessness has many causes, from asthma and infections to heart and lung disease, and severe difficulty breathing needs a 999 call.
keyPoints: NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness.
Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways.
NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath.
The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg.

body.heading: Why do people get short of breath?
body.body:
NHS inform lists asthma attacks, pneumonia and heart failure among the likely causes of sudden breathlessness. NHS inform also lists a severe allergic reaction, a collapsed lung and a blood clot in the lung as possible causes of sudden breathlessness. A collapsed lung, or pneumothorax, is a partial collapse of the lung caused by a small tear in the lung surface.

The NHS lists several possible causes of breathlessness, including COPD, scarring of the lungs, heart failure, asthma, chest infections and being overweight. In heart failure, fluid builds up in the lungs and makes breathing harder.

body.heading: What do asthma, COPD, heart failure and a lung clot look like?
body.body: Sudden breathlessness could be an asthma attack, which makes it difficult to move air in and out of the airways. The NHS lists breathlessness as the most common symptom of heart failure; it may happen after activity or at rest, may be worse when lying down, and may wake a person at night. It lists tiredness, swollen ankles and legs, and feeling lightheaded or fainting as other heart failure symptoms. An NHS trust leaflet says the most common symptom of a pulmonary embolism is breathlessness, with chest pain that is worse on breathing or coughing, and it also lists cough and fever.

body.heading: When is breathlessness an emergency?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E for severe difficulty breathing, such as being unable to speak without pausing for breath. The NHS says chest tightness or heaviness, or pain that spreads to the arms, back, neck or jaw, is also a reason to call 999 or go to A&E. The NHS adds sudden confusion, or lips or skin turning pale, blue or grey, to the signs for calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to take them or call an ambulance.

body.heading: When should breathlessness be seen urgently or soon?
body.body: The NHS says to contact NHS 111 for difficulty breathing, feeling or being sick, coughing up blood, or pain or swelling in one leg. NHS inform advises contacting the GP practice if breathlessness is new or unexplained. The NHS advises seeing a GP if breathlessness has lasted longer than a month, gets worse with normal activity or when lying down, or comes with swollen ankles.

body.heading: What does the GP ask about and test?
body.body: NHS inform's guidance asks whether breathlessness came on suddenly or slowly and whether anything triggered it, such as exercise. An NHS England pathway for persistent breathlessness lists an ECG, a chest X-ray and spirometry among the first-line tests. Spirometry is a breathing test that measures how much air a person can blow out and how fast. The same pathway says an ECG showing atrial fibrillation with breathlessness should prompt a heart specialist assessment, including an echocardiogram.

body.heading: How is breathlessness treated?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For COPD, treatment usually involves relieving symptoms with medicines such as inhalers, and pulmonary rehabilitation may help. Heart failure is managed with lifestyle changes and medicines or surgery. A blood clot in the lung can be treated with anticoagulants, which are drugs that thin the blood. NHS leaflets describe pursed-lip breathing as a technique that can help keep the airways open for longer and reduce the work of breathing, for example in COPD.

sleep-problems-what-helps.name: Sleep problems: what helps and when to get help
sleep-problems-what-helps.summary: The NHS says insomnia usually improves by changing sleeping habits, and that a GP can arrange CBT when habits alone do not help.
keyPoints: The NHS describes insomnia as regular difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early.
A steady bedtime and wake time, a dark, quiet room and winding down without screens are habits the NHS Every Mind Matters pages describe for better sleep.
The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing habits has not helped, or if sleep trouble has lasted for months.
Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the main treatment described by NHS sources; sleeping pills are rarely prescribed.

body.heading: What counts as insomnia?
body.body:
The NHS says a person who regularly finds it hard to fall asleep, stay asleep or wake up too early may have insomnia. It also says insomnia usually gets better by changing sleeping habits.

A primary care pathway from NHS South Yorkshire advises considering life events and physical or mental health problems as possible triggers of insomnia. Primary care guidance for GPs in the NHS lists physical conditions such as sleep apnoea among the possible causes of insomnia. It also suggests that a clinician asks whether a medicine could be a cause, and considers anxiety or depression as possible underlying factors.

body.heading: Which sleep habits do NHS pages describe?
body.body:
The NHS Every Mind Matters pages say a regular sleep routine can make it easier to fall asleep, because going to bed and getting up at similar times each day helps the body know when it is time to sleep. They suggest keeping the same routine on days off. They also suggest keeping phones, tablets and computers away for an hour before bed, because the light can delay sleep. Reading, meditation or breathing exercises are given as alternatives.

A dark, quiet and cool bedroom is a recurring recommendation across NHS pages. NHS pages also advise against caffeine, smoking and alcohol in the hours before bed, although the exact timing differs from page to page. Some pages advise against napping during the day and describe regular daytime exercise as helpful. For someone who worries in bed, the NHS suggests writing a list of tasks for the next day before going to sleep.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest when sleep will not come?
body.body: If a person is still awake after about 20 minutes, the NHS suggests getting up, doing something relaxing in another room, and going back to bed when sleepy.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS suggests seeing a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped insomnia, or if there has been trouble sleeping for months. A GP may refer a person for cognitive behavioural therapy, or CBT, which helps change the thoughts and behaviours that get in the way of sleep. The NHS says GPs now rarely prescribe sleeping pills for insomnia, because they can have serious side effects and a person can become dependent on them.

body.heading: What does CBT for insomnia involve?
body.body: The NHS recommends cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, known as CBT-I, as the first treatment for insomnia. CBT-I can be delivered in person, in groups or online, for example through the Sleepio programme, which is designed to be completed over six weeks; availability and cost to the patient vary by area. A primary care guideline from Buckinghamshire, Oxfordshire and Berkshire West advises that medicines are best avoided in the long-term management of insomnia.

body.heading: How much sleep do adults need, and why does it matter?
body.body: NHS sources put the amount most adults need at about 7 to 9 hours a night. One NHS page says age, health and daily routine can all affect how much sleep a person needs. NHS Every Mind Matters says getting enough sleep can support mood, energy, the immune system and overall health. A United States guide from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute adds that regularly getting too little or very poor quality sleep increases the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease and other health problems. NHS pages list feeling very tired, irritable or sleepy during the day among the signs of not sleeping enough.

body.heading: Could another sleep disorder be involved?
body.body: The NHS says a person may be referred to a sleep clinic if they have symptoms of another sleep disorder, such as sleep apnoea.

sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.name: Sore throat: causes, treatment, when to act
sore-throat-causes-treatment-and-when-to.summary: Most sore throats are caused by viruses and clear up on their own, but struggling to breathe or swallow needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic.
A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week.
NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling.

body.heading: What causes a sore throat?
body.body: NICE says acute sore throat is often caused by a viral infection, and most people get better without an antibiotic. A University Hospitals Sussex NHS leaflet lists tonsillitis, laryngitis, strep throat and glandular fever as other common causes of a sore throat. NICE suggests scoring tools (FeverPAIN or Centor) to spot people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic, and these include fever, pus on the tonsils, tender neck glands and no cough.

body.heading: How long does it last, and what helps?
body.body: A sore throat usually clears up on its own and often lasts about a week. NHS 111 Wales says a pharmacist can advise about paracetamol or ibuprofen for the pain, and a hospital trust leaflet notes that not everyone can take ibuprofen safely.

body.heading: Are antibiotics needed?
body.body: NICE says most people with a sore throat will not need an antibiotic. NICE says a scoring tool (FeverPAIN or Centor) should be used to identify people with a sore throat who may be more likely to benefit from an antibiotic.

body.heading: What are tonsillitis, glandular fever and quinsy?
body.body: A GP can often diagnose tonsillitis from the symptoms and a look at the throat, a swab can show whether bacteria are the cause, and a blood test for glandular fever is recommended if symptoms are severe or will not go away. The NHS says glandular fever is most common in people aged 15 to 24. Antibiotics do not work for glandular fever because it is caused by a virus. Quinsy is a collection of pus between the tonsil and the wall of the throat, and is a complication of tonsillitis.

body.heading: When should a GP be seen?
body.body: The NHS says to contact a GP practice if a sore throat has not started to improve after a week, and to ask for an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 for a very high temperature, feeling hot, cold or shivery, or a weakened immune system. A sore throat that does not get better within 10 to 14 days, or that gets worse rather than better, may suggest glandular fever.

body.heading: When is a sore throat an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for difficulty breathing, being unable to swallow, or drooling. Other reasons are a high-pitched noise when breathing in, a sore throat that is severe and getting worse quickly, swelling inside the mouth or throat, or trouble speaking. NHS 111 Wales advises that a person should not drive themselves to A&E but should ask someone to drive them or call 999.

statins-common-questions-answered.name: Statins: common questions answered
statins-common-questions-answered.headline: Statins: what they do and the common concerns, as the NHS describes them
statins-common-questions-answered.summary: The NHS says statins lower the cholesterol the body makes, to reduce the risk of heart attacks and strokes, and they are usually taken long term.
keyPoints: Statins work by lowering the amount of cholesterol the body makes, which helps stop cholesterol building up in blood vessels.
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease and to people who already have it.
Statins are usually taken long term, and the NHS says stopping can let cholesterol rise again.
Muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause is something the NHS says to get medical advice about.
Grapefruit juice affects some statins more than others, so the NHS says to ask a pharmacist or GP about the one prescribed.
The NHS says that stopping a statin can let cholesterol rise again, so it advises talking to a doctor first.

body.heading: What do statins do?
body.body:
Statins are medicines that lower cholesterol.

Cholesterol is a fatty substance made by the liver and carried in the blood.

According to the NHS, statins reduce how much cholesterol the body makes. This helps prevent a build-up of cholesterol in the blood vessels. High cholesterol can lead to cardiovascular disease, which includes heart attacks, strokes and peripheral arterial disease.

Atorvastatin and rosuvastatin are two of the statins the NHS describes, along with others such as simvastatin and pravastatin.

body.heading: Who are statins for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins may be offered to people at higher risk of cardiovascular disease when healthy lifestyle changes have not helped or are unlikely to help on their own. They may also be offered to people who already have cardiovascular disease, to lower the risk of a heart attack or stroke.

NICE has published a patient decision aid, "Are statins the best choice for me?", for people weighing up whether statins are right for them.

The NHS says most adults can take atorvastatin, and that it is sometimes prescribed for children aged 10 and over. Caution is needed for people with liver or kidney problems or a past allergic reaction to a statin. The NHS advises against atorvastatin in pregnancy.

body.heading: How long are statins taken for?
body.body:
The NHS says statins are usually taken long term.

For atorvastatin, the NHS says it can be taken for many years and works best when taken for a long time. It says cholesterol should fall within about four weeks if the medicine is taken as prescribed.

The NHS advises continuing atorvastatin even when a person feels well.

body.heading: What side effects can statins cause?
body.body:
For atorvastatin, the NHS lists headaches, dizziness, nausea, muscle aches and digestive upset such as diarrhoea or indigestion as common side effects.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says side effects often ease as the body gets used to the medicine, and that serious ones are rare.

The NHS lists rare serious effects including liver inflammation, pancreatitis, muscle damage and allergic reactions. It says yellowing of the skin or eyes can be a sign of liver problems, and that prompt medical attention is needed. For rosuvastatin, severe breathing or swallowing problems, or sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, are emergencies for which the NHS says to call 999.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS says to contact a doctor if side effects last more than a few days or get worse.

body.heading: What about muscle pain?
body.body:
The NHS lists muscle pain, tenderness, weakness or cramps with no clear cause as possible signs of muscle damage. For rosuvastatin it says to get medical advice promptly if these happen.

For atorvastatin, the NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for these symptoms. The NHS says that if side effects are the reason someone wants to stop, the doctor may be able to change the dose or switch medicine.

body.heading: Do grapefruit juice and other things affect statins?
body.body:
The NHS says grapefruit and grapefruit juice can affect some medicines by raising the level of the medicine in the blood, which makes side effects more likely.

The NHS treats statins differently: grapefruit juice is a particular concern with simvastatin, while atorvastatin is affected mainly by large amounts and some other statins are generally not a concern.

The NHS also says drinking a lot of alcohol regularly increases the chance of side effects and liver problems with atorvastatin.

It advises talking to a GP or pharmacist about grapefruit if it is a regular part of the diet and a medicine that is affected has been prescribed.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about stopping a statin?
body.body:
The NHS says stopping atorvastatin may cause cholesterol to rise, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

It says there are no withdrawal symptoms and no evidence that atorvastatin is addictive.

For rosuvastatin, the NHS advises talking to a doctor before stopping because of side effects, since the problem may be unrelated to the medicine. The NHS also advises not stopping a medicine without advice.

stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.name: Stomach ache: causes by area and warning signs
stomach-ache-causes-by-area-and-warning-.summary: Where a stomach ache sits helps point to causes such as appendicitis, gallstones or IBS, and sudden severe pain needs 999 or A&E.
keyPoints: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache.
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis.
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe.
The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What usually causes a stomach ache?
body.body: The NHS lists trapped wind, indigestion, constipation and a stomach bug or food poisoning as common everyday causes of stomach ache. The NHS links intense pain around the time of a period, sometimes with pain during or after sex and when pooing, with endometriosis.

body.heading: Does the area of the pain point to a cause?
body.body:
The NHS stomach ache page links pain in the lower right side of the tummy with appendicitis. NHS 111 Wales links severe pain that lasts for hours in the upper centre of the tummy, or just under the ribs on the right, with gallstones. It links ongoing cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).

NHS inform describes appendicitis as painful swelling of the appendix, and says the pain and cramping of IBS may be relieved by going to the toilet. Stomach ulcer pain is usually in the upper tummy, may feel burning and is often worse at night. Gastritis can cause pain, indigestion and feeling sick. Gastritis is inflammation of the lining of the stomach. Acute pancreatitis causes severe pain around the top of the tummy that develops suddenly, and gallstones and alcohol are its most common causes.

body.heading: What do appendicitis, gallstones and diverticular disease look like?
body.body: Appendicitis is when the appendix becomes inflamed; it usually causes pain in the lower right side of the tummy and is sometimes accompanied by nausea and loss of appetite. An NHS 111 Wales page says appendicitis needs urgent treatment in hospital. Many people with gallstones have no symptoms, but a stone can cause pain, jaundice or pancreatitis. NHS inform says diverticulitis, the inflamed form of diverticular disease, tends to cause more severe tummy pain, especially on the left side, and a fever. NHS 111 Wales advises urgent help from a GP or NHS 111 for blood or mucus in the stool, pain that gets worse or does not go away, or a high temperature or shivers.

body.heading: When is stomach pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if the pain started suddenly and is severe. Other reasons on the NHS page include struggling to breathe, confusion, and blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue. NHS inform adds chest pain and difficulty breathing to the reasons to call 999. For acute pancreatitis, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden, severe tummy pain together with any of: pain spreading to the back, bloating that does not go away, a fast heartbeat or difficulty breathing.

body.heading: When should it be checked the same day or by a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 if the ache suddenly gets much worse, if the person is pregnant, if there is blood in the poo, or if diarrhoea or vomiting has lasted several days.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: Treatment depends on the cause. For gastritis, a GP might arrange a breath test for Helicobacter pylori bacteria, a stool test or a blood test. Stomach ulcers may be treated with antibiotics for a Helicobacter pylori infection or with medicines that reduce stomach acid, such as proton pump inhibitors.

stop-smoking-nhs-support.name: Stopping smoking: the support the NHS offers
stop-smoking-nhs-support.summary: NHS stop smoking services offer nicotine replacement, medicines and professional support, and people in England can self-refer through NHS Better Health.
keyPoints: NHS stop smoking services provide nicotine replacement therapy and prescription medicines, together with professional support in the first months after quitting.
Vapes are not available as medicines on the NHS, though some local services may offer a free starter pack.
The NHS says cravings are short-lived and that withdrawal symptoms are temporary.

body.heading: What help do NHS stop smoking services provide?
body.body: NHS stop smoking services offer information and advice and professional support during the first few months after someone stops smoking. They provide nicotine replacement therapy, such as patches and gum, and medicines such as varenicline and bupropion. In England people can refer themselves to a local service through the NHS Better Health website, and can also speak to a GP. What a local service offers, such as eligibility for a free e-cigarette starter pack, varies by area.

body.heading: How do nicotine replacement and medicines work?
body.body: Nicotine replacement therapy comes as patches, gum, lozenges, microtabs, and mouth and nasal sprays. The NHS says nicotine replacement therapy gives the body nicotine without the other harmful chemicals found in cigarettes and tobacco. Varenicline works by blocking the effects of nicotine in the brain. NHS pages say that a nicotine-free medicine such as varenicline or cytisine can be combined with a nicotine product, and describe the combination as giving the best chance of success.

body.heading: Where do vapes fit in?
body.body: E-cigarettes are not currently available as medicines, so stop smoking services cannot supply them and they cannot be prescribed on the NHS. Some local stop smoking services may still offer a free starter pack.

body.heading: What happens in the body after stopping?
body.body: The NHS sets out a timeline: within about 20 minutes the pulse rate begins to return to normal. By 48 hours carbon monoxide levels in the blood have fallen to those of a non-smoker. After one year the risk of a heart attack is about half that of a person who smokes, and after ten years the risk of lung cancer is about half. NHS pages also report mental health benefits: once the withdrawal stage has passed, people report less anxiety, depression and stress.

body.heading: What are cravings and withdrawal like?
body.body: The NHS says withdrawal symptoms are temporary, usually strongest in the first week and lasting on average three to four weeks. NHS inform, the Scottish NHS site, says cravings should ease after the first two to three weeks. The NHS says an individual craving lasts only a short time. Walking, chewing sugar-free gum and deep breathing are among the coping ideas it lists.

body.heading: What other support is available?
body.body: In November 2024 NHS England announced a rollout of varenicline, a stop smoking pill, to help tens of thousands of people a year try to quit.

body.heading: Why does the NHS stress stopping?
body.body: The NHS Better Health site says the harm from smoking reaches beyond the lungs, including a higher risk of dementia and inflammation that can worsen joint pain. The relief a cigarette seems to give from stress is short-lived, and smoking can make anxiety and low mood worse over time, according to the NHS.

stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.name: Stress: how it shows up and where to get help
stress-symptoms-and-getting-help.summary: Stress is a reaction to mental or emotional pressure that can affect mood, body and behaviour, and the NHS says support is available when it affects daily life.
keyPoints: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often linked to feeling a loss of control.
Stress can show up as emotional changes, physical symptoms such as headaches and stomach problems, and changes in behaviour.
The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.
Adults in England can refer themselves to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP.

body.heading: What is stress?
body.body: The NHS describes stress as usually a reaction to mental or emotional pressure, often related to feeling a loss of control over something, though sometimes there is no obvious cause. Common triggers it lists include pressure at work, relationship or family difficulties, money worries, illness and bereavement. The NHS says most people feel stressed sometimes and some find stress helpful or even motivating, but that if it is affecting life there are things that may help. The NHS says too much stress can affect mood, the body and relationships.

body.heading: How does stress show up in the body and behaviour?
body.body: The NHS says stress can affect emotions, causing feelings such as irritability, anger and tearfulness. Physical symptoms listed include headaches, stomach problems, muscle tension and dizziness. Behaviour can change too, for example with sleep problems, loss of appetite, or drinking or smoking more.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for managing stress?
body.body: NHS pages suggest identifying the cause as the first step, then breaking large tasks into small targets and focusing on what can be changed. Controlled breathing, deep muscle relaxation and mindful breathing are listed as ways to reduce tension and some of the physical signs of stress. Talking to trusted friends, family or colleagues, or contacting a helpline, is also suggested. The NHS advises against using alcohol, cigarettes, gambling or drugs to relieve stress, because these can contribute to poor mental health.

body.heading: When does the NHS suggest getting help?
body.body: If urgent help is needed for mental health but it is not an emergency, the NHS says to use NHS 111 online or call 111 and choose the mental health option, or to ask for an urgent GP appointment. In England, adults aged 18 and over can refer themselves directly to NHS Talking Therapies without seeing a GP, and in some areas the minimum age is 16. If stress has led to thoughts of self-harm or suicide, call 999 if there is immediate danger, use NHS 111 and choose the mental health option for urgent help, or contact Samaritans free at any time on 116 123.

body.heading: What happens in the body during stress?
body.body: An NHS self-help guide describes stress as the body's reaction to feeling under threat, known as the fight or flight response, and says a certain amount of pressure can be helpful and motivating. The British Heart Foundation explains that the brain signals the body to release hormones such as adrenaline and cortisol. It says that if this response keeps being switched on again and again, over time it can take its toll on the body.

stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.name: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.headline: Stroke and TIA: spotting the signs and why 999 is the route
stroke-and-tia-spotting-the-signs.summary: A stroke and a TIA are both emergencies: the NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 even if the symptoms pass.
keyPoints: The FAST test checks for face drooping, arm weakness and speech problems, and the NHS says to call 999 if any sign is present.
A TIA, sometimes called a mini-stroke, is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to the brain, and its symptoms recover completely within 24 hours.
Symptoms of a TIA can pass, but the person still needs to be assessed in hospital, so call 999.
Treatment differs for strokes caused by a blood clot and strokes caused by bleeding, which is why a hospital scan comes first.
The Stroke Association runs a support helpline for people affected by stroke.

body.heading: What are the signs of a stroke?
body.body:
The FAST test is used across the UK to spot a stroke. It checks the face, the arms and the speech: has the mouth or eye drooped, can the person raise both arms fully and keep them there, and is their speech slurred or hard to understand.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say that any one of these signs is a reason to call 999. NHS England has found that many people wait too long to call 999, with an average of 88 minutes between the first symptom and the call.

If any one of these signs is seen, the NHS says to call 999. It also says not to wait for more symptoms to appear.

A stroke is a medical emergency, so call 999 even if symptoms seem minor or go away.

body.heading: What is a TIA, and how does it differ from a stroke?
body.body:
A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, is often called a mini-stroke. A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

NHS hospital guidance says the symptoms of a TIA recover completely within 24 hours. If symptoms last longer than that, it is classed as a stroke.

The NHS and the Stroke Association say to call 999 for a suspected stroke or TIA, even if the symptoms seem minor or go away.

A TIA is a temporary disruption of the blood supply to part of the brain.

body.heading: Why does a TIA matter if the symptoms pass?
body.body:
After a suspected TIA there is a risk of a stroke, which is why aspirin is given straight away to help prevent one.

For this reason the NHS says a suspected TIA should be assessed urgently, even if the symptoms have gone by the time the ambulance arrives. A person whose symptoms have cleared still needs to be seen in hospital.

body.heading: What happens in hospital?
body.body:
A scan is used to find out whether a stroke is caused by a blood clot (ischaemic) or by bleeding in the brain (haemorrhagic), because the treatments differ.

For an ischaemic stroke, emergency options include clot-busting medicine, called thrombolysis, and removal of the clot with a catheter, called thrombectomy. A stroke caused by bleeding is treated differently, with treatment aimed at stopping the bleeding and relieving pressure on the brain, sometimes with surgery.

Hospital teams aim to scan the brain soon after symptoms begin, which is part of why calling 999 matters.

A brain scan is done soon after symptoms begin to show whether a stroke is caused by a clot or a bleed.

Clot-busting drugs carry a risk of bleeding, so doctors weigh the risk against the benefit for each person.

Thrombectomy is used for clots that are too large for clot-busting drugs to break down.

body.heading: How is a suspected TIA treated?
body.body:
For a suspected TIA, the NHS says aspirin is usually given to lower the risk of a stroke, unless there is a medical reason to avoid it. The NHS says the person should be referred to a specialist within 24 hours of the start of their symptoms.

Care after a TIA can include a blood thinner such as aspirin, a statin, and blood pressure tablets if needed. Medicines that thin the blood or reduce clotting may be used, and sometimes surgery is offered to clear a narrowed artery in the neck.

After a TIA, treatment can include a blood thinner, a statin and blood pressure tablets if needed, and some people have surgery to unblock a narrowed neck artery.

body.heading: Where can people find support?
body.body:
The Stroke Association runs a Stroke Helpline on 0303 3033 100 for stroke survivors, their families and carers.

A GP can explain what the diagnosis means and arrange follow-up care. In an emergency, the route is always 999.

The Stroke Association helpline is free to use and supports stroke survivors, families and carers.

supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.name: Supporting someone with a mental health problem
supporting-someone-with-a-mental-health-.summary: Listening, asking open questions and offering practical help are the NHS's main suggestions for supporting someone with a mental health problem, without forcing them to talk.
keyPoints: The NHS suggests telling the person you are worried, carrying on as usual, and offering to listen.
Open questions that start with how, what, where or when give the person room to answer in their own words.
The NHS advises against forcing someone to talk or to get help.
If you or someone else is in immediate danger, call 999; NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123 offer urgent support.

body.heading: How can you start the conversation and help?
body.body: The NHS suggests telling the person that you are worried about them. It also suggests carrying on as usual, so the person is not treated differently because of what they are going through. Open questions that start with how, what, where or when are recommended. The NHS says not to force someone to talk to you. The NHS gives going with the person to professional appointments as an example of practical help.

body.heading: How can you point someone towards professional help?
body.body: For people who need more support, the NHS lists contacting a GP, calling NHS 111, or self-referring to NHS talking therapies. The NHS directs anyone who cannot cope or keep themselves safe to urgent support.

body.heading: What if the person wants to start talking?
body.body: The NHS guidance for people talking about their own mental health suggests choosing someone they trust who can offer the kind of support they need, and planning what to say. It notes that some people find it easier to talk while walking, travelling in a car or cooking, and that a person does not have to say everything at once. If the person chosen does not feel able to help, the NHS says not to take it personally.

body.heading: Where can someone get urgent help?
body.body: If someone is in immediate danger, or has been physically harmed, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent help that is not an emergency, NHS 111 has a mental health option (option 2), which trusts describe as available at any time, for yourself or on someone else's behalf. Samaritans listen at any time of day or night, and the number, 116 123, is free to call.

swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.name: Swollen ankles and legs: causes and red flags
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.headline: Swollen ankles, feet and legs: common causes and when to get help
swollen-ankles-and-legs-causes-and-red-f.summary: Swollen ankles and legs often come from sitting or standing for long periods, but can signal a clot or a heart, kidney or liver problem. The NHS names the signs that need 111 or 999.
keyPoints: The NHS lists sitting or standing for long periods, a high-salt diet, being overweight, pregnancy and some medicines among the more common causes of swollen ankles and legs.
Less often, swelling comes from a blood clot, an infection, or a heart, kidney or liver problem.
The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs does not improve after a few days of home care, gets worse, or occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.
Breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up blood or feeling faint with leg swelling may mean a clot in the lungs, which needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What commonly causes swollen ankles?
body.body: The NHS calls swollen ankles, feet and legs oedema, which is a build-up of fluid in the body’s tissues. The NHS lists sitting or standing still for long periods, a high-salt diet and being overweight as lifestyle factors. Pregnancy, varicose veins and thyroid problems can also cause swelling. Some medicines can also cause swelling.

body.heading: What are the less common causes?
body.body: Less commonly, swelling can follow an injury or an insect bite, or come from a blood clot or an infection. The NHS also lists problems with the heart, kidneys or liver as causes. The British Heart Foundation adds lymphoedema, a problem with the drainage of lymph fluid, as another cause.

body.heading: Why does one swollen leg matter more?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises seeking advice for swelling in only one leg when there is no known cause. The NHS describes deep vein thrombosis (DVT) as throbbing pain in one leg, usually in the calf or thigh, with swelling in that leg. The skin over a DVT can look red, blue or darker than usual.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if swelling in both legs has not improved after a few days of home care, if it gets worse, or if it occurs in someone with a heart, kidney or leg vein condition.

body.heading: What can ease the swelling?
body.body: The NHS says swelling in the ankles, feet or legs often goes away on its own. Its self-care advice includes raising the swollen area on a chair or pillows, gentle exercise such as walking, and avoiding long periods of standing or sitting. Wide, comfortable shoes with a low heel and washing and moisturising the feet to prevent infection are also mentioned. Treatment for swelling that does not settle depends on the cause. The British Heart Foundation says heart failure treatment includes medicines that help the heart pump more effectively and diuretics, which make you pass more urine and help relieve ankle swelling.

body.heading: Which signs mean urgent help?
body.body: NHS 111 Wales advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for swelling that is severe, painful, sudden, red or hot, or that comes with a high temperature or shivering. The same page lists swelling in the feet, ankles or legs of a person with diabetes as a reason for urgent advice. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if leg swelling comes with shortness of breath or chest pain, because a clot can travel to the lungs. Coughing up blood or feeling faint are also described as symptoms of a clot in the lungs. In pregnancy, very swollen ankles, fingers, hands or face can be a sign of pre-eclampsia, and NHS inform says to contact a midwife or GP immediately.

thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.name: Thyroid blood tests: TSH and T4 explained
thyroid-blood-tests-tsh-and-t4-explained.summary: Thyroid tests read TSH and free T4 together: a high TSH with low T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and the reverse an overactive one.
keyPoints: TSH is the most sensitive marker of thyroid status, and it is read together with free T4.
A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, and a low TSH with a high free T4 suggests an overactive thyroid.
A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism and is followed over time.
Severe illness and some medicines can change thyroid results without a thyroid disease.

body.heading: What do TSH and T4 show?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes thyroid hormones. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, or TSH, comes from the pituitary gland and tells the thyroid how much hormone to make. The British Thyroid Foundation calls TSH the most sensitive marker of thyroid status. T4 is the main thyroid hormone, and doctors usually look at free T4, the part not bound to proteins. Results are read as a pattern of TSH and free T4 together, not one number alone.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an underactive thyroid?
body.body: A high TSH with a low free T4 suggests an underactive thyroid, called hypothyroidism. The NHS says a blood test measuring hormone levels is the only accurate way to find out whether there is a problem. A GP will also ask about symptoms and may examine the neck. Thyroid UK says a low free T4 with a raised TSH will usually give a diagnosis of hypothyroidism.

body.heading: What pattern suggests an overactive thyroid?
body.body: The reverse pattern, a low TSH with a high free T4, suggests an overactive thyroid, called hyperthyroidism. The NHS describes blood tests as part of how an overactive thyroid is diagnosed.

body.heading: What if the results are borderline?
body.body: A slightly raised TSH with a normal free T4 is called subclinical hypothyroidism. It may gradually develop into clinical hypothyroidism over many years. A test for thyroid antibodies helps to judge that risk. Thyroid UK says there is no evidence that routine early treatment helps when the TSH is only a little above the reference range. A low TSH with a low free T4 may come from a problem with the pituitary gland, or from a significant illness that does not involve the thyroid.

body.heading: Can illness or medicines change the result?
body.body: Abnormal T4 levels do not always mean a condition that needs treatment. Severe illness and some medicines, such as birth control pills and steroids, can affect T4 levels.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Underactive thyroid is usually treated with daily hormone replacement tablets called levothyroxine. The NHS says this treatment is long term to prevent symptoms. NHS inform says a mild case with no symptoms may not need treatment. Regular blood tests check that the dose is right, because a wrong dose can cause side effects such as feeling sick, diarrhoea, headaches or problems sleeping. For people on replacement, TSH is the main test used to check that the treatment is adequate.

body.heading: What can cause an underactive or overactive thyroid?
body.body: In the UK the main cause of an underactive thyroid is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease. Damage to the thyroid during treatment for an overactive thyroid or thyroid cancer is another cause. Common symptoms of an underactive thyroid include tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold, constipation and low mood, and they develop slowly. Graves' disease is the most common cause of an overactive thyroid. Symptoms of an overactive thyroid include nervousness, weight loss despite a good appetite, a fast or irregular heartbeat, tremor and sleep difficulty. Treatment for an overactive thyroid can include anti-thyroid medicines, beta-blockers for symptoms such as tremor, and radioactive iodine. Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid afterwards. In Graves' disease, blood tests look for antibodies as well as hormone levels.

tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.name: Tiredness and fatigue: causes and next steps
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.headline: Tiredness that will not go away: common causes and what a GP checks
tiredness-and-fatigue-causes-and-gp-chec.summary: Tiredness is common and often has an ordinary cause such as poor sleep, stress or illness. The NHS advises a GP appointment when it lasts a few weeks without explanation.
keyPoints: The NHS lists poor sleep, an unhealthy lifestyle, hormonal changes, some illnesses and some medicines among the common causes of tiredness.
The NHS advises booking a GP appointment when tiredness has lasted a few weeks without a clear reason, affects daily life or comes with other symptoms such as weight loss.
A GP may arrange blood tests to look for conditions such as anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid.
Self-help advice from the NHS covers diet, exercise, relaxation and sleep habits.

body.heading: What counts as fatigue?
body.body: Everyone feels tired from time to time, and the NHS treats tiredness as a common symptom with many possible causes. Fatigue is described by the NHS as tiredness that is not relieved by rest and sleep. If there is no obvious reason for the tiredness and it goes on for a while without improving, the NHS says it may be a sign of a medical condition.

body.heading: What are the common causes?
body.body: The NHS names poor sleep or difficulty getting to sleep (insomnia) and an unhealthy lifestyle as common causes. Hormonal changes can also make people tired. Stress, depression and bereavement are also listed as triggers. Some medicines, including chemotherapy, can cause tiredness. Among medical conditions, the NHS mentions sleep apnoea, iron deficiency anaemia, diabetes and an overactive thyroid as possible reasons. Gasping, snorting or choking noises during sleep are one of the reasons the NHS gives for seeing a GP, because they can point to a sleep problem.

body.heading: When is it worth seeing a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises a routine GP appointment if tiredness has lasted a few weeks and the cause is unclear. A GP appointment is also advised if the tiredness affects daily life. Other symptoms alongside the tiredness, such as weight loss or changes in mood, are further reasons to book one.

body.heading: What might a GP do?
body.body: A GP will usually ask about lifestyle and general health to look for an explanation. The NHS says tests may be needed, such as blood tests to check for anaemia, diabetes or an overactive thyroid. If the cause is still unclear, a GP may refer the person to a specialist.

body.heading: What does the NHS suggest for self-care?
body.body: The NHS self-help advice covers eating a healthy diet, taking exercise, finding ways to relax and improving sleep. Caffeine can disrupt sleep, which is one reason it appears in the NHS tips. The NHS also says there is some evidence that talking therapies such as counselling or cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) may help with fatigue, and a GP can arrange a referral. Eating regular meals and healthy snacks through the day is part of the NHS advice for keeping energy steady. The NHS self-help page says regular physical activity improves energy over time. It also links excess weight with tiredness, because carrying extra weight puts extra strain on the heart. Stress uses up a lot of energy, so the NHS suggests relaxing activities. Alcohol lowers the quality of sleep, which can leave a person tired the next day.

body.heading: Could it be ME/CFS?
body.body: Myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a long-term condition whose most common symptom is extreme tiredness. There is no specific test for ME/CFS, so a diagnosis is made from the symptoms and by ruling out other conditions that could explain them.

references.title: NHS: Self-help tips to fight tiredness

troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.name: Troponin blood test: what it shows
troponin-blood-test-what-it-shows.summary: A troponin test measures proteins released when heart muscle is damaged, and a raised result does not always mean a heart attack.
keyPoints: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged.
The more damage, the more troponin reaches the blood, and levels rise over hours, so the test is often repeated.
A raised troponin may point to a heart attack, but other conditions can raise it too.
The NHS says to call 999 for chest pain that is tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw.

body.heading: What is troponin?
body.body: Troponin T and troponin I are proteins found in heart muscle. They are released into the blood when the heart muscle is damaged, for example in a heart attack. The more damage there is, the more troponin reaches the blood.

body.heading: Why is a troponin test done?
body.body: Clinicians mainly use the test to check whether a heart attack is happening or has recently happened. It is typically ordered when someone has chest pain or other signs of a heart attack. It can also be ordered for worsening angina without other signs of a heart attack, and to look for other causes of heart injury.

body.heading: How is it used in hospital?
body.body: The NHS treats an ECG as an important early test in a suspected heart attack, and says it should be done within 10 minutes of arrival at hospital. Blood tests look for troponin, which leaks slowly into the blood after damage to the heart. Levels usually rise over hours, so testing is often repeated over several hours. NICE guidance quoted by the NHS says a second troponin sample is usually taken a few hours after the first, unless the first is normal and the risk is judged low. Newer high-sensitivity tests can detect a rise sooner after chest pain begins.

body.heading: What does a normal or raised result mean?
body.body: Normal levels some hours after symptoms began make a heart attack unlikely. Very high levels most often mean a heart attack has occurred. Raised levels do not always mean a heart attack, because other heart conditions can raise troponin. A UK study reported by University Hospital Southampton found raised troponin in some people with unrelated conditions, so results need careful interpretation. After a heart attack, levels may stay high for one to two weeks.

body.heading: How do the results fit with the ECG?
body.body: The ECG and troponin results together help to identify the type of heart attack. A STEMI shows particular changes on the ECG. An NSTEMI is found when the ECG does not show those changes but blood tests show heart damage.

body.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
body.body: The NHS advises calling 999 for chest pain that feels tight or squeezing, or that spreads to the arms, neck or jaw. Severe difficulty breathing, pale, blue or grey lips or skin, and passing out also need a 999 call. The NHS says not to drive to A&E, because the person on the 999 line gives advice on what to do.

body.heading: What do NICE recommendations say about newer tests?
body.body: NICE recommends high-sensitivity troponin tests as options for ruling out a type of heart attack called NSTEMI in emergency departments. The approach can use a single sample on arrival, or a second sample about three hours later. NICE advises that a negative result should not lead to discharge without further investigation if the person looks visibly unwell or the sample was taken too early after the suspected event. NICE says sex-specific thresholds should be used for diagnosing a heart attack in men and women.

type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.name: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.headline: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes compared: causes, symptoms and treatment
type-1-and-type-2-diabetes-compared.summary: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition treated with insulin; type 2 develops when the body makes too little insulin or it works poorly.
keyPoints: In type 1 diabetes the immune system attacks and destroys the cells that make insulin.
In type 2 diabetes the body makes too little insulin or the insulin it makes does not work well.
Type 1 often develops quickly, especially in young people, while type 2 develops slowly over years.
Type 1 is treated with insulin and blood glucose checks; type 2 is managed with lifestyle changes and sometimes medicines.
There is no cure for diabetes at the moment, although type 2 can sometimes go into remission.

body.heading: What do the two types have in common?
body.body:
Diabetes is a condition in which there is too much glucose, a type of sugar, in the blood. Both type 1 and type 2 involve insulin, a hormone made by cells in the pancreas.

The two types share several symptoms: increased thirst, passing urine more often, tiredness and weight loss. The difference lies in why the problem arises and how it is managed.

body.heading: What causes type 1 diabetes?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition. The immune system attacks and destroys the cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

In young people the symptoms usually develop very quickly, over a few days or weeks. In adults, the symptoms often take longer to develop, sometimes a few months.

body.heading: What causes type 2 diabetes?
body.body:
Either the body does not make enough insulin, or the insulin it makes does not work as well as it should.

Diabetes UK lists age, family history, ethnicity and weight among the risk factors.

Type 2 develops slowly over a period of years, so the signs may not be obvious.

body.heading: How are the two types treated?
body.body:
Type 1 diabetes is treated with insulin, which is needed for life, alongside monitoring of blood glucose.

Type 2 diabetes is managed with lifestyle changes such as eating healthily, exercising and trying to lose weight, and sometimes with medicines. Medicine may be added if needed, such as metformin, and some people also need insulin.

body.heading: Can diabetes be cured?
body.body:
Diabetes UK says there is no cure for diabetes at the moment. Type 2 diabetes can sometimes be put into remission, and it can sometimes be prevented.

Remission does not mean the condition has gone for good, which is why regular checks are still part of care.

body.heading: How is diabetes checked, and who should be seen?
body.body:
Blood tests are used to diagnose and monitor diabetes. The site's pages on blood glucose and on HbA1c explain what they show, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

The NHS says to get a GP appointment as soon as possible for the main symptoms of diabetes; for a child, to contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure what to do. The NHS website sets out the symptoms to look for.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: For a child with diabetes symptoms, contact the GP practice urgently or use NHS 111 if unsure; call 999 if a child is very drowsy, confused, breathing fast or deeply, has severe tummy pain or keeps vomiting. In someone with diabetes, loss of appetite, feeling or being sick, a high temperature, stomach pain or fruity-smelling breath needs urgent medical attention, so call NHS 111 or 999 if severe. Remission means blood sugar stays below the diabetes level for at least six months without diabetes medicine.

ukhsa-diwali-urges-flu-covid-rsv-vaccina.name: UKHSA urges vaccination before Diwali
ukhsa-diwali-urges-flu-covid-rsv-vaccina.summary: On 30 October 2026 UKHSA asked eligible people celebrating Diwali to get their flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines before the festivities, saying the vaccines can take several days to provide maximum protection.
keyPoints: UKHSA published the message on 30 October 2026 for people celebrating Diwali who are eligible for flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines.
UKHSA says the vaccines can take several days to provide maximum protection.
UKHSA notes that children can have the free flu vaccine at school, or a nasal vaccine at a participating pharmacy.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
UKHSA is calling on eligible people who celebrate Diwali to come forward for flu, COVID-19 and RSV vaccines before the festival. It says the vaccines can take several days to give maximum protection, so earlier is better.

The agency also says indoor gatherings in enclosed spaces with less ventilation can help airborne viruses spread.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
UKHSA points out that eligible children can have the free flu vaccine at school, and that this year children can also have the nasal flu vaccine at a participating pharmacy. It adds that pregnant women and people aged 75 and over can have the RSV vaccine.

Not everyone is eligible for every vaccine, and the groups named above are those the release mentions. This site's influenza vaccine page describes the flu vaccine.
