ukhsa-flu-levels-low-but-higher-than-pre.name: UKHSA: flu low but above last four years
ukhsa-flu-levels-low-but-higher-than-pre.summary: UKHSA reported on 8 October 2026 that flu levels were low at the start of the season but higher than at the same point in the previous four years, and urged eligible people to be vaccinated.
keyPoints: UKHSA reported on 8 October 2026 that flu activity was low at the start of the season but higher than in each of the previous four years.
UKHSA described possible signs of an early flu season.
UKHSA says it takes a couple of weeks for the vaccine to give full protection.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
UKHSA says flu activity in September was higher than in the same period of each of the past four winters, although it remained at baseline, which means very low levels. Flu trends have been rising since August, and UKHSA says there are possible signs of an early flu season.

In a related UKHSA blog post, the agency says the rise so far has been driven largely by cases in 18 to 24 year olds. Early typing data show an equal mix of influenza A(H3N2) and A(H1N1) in England.

body.heading: What it means
body.body:
UKHSA urges people who are eligible to be vaccinated. It says the vaccine takes a couple of weeks to give full protection, so getting it sooner rather than later is better.

The blog post also notes that last season started early but was milder overall, with lower activity and mortality than the year before. This site's influenza vaccine page explains the vaccine in more detail.

underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.name: Underactive and overactive thyroid
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.headline: Underactive and overactive thyroid compared: symptoms, causes and treatment
underactive-and-overactive-thyroid-compa.summary: An underactive thyroid does not make enough thyroid hormone, while an overactive thyroid makes too much; the symptoms, causes and treatments differ.
keyPoints: An underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) means the gland does not make enough thyroid hormone; an overactive one (hyperthyroidism) means it makes too much.
Symptoms differ: an underactive thyroid can cause tiredness, feeling cold and weight gain, while an overactive one can cause nervousness, sensitivity to heat, a fast heartbeat and weight loss.
The main cause of an underactive thyroid in the UK is an autoimmune condition called Hashimoto's disease.
Underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets; overactive thyroid with medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery.
Treatment for an overactive thyroid can lead to an underactive thyroid, so follow-up blood tests matter.

body.heading: What does the thyroid do?
body.body: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones which help control the body's energy use. An underactive thyroid does not make enough of these hormones, while an overactive thyroid makes too much.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an underactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS describes an underactive thyroid as a common condition in which the thyroid does not make enough hormone. Common symptoms include tiredness, feeling colder than usual, weight gain, constipation, low mood, and dry skin or hair.

Symptoms may be mild and can develop slowly, so they are not always easy to notice.

Because the symptoms of an underactive thyroid overlap with other conditions, it cannot be diagnosed from symptoms alone.

body.heading: What are the symptoms of an overactive thyroid?
body.body:
The NHS says an overactive thyroid, also called hyperthyroidism, means the thyroid makes too much hormone. Symptoms can include nervousness, anxiety, mood swings, sleep problems, tiredness, sensitivity to heat, and a fast or irregular heartbeat.

Tremors and weight loss can also occur, and it is unlikely that one person would have all of the symptoms.

body.heading: What causes each condition?
body.body:
In the UK, the main cause of an underactive thyroid is Hashimoto's disease, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks the thyroid.

The main cause of an overactive thyroid is Graves' disease, another autoimmune condition. Thyroid nodules can also cause an overactive thyroid, though less commonly.

Other causes of an underactive thyroid include thyroiditis, neck surgery or radiotherapy, treatment for an overactive thyroid, and some medicines.

body.heading: How are they treated?
body.body:
An underactive thyroid is usually treated with levothyroxine tablets, which replace the missing hormone. The NHS says they are usually needed for life, with regular blood tests to check that the treatment is right.

An overactive thyroid can be treated with antithyroid medicine, radioactive iodine or surgery. Beta blockers can help control some of the symptoms in the meantime, but they do not stop the thyroid making too much hormone.

Radioactive iodine often leads to an underactive thyroid that then needs lifelong hormone tablets.

body.heading: How is the thyroid tested, and when should someone get help?
body.body:
Thyroid function is checked with blood tests that measure thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroid hormones. The site's pages on thyroid function tests and TSH explain them, and the laboratory report shows the reference range used.

A GP can examine the neck and arrange blood tests to check how well the thyroid is working. Thyroid storm is a rare, life-threatening flare-up of an overactive thyroid that the NHS calls a medical emergency, so it needs a 999 call.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Some people feel better soon after starting levothyroxine, while others do not notice a change in symptoms for several months. An overactive thyroid that is not treated or is poorly controlled can lead to eye problems and pregnancy complications as well as thyroid storm. A high TSH with a low thyroid hormone level in the blood could mean an underactive thyroid, while a low TSH with high thyroid hormone levels usually means an overactive thyroid. Radioactive iodine is not suitable for everyone, for example people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and surgery is usually kept for cases such as a large goitre or when other treatments cannot be used.

unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.name: Unexplained weight loss: causes and next steps
unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.headline: Losing weight without trying: possible causes and when to see a GP
unexplained-weight-loss-causes-and-next-.summary: Losing weight without changing diet or exercise has many causes, from stress to thyroid or digestive conditions. The NHS advises seeing a GP as a precaution.
keyPoints: Unintentional weight loss means losing weight without changing diet or exercise, and the NHS says it is important to get it checked by a GP.
The NHS lists mental health conditions, digestive problems, overactive thyroid and heart failure among the causes.
A GP will ask about general health and may arrange tests or scans.

body.heading: What is unintentional weight loss?
body.body: Unintentional weight loss is losing weight without changing your diet or exercise routine. NHS 111 Wales says unintentional weight loss can follow a stressful event and can sometimes signal a serious illness.

body.heading: What can cause it?
body.body: Mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, eating disorders and obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) are on the NHS list. Digestive problems are listed, including coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease. Hormone conditions such as an overactive thyroid and type 1 diabetes can cause weight loss. Heart conditions such as heart failure are also listed. Some medicines can cause weight loss as well, and cancer is another possible cause.

body.heading: When should you see a GP?
body.body: The NHS advises seeing a GP if you keep losing weight without changing your diet or exercise. NHS 111 Wales advises being seen promptly if the weight loss comes with other symptoms. NHS malnutrition advice also says to see a GP after losing a lot of weight unintentionally over a few months. A GP will ask about general health and may arrange some tests or scans.

uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.name: UTI and cystitis: what they are
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.headline: Urinary tract infection and cystitis: symptoms, treatment and when to get help
uti-and-cystitis-what-they-are.summary: A urinary tract infection (UTI) can affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys; cystitis is a UTI of the bladder, and antibiotics are not always needed.
keyPoints: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection anywhere in the urinary system, and cystitis is a UTI in the bladder.
Common symptoms are pain or burning when passing urine, needing to go more often, and cloudy urine.
Fever, pain in the back or side below the ribs, or blood in the urine can point to a more serious infection.
Antibiotics can treat UTIs, but the NHS says they are not always needed and many cases can be eased at home.
Urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP is advised for symptoms such as blood in the urine, back pain or a high temperature.

body.heading: What is the difference between a UTI and cystitis?
body.body: A urinary tract infection (UTI) is an infection in any part of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, the tubes that carry urine, the bladder and the urethra. Cystitis is the name for an infection of the bladder.

body.heading: What are the symptoms?
body.body:
The NHS lists burning or pain when passing urine, needing to pass urine more often (including at night), and cloudy urine. Cystitis can also bring lower tummy pain.

A kidney infection is more serious. Symptoms that point towards it include a high temperature, pain in the back or side under the ribs, feeling shivery or unwell, and blood in the urine.

In older people, a kidney infection may cause confusion.

A UTI can also cause blood in the urine, a fever, or feeling hot, cold and shivery.

body.heading: What causes a UTI?
body.body:
UTIs happen when bacteria, usually from the gut, get into the urinary tract. Pregnancy, using spermicide with contraception and not drinking enough fluids are among the things the NHS links with a higher chance of getting one.

People who use a urinary catheter, or who have a weakened immune system, are also at higher risk.

UTIs are more common in women, because the urethra is shorter and sits close to the anus.

body.heading: How is a UTI treated?
body.body:
The NHS says antibiotics are not always needed, and many cases can be eased at home. The NHS says paracetamol and drinking plenty of fluids can ease symptoms, and NHS guidance says there is no evidence that cranberry products help ease symptoms once an infection has started.

A pharmacist can advise on treatment and whether a GP is needed, and a GP may prescribe a short course of antibiotics.

Most kidney infections need prompt treatment with antibiotics, and some people, such as those who are pregnant or have a long-term health condition, may be treated in hospital.

body.heading: When should someone get medical help?
body.body:
The NHS advises contacting a GP or NHS 111 the same day for blood in the urine, pain in the back or side, a very high or low temperature, vomiting, or not having passed urine all day. The same applies to anyone who is pregnant, uses a catheter or has a weakened immune system.

The NHS advises seeing a GP if urinary symptoms have not improved after a few days, or if UTIs keep coming back.

Confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking can be a sign of a serious infection, and the route is 999 or A&E.

A very low temperature, feeling or being sick, or not having passed urine all day are also reasons to contact a GP or NHS 111 urgently.

The NHS says confusion, drowsiness or difficulty speaking is a reason to call 999 or go to A&E, with someone else driving rather than the person themselves.

body.heading: What else do the sources say?
body.body: Some GPs suggest waiting a couple of days before giving antibiotics for a UTI. The NHS suggests avoiding drinks that can irritate the bladder, such as coffee, alcohol and fruit juice. For kidney infections, painkillers like ibuprofen are not usually recommended, so ask a pharmacist or GP what is safe. If UTIs keep coming back, the NHS advises seeing a GP.

vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.name: Vitamin B12 and folate tests explained
vitamin-b12-and-folate-tests-explained.summary: B12 and folate blood tests help find the cause of deficiency anaemia, but a B12 result alone can miss cases, so symptoms matter too.
keyPoints: Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency can both cause anaemia in which the body makes abnormally large red blood cells.
A GP combines symptoms with blood tests that check the level of vitamin B12 and of folate.
A UK clinical guideline says a B12 blood test is not completely reliable, so two tests are requested when deficiency is suspected.
B12 deficiency is usually treated with injections of hydroxocobalamin, and folate deficiency with folic acid tablets.

body.heading: What are vitamin B12 and folate deficiency anaemia?
body.body: Vitamin B12 and folate are both needed to make healthy red blood cells. When either is lacking, the body can make abnormally large red blood cells that do not work as they should. This is called vitamin B12 or folate deficiency anaemia.

body.heading: What symptoms can it cause?
body.body: The NHS lists tiredness along with numbness, muscle weakness, psychological problems, problems with balance and coordination, pins and needles and incontinence. Folate deficiency anaemia adds symptoms such as breathlessness, pale skin and palpitations. Some effects of B12 deficiency can appear without anaemia and without a low blood level. Mouth ulcers, a sore red tongue and problems with vision or memory are also listed.

body.heading: How is it diagnosed?
body.body: A GP typically combines symptoms with blood tests. The blood tests check the level of vitamin B12 and the level of folate in the blood. A UK clinical guideline notes that a vitamin B12 blood test is not completely reliable and asks for two tests when deficiency is suspected. The same guideline says routine screening for B12 deficiency is not appropriate. The NHS says a GP should be involved when the cause is unclear, in pregnancy, or when symptoms suggest the nervous system is affected.

body.heading: What causes deficiency?
body.body: The NHS says pernicious anaemia is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in the UK. Pernicious anaemia is an autoimmune condition that affects the stomach, so B12 from food is not absorbed. Lack of B12 from the diet is uncommon, but it can happen with a vegan diet that includes no supplements or fortified foods. Some medicines, including proton pump inhibitors and metformin, can reduce B12 levels. Folate deficiency can be linked to some medicines, such as certain anticonvulsants and methotrexate.

body.heading: How is it treated?
body.body: B12 deficiency anaemia is usually treated with injections of vitamin B12, called hydroxocobalamin. When the cause is diet, treatment may be daily B12 tablets instead. Folate deficiency is usually treated with folic acid tablets. Clinicians check B12 status first, because folic acid can mask a vitamin B12 deficiency. Follow-up blood tests check that treatment is working. A GP appointment is the route for symptoms such as numbness, pins and needles or problems with balance.

vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.name: Vitamins and supplements: who may need them
vitamin-d-and-supplements-who-needs-them.summary: The NHS says a varied and balanced diet should provide enough of several vitamins, but advises supplements for some people, including vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy.
keyPoints: NHS pages advise that everyone should consider taking a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.
Some groups, including people who are rarely outdoors and people with dark skin, are advised to take vitamin D all year.
The NHS advises anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant to take a folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy.
More is not always better: the NHS warns that very high vitamin D intakes could be harmful.

body.heading: Can a balanced diet provide everything?
body.body: NHS pages say that a varied and balanced diet should provide all that is needed of some vitamins, such as vitamin A, while supplements are advised for some groups. The NHS says that from about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin.

body.heading: Who is advised to take vitamin D?
body.body: The NHS says everyone should consider a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter. In England the NHS advises all babies and children aged 1 to 4 to take vitamin D throughout the year, and NHS inform in Scotland describes babies and children under 5 as a higher-risk group. Some groups are advised to take it all year: people who are not often outdoors, such as those who are frail or housebound or living in care homes, people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors, and people with dark skin from African, African-Caribbean or South Asian backgrounds. For breastfed babies the NHS advises a daily vitamin D supplement throughout the year, and children aged 1 to 4 are also advised to take it year-round. Healthy Start vitamin products are free for eligible families.

body.heading: What does the NHS say about pregnancy?
body.body: Anyone who is pregnant or could become pregnant is advised to take a daily folic acid supplement until the twelfth week of pregnancy. The NHS says some people need a higher dose, for example those with diabetes or taking medicine for epilepsy, and that this is arranged with a doctor.

body.heading: Can too much be harmful?
body.body: For vitamin D, the NHS says there is an upper daily limit for vitamin D supplements above which they could be harmful, and this applies to adults, pregnant and breastfeeding women and children aged 11 to 17. For folic acid, the NHS says low supplement amounts are unlikely to cause harm, and that higher amounts can mask the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency.

body.heading: What do some common nutrients do?
body.body: For vitamin A, the NHS says most people should be able to get all they need from a varied and balanced diet. The NHS says vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body. It says that from about late March or early April to the end of September most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin. Iron is important for making red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body. Liver is very rich in vitamin A; the NHS says liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week, and advises people who are pregnant to avoid them.

vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.name: Vitamin D blood test: who needs one?
vitamin-d-blood-test-who-needs-one.summary: NHS guidance does not recommend routine vitamin D tests for people without symptoms, and testing is kept for specific symptoms or conditions.
keyPoints: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms.
Testing is considered for bone pain, muscle weakness, abnormal calcium results, malabsorption or kidney disease.
A lack of vitamin D can cause rickets in children and bone pain from osteomalacia in adults.
The NHS says everyone can consider a daily supplement in autumn and winter, and people at higher risk all year.

body.heading: What does a vitamin D blood test show?
body.body: The test measures the level of vitamin D in the blood, usually as 25-hydroxyvitamin D. The body makes vitamin D under the skin when it is exposed to sunlight. In the UK, levels tend to drop in winter.

body.heading: Who is tested and who is not?
body.body: NHS guidance says not to test routinely for vitamin D deficiency in people without symptoms. Testing is generally considered for bone pain or softness in adults, a condition called osteomalacia, and for unexplained muscle weakness. It is also considered for abnormal calcium or parathyroid hormone results, before some bone treatments, and in malabsorption conditions and kidney disease. People at higher risk who have no symptoms do not need routine testing but should be advised on a maintenance supplement. Higher risk applies to people over a certain age, those who get little sun and those with darker skin.

body.heading: What does a low level cause?
body.body: A lack of vitamin D can lead to bone deformities such as rickets in children. In adults it can cause bone pain through osteomalacia. An NHS medical director described more general signs of tiredness and aches and pains. In some cases the bones can become softer.

body.heading: How are the results read?
body.body: One NHS trust laboratory divides results into deficient, possibly inadequate for some people, and sufficient for almost everyone. A level in the middle band may be adequate in some people, yet treatment is advised when someone has the symptoms that prompted the test. Local guidance varies, so the report shows the range used by the laboratory. Treatment for confirmed deficiency is usually set by a clinician.

body.heading: Who is advised to take a supplement?
body.body: NHS England advice is that everyone should consider taking a daily vitamin D supplement during the autumn and winter. Scottish advice is similar and applies from age five upwards. People at higher risk are advised to take a supplement all year, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, children under five, and people with little sun exposure. People of African, African-Caribbean and South Asian origin are also in the higher-risk group. NHS guidance warns that taking too much vitamin D could be harmful. Most people buy standard supplements over the counter, because NHS England has moved away from routine prescribing for prevention.

body.heading: Where else does vitamin D come from?
body.body: Sunlight on the skin is the main source in the warmer months. Food sources include oily fish, egg yolks and fortified foods.

body.heading: What are rickets and osteomalacia?
body.body: Low vitamin D often causes no symptoms. Some people have symptoms such as tiredness and aches. In children, a deficiency can lead to rickets, where the bones are weak, soft and can become deformed. Rickets is more common in children with darker skin who spend little time in the sun. Local NHS guidance lists premature babies, exclusively breastfed babies and children taking some anticonvulsants as other higher-risk groups.

warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.name: Warfarin and apixaban: medicines and food
warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.headline: Taking warfarin or apixaban: why other medicines and food matter
warfarin-apixaban-medicines-and-food.summary: Bleeding is the main risk of both, so the NHS says other medicines, alcohol and, for warfarin, some foods and INR blood tests all matter.
keyPoints: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulants, medicines used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots.
The NHS says the amount of vitamin K-rich food should stay consistent on warfarin, and that cranberry products and grapefruit juice are avoided.
Warfarin needs regular INR blood tests, which measure how quickly the blood clots.
Both medicines can cause bleeding, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding or after a head injury.
Anyone taking either medicine should check with a pharmacist before using other medicines, herbal products or supplements.

body.heading: What are warfarin and apixaban for?
body.body: Warfarin and apixaban are anticoagulant medicines, which are used to prevent and treat harmful blood clots. An NHS trust explains that warfarin works by blocking vitamin K, which is involved in the clotting process. The same trust lists apixaban among the direct oral anticoagulants, or DOACs, a different group of anticoagulants that NICE has approved for preventing stroke in people with atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm. Both medicines make bleeding the main thing to watch for, which is why other medicines and some food and drink matter.

body.heading: Does food or drink matter with warfarin?
body.body: The NHS says some food and drink can change how warfarin works. NHS inform lists green leafy vegetables such as broccoli, spinach and lettuce, chickpeas, liver, egg yolks, mature and blue cheese, avocado and olive oil as rich in vitamin K, which can interfere with warfarin. The advice is to keep the amount eaten steady rather than cut these foods out. Cranberry juice and cranberry products, and grapefruit juice, should be avoided, because they can increase the effect of warfarin and the risk of bleeding. NHS inform also says that getting drunk or binge drinking is dangerous on warfarin, as it may increase the medicine's effect and the risk of bleeding.

body.heading: Does food or alcohol matter with apixaban?
body.body: The NHS page on apixaban says it can be taken with or without food. On alcohol, NHS hospital leaflets differ in emphasis. One says heavy or binge drinking raises the risk of bleeding. Another says apixaban does not interact with alcohol and advises drinking in moderation within UK guidelines. A pharmacist or the prescriber can say what applies to a particular person.

body.heading: Which other medicines can interact?
body.body: The NHS says to tell a doctor, anticoagulant clinic or pharmacist about any new medicine, including products bought over the counter. For warfarin, the NHS says St John's wort, a herbal remedy, and vitamin K supplements should not be taken. For apixaban, the NHS lists other anticoagulants, some antifungal medicines and antibiotics, some heart-rhythm and epilepsy medicines and transplant medicines among those that can interact. It says St John's wort should not be taken with apixaban, and that there is not enough information to show other herbal remedies and supplements are safe, so a pharmacist should be asked. On painkillers, NHS advice says aspirin and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen increase the chance of bleeding and are not taken unless a doctor has said it is fine. The NHS apixaban page says paracetamol is generally fine. NHS trust leaflets for warfarin say occasional paracetamol is acceptable but regular or prolonged use can raise the INR. A pharmacist can advise before over-the-counter remedies or herbal products are bought.

body.heading: Why does warfarin need INR blood tests?
body.body: The NHS says warfarin treatment needs regular blood tests to measure how quickly the blood clots, called the international normalised ratio, or INR. NHS trust leaflets say tests are frequent at first and are spaced out once the dose is stable. The clinic uses the result to adjust the warfarin dose, and the target depends on the condition being treated. New medicines, antibiotics, illness with vomiting or diarrhoea and changes in diet can all shift the INR, so the anticoagulant clinic is told about them.

body.heading: What are the signs of bleeding, and who should be contacted?
body.body: Bleeding is the main risk of both medicines. For warfarin, the NHS lists blood in the urine or stools, unexplained bruising, and coughing up or vomiting blood as signs of bleeding. A sudden bad headache with confusion, slurred speech or difficulty moving the arms or legs can mean bleeding in the brain. For apixaban, the NHS describes bleeding more easily than usual, such as nosebleeds, bleeding gums, heavier periods and bruising. The NHS also lists a serious allergic reaction, with swelling of the throat or tongue and difficulty breathing, as a rare side effect of both medicines. The NHS says to call NHS 111 for symptoms of bleeding, after a head injury, or for other serious side effects. NHS inform says to call 999 or go to A&E after a fall, a significant blow to the head, or if bleeding cannot be stopped. For questions that are not urgent, the GP or anticoagulant clinic can advise.

body.heading: What if a dose is missed?
body.body: NHS sources give different timing rules for a forgotten dose, and the rules vary between warfarin and apixaban and between local services, so no single rule is given here. For warfarin, NHS inform gives separate advice for evening doses, and some local anticoagulant clinics allow a different window. For apixaban, the NHS says a missed dose is taken as soon as it is remembered unless the next dose is nearly due. The sources agree that two doses should never be taken together to make up for a missed one. If unsure about a missed warfarin dose, the GP practice or anticoagulant clinic can advise, and NHS 111 can also help. For apixaban, the NHS says to tell the GP if more than the prescribed amount has been taken.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 17 September 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) published an article on patient safety in its forthcoming asthma guidelines. The guidelines themselves have not yet been published. The WHO estimates that asthma affected about 363 million people in 2023 and caused 442,000 deaths.

body.heading: What the article says about care
body.body: It says overusing reliever inhalers is linked to more asthma attacks and deaths. It also cites a Global Asthma Network survey in which 45% to 60% of people with severe symptoms were not taking inhaled corticosteroids, with larger gaps in lower-income settings. The WHO says the forthcoming guidance aims to strengthen evidence-based care and reduce avoidable harm.

who-barbados-hiv-transmission-eliminatio.summary: On 30 October 2026 the WHO announced that Barbados has eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV as a public health problem.
keyPoints: The WHO announced on 30 October 2026 that Barbados has eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV as a public health problem.
The certification follows an independent assessment that confirmed Barbados met the global targets.
The WHO reports no new HIV infections from mother-to-child transmission among infants born in Barbados from 2022 to 2024.
Barbados joins a group of 26 countries and territories recognised by the WHO for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis or hepatitis B, or for being on track to do so.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 30 October 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) announced that Barbados, in the Caribbean, has eliminated mother-to-child transmission of HIV as a public health problem. The certification follows an independent assessment confirming that Barbados met the global targets. The WHO reports that no new HIV infections from mother-to-child transmission were recorded among infants born in Barbados from 2022 to 2024.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: Barbados joins a group of 26 countries and territories that the WHO recognises for eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis or hepatitis B, or for being on track to do so; 15 of them are in the Americas. The Pan American Health Organization says that keeping this status will need continued investment, updated guidelines, stronger health information systems, expanded HIV and syphilis testing and better follow-up for women and children.

who-cancer-report-2050.name: WHO report projects rise in cancer cases
who-cancer-report-2050.headline: WHO calls for urgent action as global cancer cases are projected to nearly double by 2050
who-cancer-report-2050.summary: On 8 July 2026 the WHO published its Global status report on cancer 2026, projecting that new cancer cases will nearly double by 2050 without urgent action.
keyPoints: The WHO released its Global status report on cancer 2026 on 8 July 2026.
The WHO says annual new cancer cases could rise to nearly 35 million by 2050 without urgent action.
It estimates about 20.6 million new cases and close to 10 million deaths each year at present.
The report makes seven recommendations across three shifts: better capabilities, better protections and better value.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 8 July 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) published its Global status report on cancer 2026 and called for urgent action. The WHO says cancer now causes an estimated 20.6 million new cases and close to 10 million deaths a year, making it the second leading cause of death worldwide after cardiovascular disease. Without urgent action, it projects annual new cases rising to nearly 35 million by 2050.

The WHO says nearly four in ten cancer cases are linked to preventable risk factors.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The report sets out seven recommendations grouped under three shifts: better capabilities, better protections and better value. It points to underinvestment in prevention, unequal access to diagnosis and treatment, and insufficient social protection. The WHO's first global survey of people affected by cancer, with more than 4,000 respondents in 116 countries, found widespread psychological distress among patients and caregivers.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 11 February 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) urged countries to expand access to cataract surgery. It cited a study in The Lancet Global Health showing that one in two people worldwide facing cataract-related blindness need access to surgery. The WHO says the gap is widest in the African Region, where three in four people who need cataract surgery remain untreated.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO describes cataract surgery as one of the most cost-effective medical interventions. It notes that coverage of cataract surgery has increased by about 15% over the past twenty years, and recalls the 2021 World Health Assembly target to raise effective coverage by 30 percentage points by 2030.

who-child-obesity-guidelines.headline: WHO publishes its first global guidelines on child and adolescent obesity
who-child-obesity-guidelines.summary: On 7 October 2026 the WHO issued its first global guidelines on obesity in children and adolescents, with one document for each age group.
keyPoints: The WHO published its first global guidelines on child and adolescent obesity on 7 October 2026.
One guideline covers children aged 29 days to under 10 years and another covers adolescents aged 10 to 19 years.
The WHO strongly recommends structured changes to diet, behaviour and physical activity for children and adolescents with obesity.

The WHO says the foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is access to comprehensive support for healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change, not medicines or surgery.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) issued its first global guidelines on child and adolescent obesity on 7 October 2026. The WHO describes them as evidence-informed recommendations for managing obesity in children and adolescents.

There are two documents: one for children aged 29 days to under 10 years and one for adolescents aged 10 to 19 years. The recommendations cover diet, physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep, behaviour-change and digital health interventions, medicines, bariatric surgery, weight-management devices and combined approaches. The WHO strongly recommends structured changes to diet, behaviour and physical activity for children and adolescents with obesity.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO says medicines, surgery and devices are not the foundation of care for children and adolescents with obesity; comprehensive support for healthy eating, physical activity and behaviour change is. It presents the guidelines as part of a life-course approach that sits alongside its existing recommendations for adults.

who-contraception-options-2026.summary: On 23 September 2026 the WHO published guidelines on expanding contraceptive options, covering extended pill use, longer implant use and an extra emergency option.
keyPoints: The WHO released its guidelines on expanding contraceptive options on 23 September 2026.
The guidelines support extended use of combined oral contraceptive pills as an alternative to cyclical use.
They also support longer use of contraceptive implants and add mifepristone as an emergency contraception option.
The WHO recommends against adding quinestrol-containing contraceptive pills to national programmes.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) published "WHO guidelines on expanding contraceptive options" on 23 September 2026. The WHO now supports extended use of combined oral contraceptive pills as an alternative to cyclical use, and longer use of contraceptive implants, which it says may reduce the need for replacement procedures, clinic visits and costs.

Mifepristone is recommended as an additional emergency contraception option. The WHO recommends against adding quinestrol-containing contraceptive pills to national contraceptive programmes, and says more research is needed on ormeloxifene before it enters family planning programmes.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO also announced its first Target Product Profile for male contraceptive methods, which sets out what such products would need to achieve. The WHO frames the new guidelines as widening the safe options available to people choosing a method.

who-dementia-risk-guidelines.summary: On 15 July 2026 the WHO issued updated guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia, linking up to 45% of risk to factors that can be changed.
keyPoints: The WHO published the second edition of its guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia on 15 July 2026.
The WHO says up to 45% of dementia risk can be attributed to modifiable risk factors.
The risk factors named include tobacco, alcohol use, social isolation, physical inactivity, air pollution, high blood pressure and diabetes.
The WHO says hearing aids may be offered as part of risk-reduction strategies.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 15 July 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) released updated guidelines on reducing the risk of cognitive decline and dementia. They follow the WHO's first recommendations on the subject in 2019 and reflect a larger body of evidence.

The WHO says that up to 45% of dementia risk can be attributed to modifiable risk factors. These include tobacco, alcohol use, social isolation, physical inactivity, air pollution and noncommunicable diseases such as high blood pressure and diabetes.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO says that managing cardiometabolic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes and high cholesterol can also help reduce dementia risk, and that hearing aids may be offered as part of risk-reduction strategies. The 45% figure is an estimate of the share of risk linked to changeable factors; it is not a promise that addressing them would prevent dementia in any one person.

who-europe-world-hepatitis-day-2026.name: WHO Europe: hepatitis progress and gaps
who-europe-world-hepatitis-day-2026.headline: World Hepatitis Day 2026: WHO/Europe reports progress against hepatitis but gaps in diagnosis and treatment
who-europe-world-hepatitis-day-2026.summary: On World Hepatitis Day, 28 July 2026, WHO/Europe said the European Region has made progress against hepatitis but millions still miss diagnosis and treatment.
keyPoints: WHO/Europe published the statement on World Hepatitis Day, 28 July 2026, and it concerns the WHO European Region, not the world as a whole.
The Region has already met its hepatitis B elimination target for children under 5, with prevalence at about 0.06%.
The Region remains off track for all of its 2030 hepatitis elimination targets.
WHO/Europe says only 23% of people with hepatitis B have been diagnosed and 4.2% are receiving treatment.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On World Hepatitis Day, 28 July 2026, the World Health Organization's European regional office (WHO/Europe) reported on progress against hepatitis in the WHO European Region. It says the Region has already met its hepatitis B elimination target for children under 5 years, with prevalence at about 0.06%. New hepatitis B infections are down 54% since 2015 and new hepatitis C infections are down 28%.

The Region is still off track for all of its 2030 elimination targets. WHO/Europe estimates that 9.7 million people live with hepatitis B and 5.6 million with hepatitis C in the Region, and that only 23% of people with hepatitis B have been diagnosed and 4.2% are receiving treatment.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: WHO/Europe's regional adviser says the main gap is now finding people and getting them into care, rather than prevention. The 2026 World Hepatitis Day theme is "Hepatitis: Let's break it down", and the WHO is urging countries to remove barriers to testing and treatment.

who-flu-vaccine-2027-southern.summary: On 25 September 2026 the WHO announced which virus strains influenza vaccines should contain for the 2027 southern hemisphere season.
keyPoints: The WHO announced its recommendation for the 2027 southern hemisphere flu season on 25 September 2026, after a consultation held from 21 to 24 September.
This recommendation is for the southern hemisphere; the next one, for the 2027-28 northern hemisphere season, is due in February 2027.
The 2027 southern hemisphere viruses differ from those recommended for the 2026 southern hemisphere vaccine.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 25 September 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) announced its recommendations for the virus strains in influenza vaccines for the 2027 southern hemisphere season. The recommendation followed a consultation held from 21 to 24 September 2026. National regulators and manufacturers use the recommendations in vaccine development and licensing.

For egg-based vaccines the WHO recommends an A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like virus, an A/Darwin/1454/2025 (H3N2)-like virus and a B/Tokyo/EIS13-175/2025 (B/Victoria lineage)-like virus.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO says the 2027 southern hemisphere viruses differ from those recommended for the 2026 southern hemisphere vaccine, and that they match the components recommended for the 2026-27 northern hemisphere vaccine. A separate recommendation for the 2027-28 northern hemisphere season is planned for February 2027.

who-global-health-estimates-2023.name: WHO global health estimates to 2023
who-global-health-estimates-2023.headline: New WHO estimates show how the leading causes of death have changed since 2000
who-global-health-estimates-2023.summary: On 2 October 2026 the WHO published Global Health Estimates for 2000 to 2023: heart disease is still the top cause of death and dementia has risen to fifth.
keyPoints: The WHO published new Global Health Estimates covering 2000 to 2023 on 2 October 2026.
Noncommunicable diseases caused 74% of global deaths in 2023, up from 58% in 2000, according to the WHO release.
Ischaemic heart disease remained the leading cause of death; dementia moved up to fifth place from 19th in 2000.
Diabetes ranked sixth, lung cancers seventh and kidney diseases ninth.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 2 October 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) released new Global Health Estimates covering 2000 to 2023. The WHO says noncommunicable diseases accounted for 74% of deaths worldwide in 2023, up from 58% in 2000. Eight of the ten leading causes of death were noncommunicable diseases.

Ischaemic heart disease remained the leading cause of death. Dementia rose to fifth place from 19th in 2000, diabetes ranked sixth, tracheal, bronchial and lung cancers seventh, and kidney diseases ninth. HIV and AIDS fell to 22nd place from seventh in 2000, and COVID-19 left the top ten for the first time since the pandemic began.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO says the 2000 to 2023 estimates are not comparable with its previously released estimates, because of changes in data and methods.

who-heat-illness-mass-gatherings.headline: WHO releases guidance on preventing heat-related illness at mass gatherings
who-heat-illness-mass-gatherings.summary: On 30 September 2026 the WHO released a resource suite on preventing and managing heat-related illness at mass gatherings.
keyPoints: The WHO released the guidance suite on 30 September 2026.
The WHO's evidence review of studies from 1980 to 2025 found nearly half a million medical encounters at mass gatherings, including more than 22,000 heat-related illnesses.
The suite includes a heat-risk assessment tool, and WHO names spectators, attendees, volunteers and workers among those affected by heat at mass gatherings.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 30 September 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) released a resource suite called "Prevention and management of heat-related illness at mass gatherings". The WHO says most heat-related illnesses at major events can be prevented or treated on site when timely risk management measures are in place.

Its evidence review of studies from 1980 to 2025 found nearly half a million medical encounters at mass gatherings, including more than 22,000 heat-related illnesses.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The guidance includes a heat-risk assessment tool and is intended to complement the WHO's heat-health action plan guidance and existing national plans. The WHO urges governments, event organisers and partners to build heat risk management into health planning and event operations.

who-heat-maternal-child-indicators.summary: On 21 October 2026 the WHO released a new global framework of priority indicators for tracking the health risks of extreme heat for pregnant women, newborns and children.
keyPoints: The WHO released the framework on 21 October 2026.
The report recommends that countries monitor preterm births, stillbirths, low birthweight, hypertension in pregnancy, child deaths and health-facility visits during extreme heat.
The WHO says combining routine health data with heat-exposure data can help countries spot unusual changes during extreme heat and investigate them.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 21 October 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) released a new global framework of priority indicators for monitoring the effects of extreme heat on maternal, newborn and child health. The report recommends that countries monitor preterm births, stillbirths, low birthweight, hypertension in pregnancy, child deaths and health-facility visits during extreme heat.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: According to the release, routine health data and heat-exposure data such as air temperature can help identify possible heat-related signals. A related WHO publication organises the indicators across four areas: routine maternal, newborn and child health monitoring, public health and surveillance systems, climate and health monitoring, and measures of heat exposure.

who-hiv-hepatitis-sti-progress.name: WHO reviews HIV, hepatitis and STI targets
who-hiv-hepatitis-sti-progress.headline: WHO progress assessment: integration, innovation and community leadership key to ending HIV, hepatitis and STIs
who-hiv-hepatitis-sti-progress.summary: On 27 July 2026 the WHO published a progress assessment of its 2022 to 2030 strategies on HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections.
keyPoints: The WHO published the assessment on 27 July 2026.
The WHO names integration of services into primary health care as one of the biggest opportunities to speed progress.
It points to long-acting prevention such as twice-yearly lenacapavir.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
On 27 July 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) published a progress assessment of its Global Health Sector Strategies on HIV, viral hepatitis and sexually transmitted infections for 2022 to 2030. The WHO says integration is one of the biggest opportunities to speed progress, and that countries with the strongest results deliver HIV, hepatitis and STI care through primary health care.

It also points to innovation, including long-acting prevention such as twice-yearly lenacapavir, and to stronger community leadership and community-generated data.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO issued consolidated HIV service delivery guidelines (22 July 2026) and consolidated guidance on routine HIV surveillance (27 July 2026) in the same period. It says eliminating mother-to-child transmission of HIV, syphilis and hepatitis B remains a priority, with more countries applying for WHO validation.

who-hpv-single-dose-recommendation.name: WHO advisers back single-dose HPV schedule
who-hpv-single-dose-recommendation.headline: WHO immunization advisers recommend a single-dose HPV schedule for girls aged 9 to 14
who-hpv-single-dose-recommendation.summary: On 29 October 2026 the WHO reported that its immunization advisers, meeting on 5 to 8 October, recommend a single-dose HPV vaccine schedule for girls aged 9 to 14.
keyPoints: The WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) met from 5 to 8 October 2026.
SAGE recommends HPV vaccination of girls aged 9 to 14 years with a single-dose schedule, which it describes as the most efficient immunization strategy for cervical cancer prevention.
SAGE says countries may consider routine single-dose vaccination of girls aged 4 to 8 years.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
A message from the director of the World Health Organization's immunization department, dated 29 October 2026, reports on the October meeting of its Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE), held from 5 to 8 October. SAGE recommends human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination of girls aged 9 to 14 years using a single-dose schedule, which it describes as the most efficient immunization strategy for cervical cancer prevention.

According to the meeting highlights, countries may also consider routine single-dose vaccination of girls aged 4 to 8 years, and single-dose coverage could later extend to further target groups. The director's message adds that a single dose can be used for people up to age 30.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The 2022 SAGE position allowed one or two doses for the primary target group of girls aged 9 to 14; the October 2026 advice is for a single dose.

keyPoints: The WHO news item is dated 12 June 2026 and concerns a Lancet Series on postpartum haemorrhage (excessive bleeding after birth).
The series estimates that excessive bleeding after birth affects 27 million women and kills nearly 43,000 women every year.
It concludes that visually estimating blood loss after birth is grossly inaccurate.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 12 June 2026 the World Health Organization (WHO) published a news item on a Lancet Series about postpartum haemorrhage, which means severe bleeding after childbirth. The series estimates that excessive bleeding after birth affects 27 million women and kills nearly 43,000 women every year. It also estimates a cost to countries, health systems and families of over US$ 10 billion each year.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The series says that visually estimating blood loss after birth is grossly inaccurate and results in missing half of postpartum haemorrhage cases. It also points to missed opportunities to prevent haemorrhage before it starts.

who-pregnancy-hypertension-roadmap.headline: WHO and partners launch a global roadmap on hypertension in pregnancy
who-pregnancy-hypertension-roadmap.summary: In October 2026 the WHO and partners launched a global roadmap for 2026 to 2035 on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia.
keyPoints: The WHO news item announcing the roadmap is dated 8 October 2026.
The roadmap covers 2026 to 2035 and sets out coordinated actions on research, clinical guidance, access to medicines and diagnostics, implementation, advocacy and accountability.
The WHO says hypertensive disorders complicate an estimated 10 to 15% of pregnancies worldwide.
The roadmap points to a shortage of medicines approved specifically for preventing or treating pre-eclampsia or eclampsia.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body:
The World Health Organization (WHO) and partners launched a global roadmap on hypertensive disorders in pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia, in a news item dated 8 October 2026. The roadmap covers 2026 to 2035 and sets out coordinated actions on research, clinical guidance, access to medicines and diagnostics, implementation, advocacy and accountability.

The WHO says hypertensive disorders complicate an estimated 10 to 15% of pregnancies worldwide and are a leading cause of maternal and newborn deaths.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The roadmap highlights a gap in approved treatments: few medicines have been approved by regulators specifically to prevent or treat pre-eclampsia or eclampsia. The WHO notes that many countries still lack reliable access to basic blood-pressure measurement, testing and essential medicines. In May 2026 the WHO brought together more than 140 partners at a summit to identify 20 priority research questions.

who-youth-nicotine-warning.headline: WHO urges governments to protect young people from tobacco and nicotine addiction
who-youth-nicotine-warning.summary: On 29 May 2026, ahead of World No Tobacco Day, the WHO urged governments to protect young people from tobacco and nicotine addiction.
keyPoints: The WHO issued the call on 29 May 2026, ahead of World No Tobacco Day on 31 May.
The WHO says at least 40 million children aged 13 to 15 use tobacco products, and that use of e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches among young people continues to rise.
It urges governments to ban flavoured products, ban advertising, promotion and sponsorship, make indoor public places completely smoke- and vape-free, and step up enforcement.

body.heading: What was announced
body.body: On 29 May 2026, ahead of World No Tobacco Day on 31 May, the World Health Organization (WHO) urged governments to protect young people from addiction to tobacco and nicotine products. The WHO says at least 40 million children aged 13 to 15 use tobacco products, and that young people's use of e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches continues to rise. It says tobacco and nicotine companies are deliberately engineering products to be more appealing, easier to use and harder to quit, especially for adolescents.

body.heading: What it means
body.body: The WHO calls on governments to ban flavoured products, ban advertising, promotion and sponsorship, make indoor public places completely smoke- and vape-free, and step up enforcement.

why-antibiotics-do-not-work-for-viruses.name: Why antibiotics do not work on viruses
why-antibiotics-do-not-work-for-viruses.headline: Why antibiotics do not work for colds, flu and most coughs, and what the NHS says instead
why-antibiotics-do-not-work-for-viruses.summary: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses, so the NHS says they do not help colds, flu or most coughs and sore throats.
keyPoints: The NHS says antibiotics do not work against viral infections, which include the common cold, flu and most coughs and sore throats.
NHS England says overuse of antibiotics in recent years has played a major part in antibiotic resistance, which can lead to treatment failure.
NICE describes acute cough as usually self-limiting, getting better within about 3 to 4 weeks without antibiotics.
A WHO commentary advises finishing a prescribed course but also says shorter courses may work for some infections, so sources differ in emphasis.
For flu, NHS pages describe 999 for severe difficulty breathing, and an urgent GP or NHS 111 route for people who feel short of breath.

body.heading: What is the difference between bacteria and viruses?
body.body: Antibiotics are medicines used to treat or prevent some bacterial infections. NHS inform says they kill bacteria or stop them from reproducing and spreading. Antibiotics do not work against infections caused by viruses. NHS inform lists the common cold, flu, most coughs and most sore throats among these viral illnesses. Penicillins, the group that includes amoxicillin, are antibiotics, so they act on bacteria only.

body.heading: Why do antibiotics not help colds, flu and coughs?
body.body: The NHS common cold page says GPs do not recommend antibiotics for colds, because they will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery. NHS inform says the same about flu. NICE guidance on acute cough describes the illness as usually self-limiting, which means it gets better, within about 3 to 4 weeks, without antibiotics. NICE also notes that antibiotics make little difference to how long a cough lasts.

body.heading: What is antibiotic resistance?
body.body: Antibiotic resistance means that a strain of bacteria no longer responds to treatment with one or more types of antibiotic. NHS England says overuse of antibiotics in recent years has played a major part in it. It says resistance can lead to treatment failure, repeat GP appointments, hospital admissions and more. The UKHSA campaign Keep Antibiotics Working, listed on a Department of Health and Social Care campaign page, gives three core messages: antibiotics are not for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses; antibiotics are taken as directed by the prescriber; and leftover antibiotics are not saved, because they may not work properly and could make the problem worse.

body.heading: Should an antibiotic course always be finished?
body.body: NHS sources describe stopping a course early as a risk: one NHS page notes that if antibiotics are stopped early, bacteria can become resistant to them. A WHO commentary likewise advises patients to complete the prescribed course, because stopping early can favour drug-resistant bacteria. The same commentary says evidence is emerging that shorter courses may be effective for some infections and can slow resistance by reducing how long bacteria are exposed to antibiotics. A 2024 research review on stopping antibiotics when feeling better argues that this evidence may mean the broad public message to complete every course needs revisiting. The sources therefore differ in emphasis.

body.heading: What helps with a viral illness?
body.body: NHS guidance on flu describes rest, fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen for symptoms. A local NHS page on colds says most colds do not need a visit to the GP and that pharmacists can advise on suitable medicines. NICE lists honey as a self-care option for acute cough in people older than one year, although it describes the evidence as weak.

body.heading: What side effects can antibiotics have?
body.body: NHS trust leaflets list feeling sick, vomiting, diarrhoea and bloating as the most common side effects of antibiotics. Allergic reactions are rarer but can be serious, with swelling of the face or tongue and difficulty breathing as warning signs. One leaflet says anyone with difficulty breathing, dizziness or collapse should call 999. Severe diarrhoea can be a symptom of C. difficile infection, and the same leaflet says to contact the GP if diarrhoea continues after the course ends. A pharmacist or GP can answer questions about a particular medicine.

body.heading: When does the NHS say to get help urgently?
body.body: NHS inform says to call 999 for severe difficulty breathing. NHS England's flu page lists sudden chest pain, severe breathing trouble and coughing up blood as reasons for emergency care, by calling 999 or going to A&E. NHS inform adds lips or skin turning blue or grey, and being harder to wake than usual. NHS flu pages place people who feel short of breath, and people at higher risk of complications, in an urgent group for a same-day GP appointment or NHS 111. Questions that are not urgent can go to a pharmacist or the GP.
